Dual health plans are for people dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid and include many extra benefits that can make life easier for low-income individuals. The page says entering your ZIP code shows how much you could receive monthly; benefits and features vary by plan and area.
qs: Do dual plans give a monthly credit for groceries?
How much monthly credit could I get with a dual plan?

atoms.title: What the credit can buy
atoms.q: What can you buy with the dual plan monthly credit?
atoms.text: If you had a UnitedHealthcare dual health plan, you could use your credit to buy healthy foods like fruits and vegetables, meat, seafood, dairy products and water; choose from thousands of OTC products like toothpaste, first aid necessities, cough drops and bladder control pads; and pay utility bills like electricity, gas, water and internet.
qs: Can I pay my electric bill with my dual plan credit?
Are groceries covered by the OTC credit?

atoms.title: How the credit loads onto the UCard
atoms.q: How does the Food, OTC and Utility Bill Credit work?
atoms.text: Many members of UnitedHealthcare dual health plans get the UnitedHealthcare UCard, which makes using benefits simple. Your credit is loaded to your UCard every month. Then you use your UCard to pay for any covered items you need.
qs: How do I use my monthly credit?
When is the credit added to my UCard?

atoms.title: Where members can spend the UCard credit
atoms.q: Where can I use my UCard?
atoms.text: Many UnitedHealthcare members can use their UCard to shop at thousands of participating stores, including Walmart, Walgreens, CVS and Kroger, or at neighborhood stores. They can order online and get free home delivery on qualifying orders of $35 or more, and pay eligible utility bills online, over the phone or at a local Walmart MoneyCenter. Current members can browse OTC and healthy food products and manage their benefit account online.
qs: Which stores accept the UCard?
Is there free delivery with the UCard?

atoms.title: Plan availability of the monthly credit
atoms.q: Is the monthly credit available in every area?
atoms.text: Not every area has a UnitedHealthcare dual plan with the monthly benefit. If no plan in your ZIP code includes it, the page invites you to call 1-844-812-5967 (TTY 711), 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time, 7 days a week, to find another plan in your area with benefits that fit your needs. Details of the exact credit depend on the plan; check the number or website on the back of your UCard.
qs: Does every dual plan include the food and OTC credit?
How do I find a dual plan with a monthly benefit?

atoms.title: What full dual eligibility means
atoms.q: What does it mean to have full dual eligibility?
atoms.text: Dual eligible means someone is eligible for both Medicaid and Medicare. Full dual eligibility means you qualify for full state Medicaid benefits as well as Medicare, and you may also qualify for a Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP). Medicare pays for most covered care, while Medicaid pays some out-of-pocket costs for copays, coinsurance, deductibles and premiums. Medicaid also covers benefits a D-SNP doesn't, such as long-term care.
qs: What is full dual eligibility?
What does Medicaid pay for if I'm full dual?

atoms.title: What partial dual eligibility means
atoms.q: What does it mean to have partial dual eligibility?
atoms.text: Partial dual eligibility means a person qualifies for a Medicare Savings Program (MSP). MSPs are managed by each state's Medicaid program and cover certain Medicare costs, like Medicare Part A and Part B premiums, but people with partial dual eligibility don't receive full Medicaid medical benefits. They may also qualify for a D-SNP; Medicare pays for most care, but partial dual eligibles are responsible for out-of-pocket costs. Coverage is only available in certain areas.
qs: What is partial dual eligibility?
What is a Medicare Savings Program?

atoms.title: How Medicare Savings Programs reduce costs
atoms.q: How does a Medicare Savings Program (MSP) help partial dual eligibles?
atoms.text: When Medicare members get care, Medicare doesn't cover the full amount; the remainder, called cost share or out-of-pocket costs, is the member's responsibility and may take the form of a premium, copay, coinsurance or deductible. With MSPs, the state Medicaid program helps pay some of these costs for partial dual eligibles. The amount of help depends mainly on two things: how much the person earns (income) and how much they own (assets), such as a house.
qs: How does my state help pay Medicare costs?
What determines how much help I get from an MSP?

atoms.title: QMB: Qualified Medicare Beneficiary
atoms.q: What is the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) program?
atoms.text: The Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) program is one of 4 partial dual eligibility categories. QMB helps pay premiums for Medicare Part A (hospital insurance) and Medicare Part B (medical insurance). Members who have QMB eligibility also get cost share coverage for copays, deductibles and coinsurance.
qs: What does QMB cover?
Does QMB pay my Part A and Part B premiums?

atoms.title: SLMB, QI and QDWI partial dual categories
atoms.q: What are the SLMB, QI and QDWI programs?
atoms.text: The Specified Low Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB) program helps pay premiums for Part B (medical insurance) only. The Qualified Individual (QI) program also helps pay Part B premiums, but these members can have higher income than with SLMB. The Qualified Disabled and Working Individuals (QDWI) program helps pay Medicare Part A (hospital insurance) premiums for people who are disabled but have returned to work and, as a result, lost premium-free Part A coverage.
qs: What is the difference between QMB, SLMB and QI?
What is QDWI?

atoms.title: Getting help finding a dual-eligible plan
atoms.q: How do I find a dual-eligible health plan if I might be full or partial dual?
atoms.text: If you think you, a family member or someone you care for qualifies as a full or partial dual eligible, you can use the plan search on the page to see what plans are available in your area. If you're not sure, you can call UnitedHealthcare at 1-844-812-5967 (TTY 711), 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time, 7 days a week, and talk with a licensed agent. Coverage for partial dual eligibles is only available in certain areas.
qs: How do I find out if I'm full or partial dual?
Who can I call to find a dual plan?

atoms.title: D-SNP members must keep Medicaid eligibility
atoms.q: Do I need to keep Medicaid to stay in a D-SNP?
atoms.text: Having Medicaid coverage, in addition to qualifying for Medicare, is a requirement to enroll in a D-SNP. It applies not just when you first join: to stay eligible, you need to keep your Medicaid coverage the whole time. If you lose your Medicaid eligibility, you should soon receive a letter from your health insurance company letting you know you no longer meet the D-SNP eligibility requirements.
qs: What happens to my D-SNP if I lose Medicaid?
Do I have to stay on Medicaid to keep my dual plan?

atoms.title: Grace period after losing Medicaid
atoms.q: What happens if a D-SNP member loses their Medicaid eligibility?
atoms.text: When a D-SNP member no longer qualifies for Medicaid, they go into a grace period. Depending on the health plan, the grace period could be 30 days or up to 6 months. Members can still get care and services through their plan, and Medicare still pays for most covered care. The difference is that during the grace period the member is responsible for out-of-pocket costs such as copayments, coinsurance, deductibles and premiums that Medicaid would have paid before.
qs: How long is the grace period if I lose Medicaid?
Will I owe copays if I lose Medicaid on a dual plan?

atoms.title: Disenrollment and your options after the grace period
atoms.q: What happens if my Medicaid isn't reinstated during the grace period?
atoms.text: If the grace period ends and you aren't recertified for Medicaid, you will be disenrolled from your D-SNP or other Medicare Special Needs plan, and your plan will send another letter saying when coverage will end. You'll then have a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) to enroll in a new Medicare Advantage plan, or in Original Medicare with a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan. Your new coverage starts the month after your previous plan ends.
qs: What plan can I join if I'm removed from my D-SNP?
When does new coverage start after D-SNP disenrollment?

atoms.title: Losing full Medicaid may leave partial dual eligibility
atoms.q: Can I still get a dual plan if I lose full Medicaid benefits?
atoms.text: Partial dual eligibility is when someone qualifies for Medicare but doesn't receive full Medicaid medical benefits. If you lose your full Medicaid medical benefits but still participate in a Medicare Savings Program (MSP), you may qualify for a partial dual plan. While Medicare pays for most covered care, many partial dual eligibles are responsible for out-of-pocket costs. Coverage for partial dual eligibles is only available in certain areas.
qs: Can I keep a D-SNP with only a Medicare Savings Program?
What is a partial dual plan?

atoms.title: Dual eligible and D-SNP basics
atoms.q: What does dual eligible mean for D-SNP coverage?
atoms.text: People who qualify for both Medicaid and Medicare are known as dual eligible, because they are dually eligible for both programs. Being dual eligible may also mean someone could qualify for a Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP). D-SNPs are a type of Medicare Advantage plan that provides extra benefits beyond Original Medicare and Medicaid.
qs: What is dual eligibility?
What does a D-SNP add to Original Medicare and Medicaid?

atoms.title: D-SNP enrollment may not require waiting for AEP
atoms.q: Do I have to wait for the Annual Enrollment Period to join a dual plan?
atoms.text: The Medicare Annual Enrollment Period (AEP) happens once a year in the fall, when anyone eligible can change their health plan. But if you qualify for a Dual Special Needs plan, you may not have to wait. You may be able to enroll right away.
qs: Can I join a dual plan outside of open enrollment?
Do dual-eligible people have to wait for fall enrollment?

atoms.title: Situations that let you enroll today
atoms.q: When can I enroll in a dual plan right away?
atoms.text: You may be eligible to enroll today if you are 65 and newly eligible for Medicare or have a qualifying disability; are retiring and losing your current coverage; have moved out of your current Medicare plan's service area; have Extra Help, Medicaid or a Medicare Savings Program (MSP) or recently experienced a change in coverage eligibility; or were enrolled in a plan by Medicare or by the state and want to choose a different plan.
qs: What qualifies me for a special enrollment period for a dual plan?
Can I enroll in a D-SNP when I move?

atoms.title: Enrolling or switching if you already have both programs
atoms.q: What if I already have both Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: You can enroll or switch dual plans once per Special Enrollment Period (SEP) when enrolling into a HIDE (Highly Integrated Dually Eligible) or FIDE (Fully Integrated Dually Eligible) integrated plan, or during the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period (AEP). After you're enrolled you don't have to renew; as long as you stay eligible, your dual health plan renews automatically each year. But you do need to recertify for Medicaid every year to stay qualified.
qs: How often can I switch dual plans?
Do I need to recertify Medicaid to keep my dual plan?

atoms.title: When dual plan coverage starts
atoms.q: When will my dual plan coverage start?
atoms.text: It depends on when you enroll. If you enroll when you first become eligible, coverage begins the first day of the month you qualify for Medicare. If you enroll in a Special Enrollment Period (SEP), coverage begins the first day of the next month. If you enroll in the Annual Enrollment Period (AEP), coverage begins the first day of the next year.
qs: When does my D-SNP take effect?
If I enroll during AEP, when does coverage begin?

atoms.title: Key AEP dates for dual plans
atoms.q: What are the key dates for the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: October 1: start looking for dual health plans available where you live. October 15: first day of the Annual Enrollment Period (AEP), when you can enroll or switch to a dual health plan for the next calendar year. December 7: last day you can enroll in a plan before AEP ends. January 1: the day your new plan becomes active if you enroll during AEP.
qs: When does Medicare open enrollment start and end?
When does a plan I choose in AEP start?

atoms.title: Enroll early to use the extra benefits sooner
atoms.q: Why should I enroll in a dual plan as early as I can?
atoms.text: The sooner you enroll in a dual health plan, the sooner you can start using the extra benefits that come with it. Benefits and features vary by plan and area, and limitations and exclusions apply.
qs: Should I wait to enroll in a dual plan?
Is there a benefit to joining early?

atoms.title: What does dual eligible mean?
atoms.q: What does dual eligible mean?
atoms.text: People who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid at the same time are dual eligible; they are eligible for both health care programs. Some people receive benefits from both programs. They qualify for Medicare because of age (65 or older) or a disability, and they are eligible for Medicaid because they meet their state's requirements.
qs: What does it mean to be dual eligible?
Can you have Medicare and Medicaid at the same time?

atoms.title: Difference between Medicare and Medicaid
atoms.q: What's the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicare is a national health insurance program run by the federal government for people age 65 and older, and also some people under 65 with certain disabilities. Medicaid is a joint program funded together by states and the federal government. Children, pregnant women, elderly adults and people with disabilities, as well as eligible low-income adults, are typically covered by Medicaid.
qs: How is Medicare different from Medicaid?
Who is covered by Medicaid versus Medicare?

atoms.title: How you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid
atoms.q: How do you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: They are two separate programs with different eligibility requirements. For Medicare you need to be at least 65, or under 65 and qualify on the basis of disability or other special situations, and be a U.S. citizen or legal resident who has lived in the U.S. for at least 5 years in a row. For state Medicaid you need to be under 65 and meet requirements for low-income families, pregnant women and children, SSI, disability or other special situations, or be 65 or older and also receive Extra Help or state assistance, or be blind or have a disability but not need long-term care.
qs: What do I need to qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid?
Do I have to be a citizen to get Medicare?

atoms.title: How Medicare and Medicaid work together
atoms.q: How do Medicare and Medicaid work together?
atoms.text: Medicaid programs often cover benefits that Medicare doesn't offer, such as dental, vision and hearing coverage, transportation assistance and long-term care. Paying for certain Medicare costs is another way Medicaid can help Medicare. The Medicare-Medicaid Coordination Office, created within CMS as part of the Affordable Care Act, is responsible for making sure dually enrolled people have seamless, high quality health care.
qs: What does Medicaid cover that Medicare doesn't?
Who coordinates Medicare and Medicaid?

atoms.title: Advantages of a Dual Special Needs plan
atoms.q: What are the advantages of a Dual Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: Dual health plans offer benefits and services not typically available through Medicare or Medicaid alone. You keep your Medicaid benefits and get more benefits than Original Medicare, with as low as a $0 plan premium. UnitedHealthcare plans may cover routine dental care, a flexible monthly credit for healthy food, over-the-counter products and utility bills, eye exams plus credit for eyewear, and hearing exams plus credit for hearing devices. Some also include care coordination. Benefits vary by plan and area.
qs: What extra benefits come with a dual plan?
Is there a credit for food and utilities with a D-SNP?

atoms.title: Three D-SNP eligibility questions
atoms.q: What are the eligibility requirements for Dual Special Needs plans?
atoms.text: 1) Do you get state Medicaid benefits? (You'd have a state Medicaid card.) 2) Do you have Medicare Parts A and B? You must be at least 65, or under 65 and qualify through disability or other special situations, and be a U.S. citizen or legal resident who has lived in the U.S. for at least 5 years in a row. 3) Do you live in an area where dual plans are available? A UnitedHealthcare licensed sales agent can tell you whether you live in the service area.
qs: Am I eligible for a D-SNP?
Do I need Medicare Parts A and B for a dual plan?

atoms.title: When can you apply for a D-SNP?
atoms.q: When can you apply for a Dual Special Needs Plan (D-SNP)?
atoms.text: Dual Special Needs plans have an ongoing Special Enrollment Period (SEP) that runs for the first 9 months of the year. People who qualify can enroll or change plans once every 3 months, and enrollment changes take effect the first day of the next month. To stay eligible you must recertify for Medicaid every year; as long as you stay eligible, your dual health plan will renew automatically each year.
qs: When can I enroll in a dual plan?
Do I have to renew my dual plan every year?

atoms.title: How often can D-SNP members switch plans?
atoms.q: How often can members in Dual Special Needs plans switch plans?
atoms.text: D-SNP members can join, switch or drop their plan 1 time during each 3-month enrollment period: January to March, April to June, and July to September. A change takes effect on the first day of the next month. Members can also make changes during the Annual Enrollment Period from Oct. 15 to Dec. 7, with changes taking effect on Jan. 1 of the next year.
qs: How many times a year can I change my dual plan?
When is the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period?

atoms.title: What happens if a D-SNP member loses Medicaid?
atoms.q: What happens when a D-SNP member loses Medicaid eligibility?
atoms.text: If you're enrolled in a UnitedHealthcare dual plan and lose Medicaid eligibility, UnitedHealthcare puts you on hold for 6 months. During that time you pay the Medicare cost-sharing portion, such as copayments, coinsurance, deductibles and premiums. If you don't regain Medicaid eligibility by the end of the 6 months, you'll be unenrolled from the dual plan. You can enroll in a dual plan at any time, so if you get Medicaid back, talk with a UnitedHealthcare licensed sales agent to re-enroll.
qs: What if I lose Medicaid while on a dual plan?
How long can I keep my D-SNP after losing Medicaid?

atoms.title: Is D-SNP enrollment state-based?
atoms.q: Is D-SNP enrollment by state?
atoms.text: Yes. Enrollment for Dual Special Needs plans is state-based. D-SNPs are offered in most states but not all, and the types of D-SNPs available and the benefits each provides can change depending on the county where you live. As of January 2025, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan serves members who qualify for Medicaid or for both Medicaid and Medicare in 43 states and the District of Columbia.
qs: Are D-SNPs available in every state?
Do dual plans vary by county?

atoms.title: Standard D-SNP benefits, including dental and vision
atoms.q: What standard benefits are typically covered by UnitedHealthcare dual plans?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare dual plans typically cover preventive care and routine services at no extra cost, and offer help coordinating Medicaid benefits. Other standard benefits usually include dental, vision, hearing and transportation assistance. Dental coverage may include regular exams and cleanings plus an allowance toward fillings, root canals or implants. Vision coverage may include routine eye exams plus credits toward eyewear. Benefits vary by plan and service area.
qs: Does a dual plan include dental and vision?
Is transportation covered by a D-SNP?

atoms.title: How D-SNP costs are covered
atoms.q: Does Medicare cover D-SNP members' medical costs, and who pays the rest?
atoms.text: Since a D-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan, Medicare covers most of the costs when members get medical care. The share that's left over, which may be called a premium, copay, coinsurance or deductible, is the member's responsibility, but for people on a D-SNP, state Medicaid programs help pay these costs. If you don't have Medicaid, your exact costs may depend on the plan you choose.
qs: Will I pay copays on a dual plan?
Does Medicaid pay my Medicare costs?

atoms.title: Coordination of benefits for D-SNPs
atoms.q: What is coordination of benefits?
atoms.text: Coordination of benefits (COB) applies to people with coverage under more than one health plan and determines which plan is the primary (first) payer and which is secondary. The primary payer coordinates delivery of all benefits and the secondary payer covers what the primary doesn't. A D-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan that coordinates delivery of both Medicare and Medicaid benefits; in most cases Medicaid covers benefits and costs the D-SNP doesn't. D-SNPs also coordinate care management and disease management.
qs: What does coordination of benefits mean for dual plans?
Which plan pays first, Medicare or Medicaid?

atoms.title: D-SNP vs. C-SNP vs. Medicare-Medicaid Plan
atoms.q: What is the difference between D-SNP, C-SNP and Medicare-Medicaid Plans (MMPs)?
atoms.text: A D-SNP is for low-income people dually eligible for Medicaid and Medicare. A C-SNP (Chronic Special Needs plan) is for people with a chronic condition such as chronic heart failure, cardiovascular disorders or diabetes. With a Medicare-Medicaid Plan (MMP), all Medicare and Medicaid benefits come through 1 single plan and only full dual eligibles can enroll. With a D-SNP, members keep their Medicaid plan and benefits plus a separate Medicare Advantage plan, and both full and partial dual eligibles can join.
qs: What is the difference between a D-SNP and a C-SNP?
How is an MMP different from a D-SNP?

atoms.title: D-SNPs are network-based; no referral needed in network
atoms.q: Are D-SNPs network-based, and do I need a referral to see a specialist?
atoms.text: Yes, D-SNPs are network-based, so members get care from doctors or hospitals in their plan's network. Networks vary in size and the populations they serve, for example a network may cover an entire state or a single county, or focus on a certain health issue such as dementia. When you have a UnitedHealthcare dual plan, referrals are not needed to get care from any in-network doctors, hospitals or clinics. Drug coverage is included, but check that your drugs are covered before you enroll.
qs: Do I need a referral to see a specialist on a dual plan?
Do D-SNPs include prescription drug coverage?

atoms.title: What a Dual Special Needs plan is
atoms.q: What is a Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP)?
atoms.text: A Dual Special Needs plan, or D-SNP for short, is a type of health insurance plan for people who have both Medicare and Medicaid. If that describes you, you're dual-eligible, which is just another way of saying you can have Medicare and Medicaid at the same time.
qs: What is a D-SNP?
What does dual-eligible mean?
Can I have Medicare and Medicaid at the same time?

atoms.title: Who D-SNPs are designed for
atoms.q: Who are Dual Special Needs plans for?
atoms.text: Dual Special Needs plans are for people who could use more help. That may be because of income, disabilities, age and/or health conditions. Dual Special Needs plans are a type of Medicare Advantage plan.
qs: Is a D-SNP a Medicare Advantage plan?
Who should consider a Dual Special Needs plan?

atoms.title: D-SNPs work together with your Medicaid plan
atoms.q: How does dual coverage work with both Medicaid and Medicare?
atoms.text: A Dual Special Needs plan works together with your Medicaid health plan, and you keep all your Medicaid benefits. Most dual health insurance plans also give you more benefits and features than you get with Original Medicare. Dual Special Needs plans have a $0 premium for members with Extra Help (Low Income Subsidy).
qs: Do I keep my Medicaid benefits with a D-SNP?
How much does a D-SNP cost per month?

atoms.title: Personal care coordinator with a D-SNP
atoms.q: What is care coordination in a Dual Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: Care coordination is another important benefit of a Dual Special Needs plan. You'll have a personal care coordinator who may help you understand your Medicare and Medicaid benefits, manage your doctors, specialists and care services, and get the services you need to feel healthier.
qs: Do dual plans include a care coordinator?
Who helps me manage my doctors with Medicare and Medicaid?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare Dual Complete plans
atoms.q: How can I get a Dual Special Needs plan from UnitedHealthcare?
atoms.text: Dual Special Needs plans are offered by private insurance companies, including UnitedHealthcare. UnitedHealthcare calls its dual-eligible health plans UnitedHealthcare Dual Complete. The page states that more people choose UnitedHealthcare for a Dual Special Needs plan than any other company.
qs: What is UnitedHealthcare Dual Complete?
Which companies offer dual-eligible plans?

atoms.title: UCard for dual plan members
atoms.q: What is the UCard for dual plan members?
atoms.text: UCard is only from UnitedHealthcare. Your UCard is your member ID and more: you can use it to buy healthy food and over-the-counter (OTC) products and to pay utility bills.
qs: What can I buy with the UCard?
Is the UCard my member ID?

atoms.title: Medicaid eligibility by income, age or health
atoms.q: What is Medicaid health insurance for?
atoms.text: Medicaid is health insurance for people who meet certain conditions for income, age or health. This may include children, pregnant women, older adults and people with disabilities. UnitedHealthcare Community Plan's benefits page goes on to explain what Medicaid covers and how coverage varies by state.
qs: What is Medicaid for?
Who can use Medicaid benefits?

atoms.title: Benefits every state must offer under Medicaid
atoms.q: What does Medicaid cover in all states?
atoms.text: Some Medicaid benefits are offered in all states, and the federal government gives states money for them. States must offer benefits such as family planning services, family nurse practitioner services, freestanding birth center services, health center services, home health services, inpatient and outpatient hospital services, laboratory and X-ray services, nursing facility services, pediatric care including EPSDT, physician services, pregnancy-related services, rural health clinic services, tobacco-cessation counseling for pregnant women and transportation to medical care.
qs: What services does Medicaid cover?
Does Medicaid cover pregnancy services?
Does Medicaid provide transportation to appointments?

atoms.title: States can add optional benefits and cover more people
atoms.q: How do Medicaid benefits vary by state?
atoms.text: States use federal regulations to create and run Medicaid programs, and eligibility is based on income and the value of what you own. States may choose to offer more benefits and services through Medicaid, called optional benefits. They may also choose to provide coverage to larger groups of people.
qs: Why does Medicaid coverage differ between states?
What are optional Medicaid benefits?

atoms.title: Find Medicaid benefits for your state
atoms.q: What benefits does Medicaid cover in my state?
atoms.text: Medicaid benefits can change depending on where you live. Selecting your state on the UnitedHealthcare Community Plan site helps you find the right Community Plan to meet your health care needs and see plan details by state.
qs: How do I see my state's Medicaid benefits?
Where can I find UnitedHealthcare Community Plan benefits in my state?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid cover home health care?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover home health care?
atoms.text: Yes. The federal government requires all 50 states to offer some Medicaid home health care benefits. The types of home health care services offered depend on where you live. Home health services also appear on the list of benefits that states must offer.
qs: Will Medicaid pay for home health care?
Is home health required in every state's Medicaid?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid cover dental care?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover dental care?
atoms.text: Medicaid offers dental benefits to all youth under age 21. Adult dental coverage is optional and varies by state, so whether an adult enrollee has dental coverage depends on where they live and which benefits their state chooses to offer.
qs: Does Medicaid pay for dental work for adults?
Are children's dental services covered by Medicaid?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid cover pregnant women and babies?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid provide coverage for pregnant women and babies?
atoms.text: Medicaid covers low-income pregnant women in all states. If a pregnant woman is covered by Medicaid, their baby is too. The baby is enrolled in Medicaid for the first year of their life.
qs: Is my baby covered by Medicaid if I am?
Does Medicaid cover pregnancy in every state?

atoms.title: Does CHIP cover pregnant women and children?
atoms.q: Does CHIP cover pregnant women and children?
atoms.text: The Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) also covers pregnant women and babies in some states. CHIP may cover those who don't qualify for Medicaid. Each state offers CHIP coverage and works closely with its state Medicaid program.
qs: Can I get CHIP if I'm pregnant?
Does CHIP cover people who don't qualify for Medicaid?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid cover dental care for adults?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover dental care for adults?
atoms.text: Each state manages its own Medicaid program, so each state can choose what dental benefits it provides to adult Medicaid enrollees. Most states cover emergency dental services for adults, but less than half of U.S. states currently provide comprehensive dental care. There are no minimum requirements for Medicaid dental coverage for adults.
qs: Will Medicaid pay for my dental care as an adult?
Do all states cover adult dental under Medicaid?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid cover children's dental care?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover children's dental care?
atoms.text: Medicaid covers dental services for children under age 21 who are enrolled in Medicaid. State agencies can design their dental programs but must cover more than just emergency services. All children's dental programs need to include relief of pain and infections, restoration of teeth and maintenance of dental health. Medically necessary dental care is covered whether or not it is in a state's Medicaid plan.
qs: What dental care do Medicaid kids get?
Is dental required for children under 21 on Medicaid?

atoms.title: Does CHIP cover dental care?
atoms.q: Does CHIP cover dental care?
atoms.text: In some states, CHIP dental benefits are the same as the state's Medicaid program. In other states, CHIP is a separate program and a state can offer children's dental benefits equal to one of 3 options: the most popular federal employee dental plan for dependents, the most popular plan selected for dependents in the state's employee dental plan, or dental coverage from the most popular private insurance plan in the state.
qs: What dental benefits does CHIP include?
Is CHIP dental coverage the same as Medicaid?

atoms.title: Children's dental services commonly covered
atoms.q: What children's dental services does Medicaid cover?
atoms.text: There's no standard list of children's Medicaid dental services; states choose what is covered and how often. Some cover checkups and cleanings 2 times a year, others only 1 routine visit. Common treatments include dental exams and X-rays, dental sealants (thin plastic coatings painted on molars) and fluoride treatments. Medicaid will typically cover other services when medically necessary, such as braces or wisdom tooth removal, though guidelines vary by state.
qs: Does Medicaid cover braces for kids?
Are dental sealants covered by Medicaid?

atoms.title: Why regular dental visits matter
atoms.q: Why is oral health important?
atoms.text: The health of your mouth, teeth and gums is linked to your overall health. Tooth decay and gum disease can lead to bad breath, mouth infections and loss of teeth, and there may also be a link between oral infections and diabetes, heart disease and stroke. Besides brushing and flossing each day, it's important to visit the dentist for regular checkups and cleanings so problems can be caught early.
qs: Why do I need regular dental checkups?
Is oral health linked to heart disease?

atoms.title: Barriers to children's dental care
atoms.q: What makes it hard for children on Medicaid to get dental care?
atoms.text: Millions of children and teens qualify for free or low-cost health and dental coverage through Medicaid and CHIP, but access to care is a challenge. Some children may not have a dentist in their neighborhood or may lack transportation. Some families don't know children need to see a dentist regularly, even without obvious problems, or that their children are eligible for dental services. Language barriers can also make it harder. The page points families to InsureKidsNow.gov to find a dentist who accepts Medicaid and CHIP.
qs: How do I find a dentist that takes Medicaid for my child?
Why don't kids on Medicaid always get dental care?

atoms.title: What Medicaid home health care is
atoms.q: What is Medicaid home health care?
atoms.text: Medicaid home health care services help elderly people stay living in their own homes. Typically, people who are able to live at home prefer that to a nursing home or care facility, but some may need extra help to live safely at home. That's where Medicaid in-home care comes in. In-home care can also be provided at the home of a friend or relative, an adult foster care home or an assisted living facility.
qs: What is Medicaid in-home care?
Can Medicaid in-home care be provided outside my own home?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid cover home health care?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover home health care?
atoms.text: The federal government requires all 50 states to offer some kind of home health benefits through Medicaid. But Medicaid programs change from state to state, so the amount of in-home care and the types of services available depend on where you live. Even if certain in-home services aren't covered by a state's regular Medicaid plan, they may still be offered through Home and Community Based Services (HCBS) programs.
qs: Will Medicaid pay for a home health aide?
What are HCBS programs?

atoms.title: Types of Medicaid in-home care services
atoms.q: What home health services are covered by Medicaid?
atoms.text: Services typically available in most states include home health care (medical care at home), personal care help with bathing, grooming, dressing, eating and mobility, homemaker services like housekeeping and meal preparation, physical, speech and occupational therapy, adult day care, accessibility modifications such as ramps and grab bars, medical equipment and supplies, nutrition services, personal emergency response services, transportation assistance, hospice care and family and caregiver support including respite care.
qs: Does Medicaid pay for wheelchair ramps?
Does Medicaid cover respite care for caregivers?
What in-home services can Medicaid provide?

atoms.title: Who can deliver Medicaid in-home services
atoms.q: Who provides Medicaid in-home care?
atoms.text: Some in-home care services, like skilled nursing care and occupational, physical or speech therapy, are delivered by medical professionals. Other services, such as doing chores around the house and making meals, can be provided by family members, friends or paid caregivers.
qs: Can a family member be paid by Medicaid to provide care?
Who delivers home health services?

atoms.title: How many hours of home care does Medicaid cover?
atoms.q: How many hours of home health care does Medicaid cover?
atoms.text: The rules depend on the state where you live, and how much care you can get may also depend on the type of Medicaid program you're enrolled in. The level of home health care Medicaid provides is typically based on the needs of the individual. Some programs may pay for a personal care assistant for several hours a day on multiple days a week, while others may only cover adult day care for a few days each week.
qs: How many hours of in-home care will Medicaid pay for?
Does Medicaid pay for a personal care assistant?

atoms.title: Two requirements for home health Medicaid
atoms.q: How do I qualify for Medicaid home health care?
atoms.text: There are 2 main requirements. 1) Financial requirements: each state has limits for how much you can earn or the value of what you own, though the limit for HCBS services may be higher than for regular Medicaid. 2) Medical need: most state Medicaid programs require recipients to show they need in-home medical care or help with bathing, dressing, eating and other daily activities. To qualify for HCBS programs, recipients typically need the same level of care as provided in a nursing home.
qs: What do I need to qualify for Medicaid home care?
Do I need a nursing-home level of care for HCBS?

atoms.title: D-SNPs can add extra support at home
atoms.q: Can a Dual Special Needs plan help with home care?
atoms.text: If you qualify for both Medicaid and Medicare, you could get a Dual Special Needs Plan (D-SNP). A D-SNP works together with your Medicaid health plan, so you keep all your Medicaid benefits and also get many extra benefits that Original Medicare doesn't cover. Dual Special Needs plans have a $0 premium for members with Extra Help (Low Income Subsidy). Benefits and features vary by plan and area.
qs: Can I get extra home support if I have Medicare and Medicaid?
What is Extra Help with a D-SNP?

atoms.title: Coverage differences between states
atoms.q: How do Medicaid coverage rules differ by state?
atoms.text: Each state may cover services and provide benefits a little differently. Each state decides who can get Medicaid and whether it can help more people, though states usually cover older people, children, pregnant women and people with disabilities. All states pay for basic health care like doctor visits and hospital stays, and some also cover extras like vision and dental care. Some states may have conditions that must be met to maintain Medicaid eligibility for certain groups.
qs: Why is Medicaid different in each state?
Do all states cover dental and vision?

atoms.title: Care delivery differences: copays, providers, long-term care
atoms.q: How does the way Medicaid delivers care vary by state?
atoms.text: In some states people might pay a small fee (a copay) when they go to the doctor, while in other states they don't pay when they get care. States choose which doctors and hospitals can use Medicaid, which can change how easy it is to find care. For long-term care, some states have special programs that provide care at home for older people, while others use nursing homes. States may also look at what you own, like savings or a house, if you need care for a long time.
qs: Do I pay a copay with Medicaid?
Does Medicaid long-term care differ by state?

atoms.title: Extra services that vary by state
atoms.q: Which Medicaid benefits vary by state?
atoms.text: Extra services states may or may not cover include: dental (some states cover full dental benefits while others only pay for urgent dental care); vision (some pay for eye exams and glasses, others don't); prescriptions (each state decides how much it pays); non-emergency medical transportation (some states provide rides to appointments, others don't); and physical therapy (coverage amount varies by location).
qs: Does my state's Medicaid give rides to appointments?
Does Medicaid cover glasses in every state?

atoms.title: Spend-down, private plans and income limits
atoms.q: How do eligibility rules vary across Medicaid programs?
atoms.text: In some states, people with higher incomes can lower their countable income by subtracting medical costs to qualify, which is called a spend-down program. Some states use private health plans to manage Medicaid services, which can affect the care you get and which doctors you can see. Income limits also vary: some states let people with higher incomes get Medicaid, while others only help those with very low incomes.
qs: What is a Medicaid spend-down?
Do private insurers run Medicaid in my state?

atoms.title: Medicaid expansion changes coverage by state
atoms.q: How does Medicaid expansion affect coverage in different states?
atoms.text: The Affordable Care Act lets states choose to expand Medicaid to cover more low-income adults, especially those without children, by raising the income limit. States can expand Medicaid to adults who earn up to 138% of the poverty level, which the page says is about $20,780 a year per person or $35,630 for a family of 3. In states that expand, more adults can get care and fewer people are left without insurance. In states that do not expand, fewer adults can get Medicaid.
qs: What income qualifies for Medicaid in expansion states?
What happens in states that don't expand Medicaid?

atoms.title: Signing up for Medicaid varies by state
atoms.q: Is the Medicaid sign-up process the same in every state?
atoms.text: Each state has its own way to renew or sign up for Medicaid, so the steps might be a little different depending on where you live. Some states use private health plans to help you get care; these plans help you find doctors and get check-ups, but you might only be able to go to certain doctors that work with the plan. Some states ask the federal government for permission to try new ways of running Medicaid, called a waiver.
qs: What is a Medicaid waiver?
Do I apply for Medicaid the same way in every state?

atoms.title: Medicaid covers nearly half of U.S. births
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover pregnancy?
atoms.text: Medicaid covers nearly half of all births in the United States each year and is the main source of health care coverage for low-income pregnant women. Medicaid coverage for mothers starts during pregnancy and lasts for at least 60 days after giving birth.
qs: Does Medicaid cover pregnant women?
How long does Medicaid cover mothers after birth?

atoms.title: States can extend postpartum coverage to 12 months
atoms.q: Can Medicaid cover mothers for 12 months after birth?
atoms.text: In 2023, Congress provided a way for states to extend Medicaid coverage to mothers for 12 months after giving birth. More than half of U.S. states have chosen to do this, according to the page, and more states were expected to do so in 2023.
qs: Is there 12 months of postpartum Medicaid?
Which states extended postpartum Medicaid?

atoms.title: Who qualifies for Medicaid pregnancy coverage?
atoms.q: Who can qualify for Medicaid pregnancy coverage?
atoms.text: Eligibility depends on where you live. State Medicaid programs must cover pregnant women who earn 133% of the federal poverty level (FPL) or less, but some states may cover people who earn more. Women who earn too much for Medicaid but not enough to afford private insurance may be able to get maternity coverage through the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP). Lawful immigrants may also be able to get coverage through CHIP. Women should apply as soon as they find out they're pregnant.
qs: What income qualifies me for pregnancy Medicaid?
Can I get CHIP if I'm pregnant and over the Medicaid limit?

atoms.title: Maternity services Medicaid covers
atoms.q: What maternity care services does Medicaid cover?
atoms.text: Medicaid covers pregnant women before, during and after giving birth. That includes routine checkups, and most states also cover prenatal vitamins and ultrasound exams. If a woman needs other medically necessary care during pregnancy, Medicaid will cover those services. Medicaid covers all care during delivery, including the cost of the hospital stay or birth center, and care after giving birth in the postpartum period.
qs: Does Medicaid cover prenatal vitamins and ultrasounds?
Does Medicaid cover delivery in a birth center?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare Healthy First Steps
atoms.q: What is UnitedHealthcare Healthy First Steps?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare Healthy First Steps helps all pregnant women find providers and connect to local resources. It also provides extra help during high-risk pregnancies and for at least 2 months after delivery. It is one of the value-added programs UnitedHealthcare may offer female Medicaid members; benefits vary by plan and service area.
qs: What is Healthy First Steps?
Does UnitedHealthcare help with high-risk pregnancies?

atoms.title: Extra maternity programs for Medicaid members
atoms.q: What extra pregnancy services does UnitedHealthcare offer Medicaid members?
atoms.text: Beyond standard Medicaid benefits, UnitedHealthcare's value-added programs may include Digital Education & Rewards, with customized education through each stage of pregnancy and rewards for attending visits; Home Delivered Meals after leaving the hospital; In-Home Care Services; Breastfeeding Support with up to 6 virtual visits; and supplies such as diapers, car seats and breast pumps. Benefits vary by plan and service area.
qs: Does my Medicaid plan give me a breast pump or car seat?
Are there rewards for going to prenatal visits?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid cover doulas?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover doulas?
atoms.text: A doula is a non-clinical person who provides support for women before, during and after labor. More than half of all states either provide Medicaid coverage for doula care or are working toward offering it. UnitedHealthcare is working to offer doula care in states where it's not covered by Medicaid, partnering with The Doula Network to test doula care programs in 5 states: Arizona, Kansas, Kentucky, Texas and Washington.
qs: Will Medicaid pay for a doula?
Where is UnitedHealthcare testing doula care?

atoms.title: What CHIP is and who it is for
atoms.q: What is the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP)?
atoms.text: CHIP is a federal and state program that gives health coverage to children who don't have insurance. It's for families who earn too much to get Medicaid but not enough to pay for other health plans. It offers low-cost or no-cost coverage for infants, children and teens. Each state runs its own CHIP program with rules about who qualifies and what's covered.
qs: What is CHIP?
Who is CHIP for?
What if my income is too high for Medicaid but I can't afford insurance?

atoms.title: How CHIP plans are designed and funded
atoms.q: How does CHIP work?
atoms.text: CHIP plans are designed to provide health coverage for eligible children through Medicaid and separate CHIP programs. They help children get coverage if their family's income is too high for Medicaid but too low to pay for private insurance. CHIP is funded by money from the state and federal government's Medicaid program.
qs: How is CHIP funded?
Is CHIP part of Medicaid?

atoms.title: Services CHIP typically covers
atoms.q: What services does CHIP cover?
atoms.text: CHIP benefits differ by state, but most states offer coverage for a range of services, including well-baby doctor visits, dental and vision care, prescriptions, vaccinations, hospital and emergency care, lab and X-rays, and behavioral health care.
qs: Does CHIP cover dental and vision?
What does CHIP pay for?

atoms.title: CHIP is available in all 50 states
atoms.q: Which states have CHIP plans?
atoms.text: CHIP is available in all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and 5 U.S. territories. Each state runs its own program and has rules about who can join and what's covered, so benefits can vary depending on where you live. UnitedHealthcare Community Plans offer CHIP plans in Colorado, New York, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas.
qs: Is CHIP available in my state?
In which states does UnitedHealthcare offer CHIP?

atoms.title: Applying for CHIP or Medicaid depends on state
atoms.q: Should I apply for CHIP or Medicaid for my child?
atoms.text: In some states, you can apply for a CHIP plan for children. In other states, you can apply for a Medicaid plan that includes health insurance for children. A child can also be enrolled in both Medicaid and CHIP, if eligible.
qs: Can a child have both Medicaid and CHIP?
Do I apply for CHIP or Medicaid for kids in my state?

atoms.title: Does my child qualify for CHIP?
atoms.q: Does my child qualify for CHIP?
atoms.text: CHIP is for children who can't get insurance elsewhere. Your child may qualify even if you don't receive Medicaid. Your state decides if your child qualifies and what's covered, based on financial and non-financial information. Three groups may be covered: children, pregnant women, and targeted low-income children, generally those whose household income is above the state's Medicaid level but still low enough for CHIP.
qs: Who qualifies for CHIP?
Can my child get CHIP if I'm not on Medicaid?

atoms.title: What does CHIP cost?
atoms.q: What does CHIP cost?
atoms.text: Routine health and dental check-ups are available with CHIP plans at no extra cost. Depending on your state's coverage, you may still have to pay a small amount for other services when your child gets care. Some states charge a monthly fee for CHIP coverage, but you won't have to pay more than 5% of your family's income for the year.
qs: How much does CHIP cost?
Is there a monthly premium for CHIP?

atoms.title: How long can a child stay on CHIP?
atoms.q: How long can a child stay on CHIP?
atoms.text: CHIP usually covers eligible children up to age 19, but rules vary by state. You'll be notified every year to renew your CHIP coverage. Eligibility rules, including the age limit, are set by each state, so families should check their own state CHIP program for details.
qs: Until what age is a child covered by CHIP?
Do I need to renew CHIP every year?

atoms.title: How to apply for CHIP
atoms.q: What is the CHIP application process?
atoms.text: You can apply for and enroll in CHIP at any time. If you qualify, coverage starts right away and you won't need to buy any other insurance. Apply by finding a CHIP program by state on Medicaid.gov, by creating an account or signing in with the ACA Health Insurance Marketplace, or by filling out an application. If anyone in your household qualifies for CHIP after a Marketplace application, your information is sent to your state agency, which will contact you about enrollment.
qs: How do I apply for CHIP?
When can I enroll my child in CHIP?

atoms.title: Can a non-parent apply for a child's CHIP?
atoms.q: Can I apply for CHIP if I'm not the child's parent?
atoms.text: Legal guardians, including grandparents, aunts or uncles, can apply for CHIP. If your child doesn't qualify at first, keep trying. Rules can change and your child may qualify later. Each state decides whether a child qualifies.
qs: Can a grandparent apply for CHIP?
Can a legal guardian enroll a child in CHIP?

atoms.title: Documents needed to apply for CHIP
atoms.q: What documents are needed to apply for CHIP?
atoms.text: Check with your state, but you may need the applicant's name, date of birth and Social Security number; proof of income, like pay stubs or W-2s; monthly payments for rent, mortgage or utilities; proof of address, citizenship or immigration status; and current insurance and government benefits.
qs: What do I need to apply for CHIP?
Do I need proof of income for CHIP?

atoms.title: How to renew your child's CHIP coverage
atoms.q: How can I renew my child's CHIP coverage?
atoms.text: 1) Update your contact information so your state has your current mailing address, phone number and email. 2) Check your mail for a letter from your state's Medicaid or CHIP office saying whether you need to fill out a renewal form. 3) Complete and return the renewal form, with required documents, to your state right away to avoid gaps in coverage.
qs: How do I renew CHIP?
What should I do when I get a CHIP renewal letter?

atoms.title: Medicaid is health insurance with eligibility rules
atoms.q: Who is Medicaid for?
atoms.text: Medicaid is health insurance. You can get it if you meet certain requirements. It could be right for you if you have a low income. It's also for children, pregnant women, older adults and people with disabilities. Learning about Medicaid eligibility is the first step when looking into Medicaid plans.
qs: Am I eligible for Medicaid?
What is Medicaid eligibility?

atoms.title: Groups eligible for Medicaid
atoms.q: Who's eligible for Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicaid eligibility rules are different in each state. If a person meets the criteria in their state, they can enroll in Medicaid. People who are eligible include children under age 18 in families with very low income, children in foster care, people who are pregnant and have very low income, certain parents or caretakers with very low income, most older adults (65 and over) who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), and people with disabilities who receive SSI.
qs: Who qualifies for Medicaid?
Do people on SSI qualify for Medicaid?
Are foster children eligible for Medicaid?

atoms.title: How the MAGI income test works
atoms.q: What is the income limit for Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicaid income limits vary from state to state, and household size also affects income eligibility. The Affordable Care Act established Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) as a way to determine income eligibility. MAGI is based on adjusted gross income plus tax-exempt interest. Assets and resources like bank accounts, homes or vehicles are not counted, and certain income like SSI and child support is not considered. You may be eligible if your MAGI is at or below a set percentage of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL), which depends on your state.
qs: What is the income limit for Medicaid?
Do assets count for Medicaid eligibility?
What is MAGI?

atoms.title: Medicaid work requirement starts January 1, 2027
atoms.q: Is there a Medicaid work requirement?
atoms.text: In 2025, the president signed a bill that changed the Medicaid program and put a new Medicaid work requirement into place, starting on January 1, 2027. The new rules are for people aged 19-64 who enroll in Medicaid. They'll need to show that they are working 80 hours per month, or doing other qualifying activities such as paid work, educational programs, job training or community service.
qs: Do I have to work to keep Medicaid?
How many hours do I need to work for Medicaid?
When do Medicaid work requirements begin?

atoms.title: Who is exempt from the Medicaid work requirement
atoms.q: Who does not have to meet the Medicaid work requirement?
atoms.text: People who are medically frail, pregnant or postpartum, or parents and caretakers of children 13 or younger do not have to meet the Medicaid work requirements that begin January 1, 2027.
qs: Are pregnant women exempt from Medicaid work requirements?
Do parents of young children have to work for Medicaid?

atoms.title: What Medicaid expansion is
atoms.q: What is Medicaid expansion?
atoms.text: Medicaid expansion was part of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), a law signed in 2010 with the goal of helping make health insurance more affordable for people with low incomes. Expansion began in 2014. Each state decided individually whether to adopt it, so your eligibility may depend on whether your state has expanded its program.
qs: What is Medicaid expansion?
Did every state expand Medicaid?

atoms.title: Does Medicaid eligibility vary by state?
atoms.q: Does Medicaid eligibility vary by state?
atoms.text: Yes. Each state has different eligibility requirements for Medicaid, based on income, household size, disability, family status or other factors. To find out if you're eligible, visit the website for Medicaid in your state and check the eligibility requirements.
qs: Is Medicaid different in each state?
How do I find my state's Medicaid requirements?

atoms.title: Do you lose Medicaid with a dual plan?
atoms.q: If I get a dual health plan, do I lose my Medicaid benefits?
atoms.text: No. People who have both Medicaid and Medicare can get a dual health plan. This lets you keep all your Medicaid benefits, plus get extra Medicare benefits too. A dual health plan is designed for people who are covered by both programs.
qs: Will I lose Medicaid if I join a dual plan?
Can I keep Medicaid and get Medicare benefits?

atoms.title: Medicaid renewal also called redetermination
atoms.q: What is Medicaid renewal?
atoms.text: Medicaid renewal is also called Medicaid redetermination. This is when the state checks if you still qualify to get Medicaid benefits. Yearly renewals are how states confirm that members still meet the requirements to keep Medicaid benefits.
qs: What is Medicaid redetermination?
Is renewal the same as redetermination?

atoms.title: People with disabilities and low incomes qualify for Medicaid
atoms.q: Can I get Medicaid if I have a disability?
atoms.text: People with disabilities or chronic conditions and low incomes are eligible for Medicaid. All states also provide aged, blind and disabled (ABD) Medicaid benefits. ABD Medicaid is for adults 65 and older or anyone who is disabled according to Social Security. You also need to meet the financial eligibility requirements in your state.
qs: Does a disability qualify me for Medicaid?
What is aged, blind and disabled Medicaid?

atoms.title: SSI leads to Medicaid, SSDI leads to Medicare
atoms.q: Do I get Medicaid or Medicare if I receive disability benefits?
atoms.text: Whether you qualify for Medicaid or Medicare depends on the type of disability benefits you get. If you have Supplemental Security Income (SSI) disability, you'll be eligible for Medicaid coverage; in many states you'll get Medicaid automatically, but in others you'll need to sign up. If you get Social Security Disability Income (SSDI), you'll qualify for Medicare.
qs: Does SSI qualify me for Medicaid?
Do I get Medicare if I get SSDI?

atoms.title: More than 10 million qualify for Medicaid by disability
atoms.q: How many people qualify for Medicaid because of a disability?
atoms.text: More than 10 million people qualify for Medicaid based on having a disability, citing MACPAC (the Medicaid and CHIP Payment and Access Commission). There are also more than 12 million people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid, known as dual-eligibles.
qs: How many people are dual eligible?
How many people have Medicaid because of disability?

atoms.title: Disability medical requirements are the same across programs
atoms.q: What conditions qualify as a disability?
atoms.text: No matter whether you have SSI, SSDI, Medicaid, ABD Medicaid or Medicare, the medical requirements are the same. First, you must meet the non-medical disability requirements, based mainly on work history and Social Security taxes paid. Then monthly disability benefits are paid if a medical condition is expected to last at least 1 year or result in death.
qs: How long must a condition last to count as a disability?
What are the requirements for Social Security disability?

atoms.title: Disorder categories that may qualify as a disability
atoms.q: Which health disorders may qualify adults for Social Security disability?
atoms.text: The page lists general categories for adults over 18, noting the list is not complete and the Social Security Administration website has the full list. Categories include musculoskeletal, special senses and speech, respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, kidney, blood, skin, endocrine, congenital disorders, neurological, mental disorders, cancer and immune system disorders. A separate childhood listing covers impairments for children.
qs: What medical conditions count as a disability?
Is cancer a qualifying disability?

atoms.title: Under 65 with disability: Medicare after 24 months
atoms.q: Can I get Medicare if I'm under 65 and have a disability?
atoms.text: People under age 65 with disabilities automatically qualify for Original Medicare (Parts A and B) after they've received disability benefits from Social Security for 24 months. If you also qualify for Medicaid, your state Medicaid program may help pay for costs and services Medicare does not cover. For services covered by both, such as doctor visits, hospital care, home care and skilled nursing facility care, Medicare pays first and Medicaid may pay added costs afterward.
qs: How long until I get Medicare on disability?
Does Medicare or Medicaid pay first?

atoms.title: Dual Special Needs plans for people with disabilities
atoms.q: What is a Dual Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: Dual Special Needs plans are for people who could use extra help because of income, disabilities, age and/or health conditions. They are a special type of Medicare Advantage plan. They include everything you get with Original Medicare, plus prescription drug coverage and many other extra benefits, and you could get it all with as low as a $0 plan premium. The page says many people who could qualify don't know these plans exist.
qs: What plan is for people with Medicare and Medicaid and a disability?
Do dual plans cost anything?

atoms.title: Who is eligible for Medicaid
atoms.q: Who is eligible for Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicaid is a federal and state program that provides health care coverage to qualified individuals. Eligible people include pregnant women with low income, children of low-income families, children in foster care, people with disabilities, seniors with low income, and parents or caregivers with low income. Because programs are state-run, states can choose to provide Medicaid to more people.
qs: What groups does Medicaid cover?
Can states cover more people than the federal minimum?

atoms.title: Do you lose Medicaid with a dual health plan?
atoms.q: If you get a dual health plan, do you lose your Medicaid benefits?
atoms.text: No. A dual health plan won't change your Medicaid benefits in any way. Dual health plans are for people who have both Medicaid and Medicare. You keep the same Medicaid plan and all the same Medicaid benefits you get now, and you could get more Medicare benefits. A dual health plan doesn't replace your Medicaid plan.
qs: Will a dual plan take away my Medicaid?
Does a D-SNP replace my Medicaid plan?

atoms.title: How you can have both Medicaid and Medicare
atoms.q: How can I have both Medicaid and Medicare?
atoms.text: To get a dual health plan, you need to qualify for both Medicaid and Medicare. You qualify for Medicaid based on low income, and must meet the income requirements in your state. You qualify for Medicare based on age (65 or older) or due to having a disability. People who qualify for both are dual-eligible, which also makes them eligible for a dual health plan.
qs: What makes someone dual-eligible?
Do I need low income to get a dual plan?

atoms.title: A dual health plan is a Medicare Advantage plan
atoms.q: What type of plan is a dual health plan?
atoms.text: If you already have Medicare coverage, you probably have Original Medicare. A dual health plan is a special kind of Medicare plan, called a Medicare Advantage plan. It includes everything you get with Original Medicare, plus prescription drug coverage and many other extra benefits and features on top, and you could get it all with as low as a $0 plan premium. Benefits and features vary by plan and area.
qs: Is a dual plan the same as Original Medicare?
Does a dual plan include prescription coverage?

atoms.title: Switching to a dual plan can be easy
atoms.q: Is it hard to switch to a dual health plan?
atoms.text: If you qualify for a dual health plan, you may have quite a lot of medical needs, so it's understandable to hesitate about switching. The whole point of dual plans is to help make life easier. UnitedHealthcare says it has helped many people switch and knows how to make enrolling in a dual health plan as easy as possible. To start, enter your ZIP code to search for dual plans in your area.
qs: How hard is it to switch to a dual plan?
What is the next step to get a dual health plan?

atoms.title: Who Medicaid expansion covers
atoms.q: Who is covered by Medicaid expansion?
atoms.text: Medicaid expansion gave states the chance to provide Medicaid coverage to people who earn up to 138% of the federal poverty level (FPL). It opened access mainly to 2 low-income groups: adults who don't have any children, and people who in the past earned too much to qualify for state Medicaid. The page states that for 2023 the FPL is $13,590 for individuals and $27,750 for a family of 4.
qs: What income qualifies for Medicaid expansion?
Can adults without children get Medicaid?

atoms.title: Federal poverty level (FPL) explained
atoms.q: What is the federal poverty level?
atoms.text: FPL stands for federal poverty level, a measure of income. It is the cutoff to qualify for Medicaid and other government benefits. The federal government updates the FPL each year.
qs: What does FPL mean?
How is Medicaid income eligibility measured?

atoms.title: How Medicaid expansion is funded
atoms.q: How is Medicaid expansion funded?
atoms.text: Each state runs its own Medicaid program, and the federal government provides states at least half of the funding needed. For costs specifically related to Medicaid expansion, the federal government paid 100% for the first few years, and that share was gradually reduced. As of 2020 and every year going forward, the federal government pays 90%, so for every extra dollar a state spends on expansion, the federal government covers 90 cents.
qs: Who pays for Medicaid expansion?
What share of expansion costs does the federal government cover?

atoms.title: 38 states and D.C. adopted expansion; 12 did not
atoms.q: Why don't all states have Medicaid expansion?
atoms.text: In 2012, the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government could not force states to expand Medicaid under the ACA because it would cost states money, so each state could choose. At the time of the page, 38 states plus Washington, D.C. had adopted Medicaid expansion and 12 states had not.
qs: Which states expanded Medicaid?
Why did some states not expand Medicaid?

atoms.title: The Medicaid coverage gap
atoms.q: What is the Medicaid coverage gap?
atoms.text: The Medicaid coverage gap affects people in states that chose not to expand Medicaid. These people earn too much to qualify for Medicaid in their state, but still can't afford the cost of an individual or family Marketplace (ACA) plan. Roughly 2.2 million people fall into this gap, according to the page.
qs: What is the coverage gap in Medicaid?
How many people are in the Medicaid coverage gap?

atoms.title: Findings of the Menges Group expansion study
atoms.q: What has been the impact of Medicaid expansion?
atoms.text: A study by The Menges Group, published in August 2021, compared states that adopted Medicaid expansion with states that did not. Key findings: more than 9 million people who would otherwise be uninsured got coverage; from 2013 to 2019, the share of Medicaid costs paid by states grew less in expansion states (19.5% versus 26.4%); expansion helped lower the COVID-19 death rate among people aged 18 to 64; and hospital revenues appear to have increased considerably in expansion states.
qs: Did Medicaid expansion reduce the number of uninsured?
What did the Menges Group find about Medicaid expansion?

atoms.title: Expansion and Dual Special Needs plan eligibility
atoms.q: How does Medicaid expansion help people who also have Medicare?
atoms.text: Medicaid expansion made it possible for more people to get coverage through Medicaid, including some who are also eligible for Medicare. Those people would most likely also qualify for a Dual Special Needs plan, a Medicare Advantage plan that works together with your Medicaid health plan. You keep all your Medicaid benefits, and most dual plans give more benefits and features than Original Medicare, with as low as a $0 plan premium.
qs: Can Medicaid expansion make me eligible for a dual plan?
Do I keep Medicaid benefits with a Dual Special Needs plan?

atoms.title: What Medicaid redetermination is
atoms.q: What is Medicaid redetermination?
atoms.text: Medicaid redetermination, also called Medicaid renewal or recertification, is when people who have Medicaid benefits are asked to show they still qualify in their state. Your coverage will renew only if the state can confirm that you still qualify. In some cases the state can do this automatically. If it can't, it will request more information. If you no longer qualify, or don't respond to a renewal notice, your coverage can end.
qs: What does Medicaid redetermination mean?
Why do I have to renew Medicaid?
Can I lose Medicaid if I don't respond to a renewal notice?

atoms.title: Four steps of Medicaid renewal
atoms.q: What are the steps of Medicaid renewal?
atoms.text: 1) Receive a renewal notice, usually 60 to 90 days before your coverage ends, by mail, email or your state's online portal. 2) Complete the renewal form if your state sends one, confirming household members, income, address and contact information, and other health coverage. 3) Submit documents if your income or household changed, such as pay stubs, benefit letters, a recent tax return or proof of a new address. 4) Receive a renewal decision; if you still qualify, coverage continues.
qs: How does Medicaid renewal work?
When will I get my Medicaid renewal notice?
What documents might I need to renew Medicaid?

atoms.title: Ex parte (automatic) Medicaid renewal
atoms.q: Does Medicaid automatically renew?
atoms.text: Some states renew coverage automatically using information like tax or Social Security records. This is called ex parte renewal, also known as administrative, passive or auto-renewal. A government agency, most commonly Medicaid or CHIP, renews your coverage without requiring you to fill out forms or submit new documents. Automatic renewal is not always possible, because some income may not show up in state records. If the state can't verify your information, it will send a form or ask for more documents.
qs: Does Medicaid renew by itself?
What is ex parte renewal?

atoms.title: Renewal every 6 months for some adults from 2027
atoms.q: Will Medicaid renewals change in 2027?
atoms.text: Starting in 2027, some adults in Medicaid expansion programs will need to renew coverage every 6 months instead of once a year. Some pregnant people, older adults and people with disabilities will still renew once a year. The page notes that rules can vary by state, so members should check their state's Medicaid program for details.
qs: Do I have to renew Medicaid every 6 months?
Who still renews Medicaid once a year?

atoms.title: 2027 work rule for some adults 19-64
atoms.q: What is the new Medicaid work rule?
atoms.text: Starting in 2027, some adults may need to meet a work rule to get or keep Medicaid. This may apply to some adults aged 19 to 64. You may meet the rule by working, going to school, getting job training or doing community service. In most cases, you need to complete 80 hours each month. If the state can't confirm you meet the requirements, it may give you time to respond, and if you lose coverage you may be able to apply again.
qs: How many hours do I need to work for Medicaid in 2027?
Does school count toward the Medicaid work rule?

atoms.title: Who is exempt from the work rule
atoms.q: Who doesn't have to follow the Medicaid work rule?
atoms.text: Some people do not have to follow the Medicaid work rule. This may include people who recently gave birth or are pregnant, have serious health needs, care for a child aged 13 or younger, or care for a person with a disability. States may also give short-term exceptions, which can include a hospital stay, a disaster or high unemployment in your area.
qs: Can I get an exception to the Medicaid work rule?
Are caregivers exempt from Medicaid work requirements?

atoms.title: How do you find your Medicaid renewal date?
atoms.q: When is Medicaid renewal?
atoms.text: Your Medicaid renewal date depends on when you first signed up or last renewed, so it's different for each person. You can find it by logging into your state's Medicaid portal or your UnitedHealthcare member account, calling your state Medicaid helpline, or looking at the most recent notice from your state agency. Your state must send at least one renewal notice before coverage ends. If you don't get one, contact your state right away; you still need to renew on time.
qs: How do I find out when my Medicaid renews?
What if I never got a Medicaid renewal notice?

atoms.title: Four ways to renew Medicaid
atoms.q: How can I renew Medicaid?
atoms.text: Renewing Medicaid may be easier than applying for the first time. Online is typically the fastest, through your state's benefits portal; keep your confirmation number. By phone, call your state Medicaid helpline with your Medicaid ID number, income and household information ready. By mail, sign and return the paper form, using certified mail if the deadline is close. In person, visit your local Medicaid office or a community health center.
qs: Can I renew Medicaid online?
How do I renew Medicaid by mail or phone?

atoms.title: What if you miss the Medicaid renewal deadline?
atoms.q: What happens if you don't renew Medicaid in time?
atoms.text: Missing the renewal deadline does not always mean you lose coverage for good. Many states give you 90 days after your coverage ends to renew, and if you still qualify your coverage may be restored, often back to the date it ended. You could also appeal if you think you still qualify, and many states give you 90 days to ask for a hearing. If too much time has passed, you can apply again; coverage often starts the first day of the month you apply.
qs: Can I get Medicaid back if I missed renewal?
How long do I have to renew after coverage ends?
Can I appeal a Medicaid termination?

atoms.title: Common reasons Medicaid renewal fails
atoms.q: What are common Medicaid renewal mistakes?
atoms.text: Common reasons renewal does not go through include not answering the renewal notice (even if nothing changed, you still need to respond, and an out-of-date address, email or phone number may cause you to miss it); missing information, such as proof of income that the state requests; and no longer qualifying, for example after household changes like marriage, divorce, someone moving in or out, or a child aging out of coverage.
qs: Why was my Medicaid renewal denied?
How can I avoid losing Medicaid at renewal?

atoms.title: Marketplace options after losing Medicaid
atoms.q: What can I do if I no longer qualify for Medicaid?
atoms.text: If your state says you no longer qualify, your coverage may end, and your state may share your contact information with the ACA Marketplace, which may contact you by mail, phone, text or email. You may be able to get Marketplace coverage with savings if you lost or will soon lose Medicaid or CHIP, or applied through your state and were denied. If you lose Medicaid because you did not meet work requirements, you may not qualify for premium tax credits. You can apply again at any time.
qs: Where do I get insurance if I lose Medicaid?
Can I get Marketplace savings after losing Medicaid?

atoms.title: Two main steps to enroll in Medicaid
atoms.q: How do I enroll in Medicaid?
atoms.text: There are 2 main steps. 1) Apply for Medicaid benefits in your state. Each state manages its own Medicaid program, so you apply through your state to find out if you're eligible. 2) Enroll in a Medicaid plan. Once you find out you're eligible for Medicaid, you can pick a Medicaid plan.
qs: What are the steps to get on Medicaid?
Do I apply first or pick a plan first?

atoms.title: Personal, financial and medical information to apply
atoms.q: What do you need to apply for Medicaid?
atoms.text: Each state requires different information for a Medicaid application. Be ready to provide personal information (name, date of birth and Social Security number of household members, and proof of citizenship), financial information (rent or mortgage, expenses such as utilities and daycare, vehicle information, bank statements and income such as pay stubs) and medical information (proof of disability or records of a lasting medical condition, and recent medical bills).
qs: What documents do I need for a Medicaid application?
Do I need proof of citizenship for Medicaid?
What financial information is required to apply?

atoms.title: Picking a Medicaid health plan after approval
atoms.q: How do you enroll in a Medicaid plan?
atoms.text: After you apply for Medicaid in your state and find out you're eligible, you can pick the Medicaid health plan you want. Sometimes a state may automatically enroll people in a Medicaid plan. If that happens, you may be able to switch to a different plan if there is another you prefer. You can choose your state to see available UnitedHealthcare Community plans and review the benefits included in each.
qs: How do I choose a Medicaid health plan?
What if my state picked a plan for me?

atoms.title: When can you enroll in Medicaid?
atoms.q: When can you enroll in Medicaid?
atoms.text: You can enroll in Medicaid at any time during the year. That's also true for the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP). If you've had a life change, like getting married or moving to a different state, you could qualify for Medicaid and should apply right away.
qs: Is there an open enrollment period for Medicaid?
Can I apply for Medicaid any time of year?

atoms.title: Pregnant people should apply right away
atoms.q: When should a pregnant person apply for Medicaid?
atoms.text: Pregnant people should apply for Medicaid as soon as they find out they're pregnant. Medicaid pregnancy coverage is available to help keep you and your baby healthy throughout your pregnancy and beyond. Your newborn will automatically be enrolled in Medicaid, too.
qs: Is my newborn automatically covered by Medicaid?
When should I apply for Medicaid if I'm pregnant?

atoms.title: When can you change your Medicaid plan?
atoms.q: When can you change your Medicaid plan?
atoms.text: After you first enroll as a new Medicaid member, you'll typically have 90 days to change your plan. If you don't choose a health plan, your state will assign you to a plan. After that, most Medicaid members can only switch their health plan once per year. Your Medicaid agency will let you know when you can change your coverage.
qs: How long do I have to switch Medicaid plans?
Can I change my Medicaid health plan?

atoms.title: Auto-enrollment (auto-assignment) in Medicaid
atoms.q: What is auto-enrollment in Medicaid?
atoms.text: Auto-enrollment, also called auto-assignment, is when a state automatically assigns a group of people to a specific Medicaid plan. This can happen when a new health plan becomes available, or if a health insurance company stops offering a Medicaid plan in a certain area. If someone is auto-assigned to a plan and prefers a different Medicaid plan, they'll have 90 days to switch.
qs: Why was I assigned to a Medicaid plan?
Can I switch if I was auto-assigned?

atoms.title: Do you re-enroll in Medicaid every year?
atoms.q: Do you have to re-enroll in Medicaid every year?
