atoms.text: Current employer groups manage benefits through the uhceservices portal, which UnitedHealthcare says should be accessed from a desktop or tablet device. Employers can also sign in to Employer eServices to manage their benefits. Education materials and benefit information are available through UnitedHealthcare's employer resources.
qs: How do I log in to uhceservices?
Where do employers manage their UnitedHealthcare benefits online?

atoms.title: How to contact a UnitedHealthcare representative
atoms.q: How can an employer reach a UnitedHealthcare representative about group coverage?
atoms.text: Employers can fill out the UnitedHealthcare contact form to have a representative reach out, or call a UnitedHealthcare representative at 1-800-650-5826. Current employer groups can use the same number to get help with their plan.
qs: What phone number do employers call for UnitedHealthcare group plans?
How do I talk to a UnitedHealthcare rep about employee benefits?

atoms.title: Why work with UnitedHealthcare
atoms.q: What does UnitedHealthcare say sets it apart for employers?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says employers can learn what sets it apart as an industry leader by looking at three areas: lowering costs, expanding care access and advancing innovation. It also notes that its e-service platforms are meant to make benefits administration easier for employers to manage and support.
qs: Why choose UnitedHealthcare as an employer carrier?
What does UnitedHealthcare offer to simplify benefits administration?

atoms.title: Group health plans for 2 to 50 employees
atoms.q: What group health insurance does UnitedHealthcare offer small businesses?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers group health insurance plans for business owners with 2 to 50 employees. The plans are designed to help a small business save money and support employees' health and well-being needs, and they can help the business retain and recruit talent.
qs: Does UnitedHealthcare offer health insurance for a business with 2 employees?
What is group health insurance for small business owners?

atoms.title: Small business reach and network size
atoms.q: How many small business employees does UnitedHealthcare cover, and how large is its network?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says it is the carrier of choice for over 235,000 employers and provides health care coverage to more than 2.5 million small business employees (internal analysis, March 2025). Its nationwide provider network includes more than 1.8 million physicians and health care professionals and over 5,600 hospitals (as of March 31, 2025).
qs: How big is UnitedHealthcare's network for small business plans?
How many small business employees does UnitedHealthcare insure?

atoms.title: Surest, fully insured and level funded for small business
atoms.q: What plan types can small businesses choose from at UnitedHealthcare?
atoms.text: Small businesses can choose among three product types. Surest plans offer clear upfront copays with no deductibles or coinsurance. Fully insured plans have the insurance company manage employee claims for a fixed monthly premium and take on the financial risk. Level funded plans are based on employees' actual medical claims, so the plan could get a potential year-end surplus if claims are lower than expected.
qs: What is the difference between Surest, fully insured and level funded?
What small business health plan options does UnitedHealthcare have?

atoms.title: Surest plans for small business
atoms.q: What are Surest plans?
atoms.text: Surest plans give employees more control over their health care experience. They feature clear, upfront copays and no deductibles or coinsurance. UnitedHealthcare says the benefits are designed to be easy to understand, without shifting costs to employees.
qs: Do Surest plans have a deductible?
How do Surest copays work for small businesses?

atoms.title: What a fully insured plan is
atoms.q: What is a fully insured health plan for a small business?
atoms.text: With a fully insured plan, the insurance company manages all employee claims for a fixed monthly premium. The insurer takes on the financial risk and handles administrative tasks. UnitedHealthcare says this can help make costs more predictable and simplify operations for the employer.
qs: What does fully insured mean?
Who pays claims in a fully insured group plan?

atoms.title: No-cost programs in small business plans
atoms.q: What no-cost programs come with UnitedHealthcare small business plans?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare lists several no-cost programs and services for employees: 24/7 Virtual Visits to access health care professionals anytime, anywhere; UnitedHealthcare Rewards, which gives incentives for completing healthy actions; and the Vital Medication Program, which eliminates out-of-pocket costs for essential medications like insulin, epinephrine, glucagon, naloxone and albuterol.
qs: Does UnitedHealthcare cover insulin with no out-of-pocket cost?
What wellness perks come with small business plans?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare Small Business Store
atoms.q: What is the UnitedHealthcare Small Business Store?
atoms.text: The Small Business Store is a one-stop digital shop where a small business can research plan options, compare prices, get plan recommendations and purchase a group health plan. A team of licensed agents is available by live chat or by scheduled appointment. The store is not available in AK, HI, NV or VT, where businesses can request a quote instead.
qs: Can I buy small business health insurance online from UnitedHealthcare?
Which states don't have the Small Business Store?

atoms.title: Employers rate health benefits as important
atoms.q: How important do employers say health care benefits are?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare cites the SHRM Employee Benefits Survey (accessed April 2025) finding that 88% of employers rate health care-related benefits as extremely important or very important to their workforce. It says group health insurance can help retain and recruit talent.
qs: Do employers think health benefits matter for hiring?
What percentage of employers value health benefits?

atoms.title: Dental, vision and life add-on coverage
atoms.q: Can small businesses add dental, vision and life insurance?
atoms.text: Yes. UnitedHealthcare says small businesses can offer additional benefit options such as dental, vision and life insurance coverage alongside their health plan, to provide the tailored benefit solutions their employees want.
qs: Does UnitedHealthcare offer dental and vision for small groups?
What extra benefits can a small business add?

atoms.title: SHOP Marketplace for small employers
atoms.q: What is the SHOP Marketplace?
atoms.text: The Small Business Health Options Program (SHOP) is an online marketplace established under the Affordable Care Act. Eligible small business employers can choose coverage options for their employees, and employees can shop for group health insurance too. UnitedHealthcare offers SHOP plans.
qs: What is SHOP health insurance?
Does UnitedHealthcare offer SHOP plans?

atoms.title: Plans for businesses with more than 50 employees
atoms.q: What if my business has more than 50 employees?
atoms.text: Businesses with more than 50 employees can request a quote from UnitedHealthcare to explore group medical plans for their employees and business, plus supplemental plans for dental, vision, disability and more.
qs: Where do I get a quote for a group with over 50 employees?
What does UnitedHealthcare offer mid-size employers?

atoms.title: What a caregiver is
atoms.q: What is a caregiver?
atoms.text: A caregiver may be a family member, friend or neighbor. It is generally a person who provides unpaid assistance with activities of daily living and sometimes medical tasks, too. Every care situation is different, and caregiving may have been expected for a long time or may have come as a surprise.
qs: What does it mean to be a caregiver?
Who counts as a caregiver?

atoms.title: Informal caregiver role
atoms.q: What is an informal caregiver?
atoms.text: An informal caregiver is a non-professional who provides care voluntarily, typically a friend, partner or family member. Caregivers often help with day-to-day tasks as well as decision making and working with a formal care team.
qs: What is an informal caregiver?
What does an unpaid caregiver do?

atoms.title: Common caregiver activities
atoms.q: What tasks do caregivers help with?
atoms.text: Caregiver activities include hands-on care such as dressing, bathing, grooming, toileting, moving safely, meal prep and feeding; errands such as groceries, laundry and cleaning; health matters such as communicating with health professionals, organizing appointments and managing medications; transportation to appointments; financial and legal matters; emotional and social support; and advocacy, including learning about the condition and making care decisions.
qs: What does a family caregiver do?
What tasks are involved in caregiving?

atoms.title: Care Organizer for caregiving information
atoms.q: Is there a tool to organize caregiving information?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers a Care Organizer, available as a downloadable PDF, to help caregivers keep track of caregiving information. It helps gather important details in one place, from lists of providers and medications to home and financial information. Caregivers can also use care guides for specific health care needs.
qs: Where can I find a caregiver organizer?
How do I keep track of a loved one's medications and providers?

atoms.title: Self-care for caregivers
atoms.q: Why is self-care important for caregivers?
atoms.text: Being a caregiver can feel like a lot of responsibility, and it is natural to feel stressed or burdened. Caring for your own health and well-being is as important as other tasks. Caregiver support resources can help you understand your responsibilities and options for assistance, consider when to hire a professional in-home caregiver, balance duties with self-care, stay organized and communicate better with your loved one.
qs: How can caregivers take care of themselves?
When should I hire an in-home caregiver?

atoms.title: Caregiver support topics library
atoms.q: What caregiver support topics does UnitedHealthcare cover?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare's caregiver library includes support topics such as getting paid for the care you provide, caring for a caregiver, caregiver burnout and coping strategies, resources for new caregivers and letting go of caregiver guilt. Family caregiving topics include signs an aging parent may need help, adjusting to an elder care facility, moving an aging parent in, sharing caregiving duties as a family and communication tips.
qs: How do I know when my aging parent needs help?
How can family members share caregiving duties?

atoms.title: Caregiver support organizations and respite care
atoms.q: Where can caregivers find local support?
atoms.text: Caregivers can find programs from both national and local organizations. These resources include caregiver support groups and events, home care services, respite care, adult day centers, geriatric case managers and more.
qs: Where can I find caregiver support groups?
What is respite care?

atoms.title: Financial, legal and insurance help for caregivers
atoms.q: Where can caregivers get help with insurance and legal paperwork?
atoms.text: Many caregivers help with financial, legal and health insurance matters, such as signing someone up for Medicare, Medicaid or other health insurance. There may be paperwork and authorizations to complete before helping with more complex issues like advance care planning. UnitedHealthcare offers an advance care planning worksheet as a downloadable PDF.
qs: What is advance care planning?
How do I help a parent sign up for Medicare?

atoms.title: Can caregivers get support through insurance?
atoms.q: Can caregivers get support through the insurance of the person they care for?
atoms.text: If the person you are caring for has UnitedHealthcare insurance, several programs may help caregivers: Medicare Made Clear explains how Medicare works and what is covered; the Just Plain Clear glossary defines thousands of health care terms in plain language; the Pharmacy Locator helps Medicare members find pharmacies, with home mail delivery on some plans; and the Drug Cost Estimator helps Medicare members estimate drug costs.
qs: What tools help me manage a parent's Medicare plan?
Is there a drug cost estimator for Medicare?

atoms.title: What caregiver burnout is
atoms.q: What is caregiver burnout?
atoms.text: Caregiver burnout is a state of physical, emotional and/or mental exhaustion that can create an overall sense of stress and negativity. Caring for a loved one can be rewarding but also very stressful, and the emotions behind this stress (caregiver burden) can feel overwhelming. Negative thoughts and feelings are normal, and caregivers are encouraged to give themselves grace.
qs: What is caregiver burnout?
Is it normal to feel negative as a caregiver?

atoms.title: Common causes of caregiver burnout
atoms.q: What causes caregiver burnout?
atoms.text: Common causes include role confusion, which means separating your role as caregiver from your role as a spouse, parent or friend; unrealistic expectations, such as expecting improvement in someone with Alzheimer's or ALS; lack of control over limited time, resources and skills; unreasonable demands that you feel obligated to take on; and lack of self-awareness about reaching a breaking point.
qs: Why do caregivers burn out?
What triggers caregiver stress?

atoms.title: Signs of caregiver burnout
atoms.q: What are the signs of caregiver burnout?
atoms.text: Caregiver burnout can look like any high-stress situation. Signs to watch for include feeling overwhelmed or worried, often feeling tired, getting too much or too little sleep, gaining or losing weight, easily becoming upset, losing interest in activities you used to enjoy, often feeling sad, frequent headaches or bodily pain, and abusing alcohol or drugs, including prescription medications.
qs: How do I know if I'm burned out as a caregiver?
What are symptoms of caregiver stress?

atoms.title: Coping with caregiver emotions
atoms.q: How can caregivers cope with the emotions of caregiving?
atoms.text: Finding healthy ways to navigate the many emotions of being a caregiver supports physical and mental well-being, and when you can show up as your best self, the person you care for benefits too. UnitedHealthcare's page offers coping guidance for four emotions caregivers commonly face: anger, depression, fear and guilt.
qs: How do I cope with caregiver guilt?
What are healthy ways to handle caregiver anger?

atoms.title: Respite care for caregivers
atoms.q: What is respite care?
atoms.text: Respite care is a way to give yourself a temporary break from caregiver duties and comes in many forms. You can ask a friend or family member to care for your loved one for a few hours a day or week, or you can look into an official respite care facility. There are many options, which can make finding the right support easier than expected.
qs: What is respite care for caregivers?
How can I get a break from caregiving?

atoms.title: Who to see for help with caregiver burnout
atoms.q: Who can I see for help with caregiver burnout?
atoms.text: If you are struggling with physical or mental symptoms of caregiver burnout, schedule an appointment with your primary care provider, who can recommend healthy ways to deal with the stress. Mental health programs may also be available to help with coping. Options can include talking to a therapist, journaling, lifestyle changes or finding a way to share caregiving duties with another person.
qs: Who do I talk to about caregiver burnout?
Can a therapist help with caregiver stress?

atoms.title: Health benefits of regular exercise
atoms.q: What are the benefits of regular exercise?
atoms.text: Physical activity may help control or reduce cholesterol and blood pressure, increase flexibility, lower the risk of diabetes, stroke and cardiovascular disease, prevent bone loss, build muscle tone and strength, and increase energy levels. UnitedHealthcare notes that the physical benefits of exercise may go beyond losing weight.
qs: Why is exercise good for you?
How does exercise help blood pressure?

atoms.title: How to start a fitness plan
atoms.q: How do I start an exercise routine?
atoms.text: Making a change is more manageable when you set achievable goals that fit your lifestyle. UnitedHealthcare suggests starting small, such as 5 minutes of exercise a day and working up to 10 or 15 minutes, finding a buddy such as a friend, coworker or neighbor for support, and signing up for a rewards program that rewards you for meeting health and activity goals.
qs: How do I start working out?
How much exercise should a beginner do?

atoms.title: Rewards for meeting health and activity goals
atoms.q: Can my health plan reward me for exercising?
atoms.text: Many health insurance providers offer programs that reward you for meeting health and activity goals, which may help you stay motivated. Rewards may include things like gift cards or money toward your health savings account. If you are a UnitedHealthcare member, you can explore UnitedHealthcare's wellness and rewards programs.
qs: Does insurance reward you for working out?
What are wellness rewards programs?

atoms.title: Slow and steady weight loss
atoms.q: How fast should I lose weight?
atoms.text: According to the CDC, slow and steady wins the race: people who lose 1 to 2 pounds per week have better odds of keeping the weight off long-term. UnitedHealthcare adds that it is not about how fast you lose weight but how consistent you are with your routine and how much you modify your diet.
ents: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
qs: How many pounds a week is healthy to lose?
How do I keep weight off long term?

atoms.title: Exercise tips for boosting metabolism and burning calories
atoms.q: What exercise burns the most calories?
atoms.text: When you lift weights, your muscles burn more calories at rest than other tissues, speeding up your resting metabolism. A workout that gets your heart pumping, such as jogging, biking, speed walking or aerobic exercise, may burn the most calories per session. Strength training may be more likely to help you burn more calories as the day goes on.
qs: Does lifting weights boost metabolism?
Is cardio or strength training better for burning calories?

atoms.title: Wider benefits of healthy habits like exercise
atoms.q: What else can exercise improve besides physical health?
atoms.text: Regular physical exercise may help improve your relationships, lower your health care costs, supercharge your creativity and bring feelings of joy, because exercise releases endorphins, which can make you feel happy. UnitedHealthcare encourages adding new healthy habits to your everyday routine to experience these benefits.
qs: Does exercise improve mood?
Can exercise lower health care costs?

atoms.title: Easy ways to fit exercise into your day
atoms.q: How can I fit exercise into a busy schedule?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare suggests sneaking exercise into your day by doing squats while you brush your teeth or blow dry your hair, parking a little farther away, considering how much you stand during the day, scheduling walk breaks, and playing active games with the kids, such as chasing them around the yard or playing sports.
qs: What are easy ways to be more active?
How do I exercise with no time?

atoms.title: Staying motivated with an exercise routine
atoms.q: How do I stay motivated to exercise?
atoms.text: To keep up an exercise routine, schedule workout time on your calendar but do not be so rigid that you get discouraged when life gets in the way. Focus on putting on your shoes and getting to your destination rather than dwelling on the workout, and do not compare yourself to others since many people's fitness journeys look different. Remember why you started.
qs: How do I stick with a workout plan?
What if I miss a workout?

atoms.title: Why well-child visits matter
atoms.q: Why are well-child visits important?
atoms.text: Regular wellness checks, screenings and tests help support a child's health and track development so parents can understand how to help as the child grows. Well-child visits help keep up with fast growth to make sure it is healthy and on track. Topics include vaccines, screenings for each stage of development, and when to schedule regular preventive care visits.
qs: Why does my child need a well visit?
What happens at a well-child checkup?

atoms.title: Are child well visits covered?
atoms.q: Are child well visits covered by insurance?
atoms.text: Most health insurance plans are required to cover preventive care, which includes child well visits. As long as your child sees a network provider and the visit only covers preventive care, these visits will not cost you anything out of pocket. Most health plans cover early child well visits or provide assistance, so call the number on your insurance card for more information.
qs: Do I pay for well-child visits?
Is a pediatric checkup free with insurance?

atoms.title: Vaccines at well-child visits
atoms.q: How do vaccines work at well-child visits?
atoms.text: During a well-child visit, your child's care provider explains which vaccines your child is able to get. Vaccines may help reduce the risk of infection by working with the body's natural defenses to safely develop immunity to disease. Some vaccines, like a flu shot, may be recommended yearly, while others are recommended based on age.
qs: What vaccines does my child need?
How often does a child need a flu shot?

atoms.title: Screenings and milestones from birth to 24 months
atoms.q: What happens at well-child visits from birth to 24 months?
atoms.text: Visits in the first 2 years happen fairly often. Birth to 6 months includes hearing, vision and blood screenings, with milestones like social smile, cooing and rolling over. At 9 to 15 months, screenings add anemia and lead, and milestones include standing or walking and starting to talk. At 18 to 24 months, autism screening is added, with milestones like climbing and using a fork or spoon.
qs: What screenings does a baby get?
When is autism screening done?

atoms.title: Screenings and milestones from ages 2 to 4
atoms.q: What happens at well-child visits from ages 2 to 4?
atoms.text: Well-child visits for ages 2 to 4 follow an annual schedule. At 2 and 2 1/2 years, screenings include hearing, vision, autism or development, oral health, and anemia and tuberculosis for high-risk children. At 3 and 4 years, screenings include hearing, vision, oral health and development. Milestones include using phrases at 3 and dressing themselves and identifying emotions at 4.
qs: What screenings does a 3-year-old get?
How often should a toddler see the doctor?

atoms.title: Screenings and milestones from ages 5 to 10
atoms.q: What happens at well-child visits from ages 5 to 10?
atoms.text: At age 5, screenings include hearing, vision, oral health and development. From ages 6 through 10, screenings include hearing, vision, oral health and behavioral, social and emotional screenings. Every visit includes a physical exam, vaccines, and height, weight and BMI. Providers discuss topics such as physical activity, eating habits, safe media use, puberty and drug and alcohol awareness.
qs: What does a 7-year-old's checkup include?
When do behavioral screenings start for kids?

atoms.title: Safety topics at well visits to age 4
atoms.q: What topics do providers discuss at early well-child visits?
atoms.text: From birth to 24 months, providers discuss topics like sleep habits, hygiene, car seats, when to start solid foods, nutrition, child care, infant CPR, dental checks, child-proofing, sun protection, water safety, potty training and screen time. From ages 2 to 4, topics include school readiness, injury prevention, food security and a safe environment.
qs: What safety topics come up at baby checkups?
When should I start solid foods?

atoms.title: Preventive care checklists for children
atoms.q: Where can I find a well-visit checklist for my child?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers a child well visit checklist to help parents prepare and have a more helpful appointment. Checklists for preventive care visits are available for every age, from 1 month to adulthood. Making preventive visits part of your family's routine can set your child up for success in their own health care journey.
qs: Is there a checklist for my child's doctor visit?
What should I ask at a well-baby visit?

atoms.title: Healthy First Steps for Community Plan families
atoms.q: How does Healthy First Steps help with child well visits?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare Community Plan members may have access to the Healthy First Steps program, which can help find a care provider, schedule well-child visits and connect with educational and community resources. To get started, call 1-800-599-5985, TTY 711, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The program is only available in certain states.
qs: Who can use Healthy First Steps?
Where can Medicaid families get help scheduling well visits?

atoms.title: Help with transportation and food
atoms.q: What if I need help getting to appointments or getting food?
atoms.text: If you need help getting to an appointment, or getting formula or healthy food, call the number on your insurance card. If you are having a hard time getting food or are experiencing unemployment, your care provider may be able to connect you with resources that can help.
qs: Can my plan help with rides to appointments?
Where can I get help with baby formula?

atoms.title: 1 in 10 Americans live with diabetes
atoms.q: What does it mean to live with diabetes?
atoms.text: For the 1 in 10 Americans living with diabetes, it means managing blood sugar (glucose) levels. Glucose is the main source of energy for the body's cells, and insulin plays an important role in managing it. Whether newly diagnosed or living with diabetes for some time, careful diabetes management may make a world of difference.
qs: How common is diabetes?
What is glucose?

atoms.title: Common symptoms of diabetes
atoms.q: What are the symptoms of diabetes?
atoms.text: Symptoms include feeling thirsty or hungry, peeing more often, feeling tired, itchy skin, dry mouth, unintended weight loss, blurry vision, frequent infections, cuts that heal slowly, breath that smells like acetone or nail polish remover (a sign of ketones rising to unsafe levels), nausea and abdominal pain. Call your doctor right away if you have these symptoms.
qs: What are early signs of diabetes?
What does diabetes feel like?

atoms.title: Why diabetes symptoms need quick action
atoms.q: Why should diabetes symptoms be treated quickly?
atoms.text: Without medical intervention, a person with diabetes may suffer from damaged organs, lose consciousness and even slip into a life-threatening coma, also called diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Being able to act quickly may potentially save a person's life.
qs: What is diabetic ketoacidosis?
Can untreated diabetes be life-threatening?

atoms.title: What prediabetes is
atoms.q: What is prediabetes?
atoms.text: Prediabetes is when your blood sugar levels are high, but not high enough to be considered diabetes. If prediabetes is left unchecked, it can turn into type 2 diabetes. There are positive steps you can take to get prediabetes under control.
qs: What is prediabetes?
Can prediabetes turn into diabetes?

atoms.title: What type 1 diabetes is
atoms.q: What is type 1 diabetes?
atoms.text: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune condition in which the body mistakenly attacks and destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin. It was once known as juvenile diabetes because most people diagnosed are in elementary school or are preteens. There is no way to prevent type 1 diabetes, and symptoms may appear quickly.
qs: What causes type 1 diabetes?
Can type 1 diabetes be prevented?

atoms.title: What type 2 diabetes is
atoms.q: What is type 2 diabetes?
atoms.text: Type 2 diabetes, the most common form of diabetes, is when your body does not use insulin properly. Some people are prediabetic before becoming diabetic. It used to be known as adult-onset diabetes, but today more kids are being diagnosed, possibly because of the rise in childhood obesity. No one knows exactly what causes diabetes, but there are known risk factors.
qs: What is type 2 diabetes?
What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes?

atoms.title: Exercise and diet in managing diabetes
atoms.q: Can exercise and diet help manage or prevent diabetes?
atoms.text: When it comes to managing, delaying or preventing diabetes, exercise and diet can both play a big role. These are two areas where you have ways to help control your health. UnitedHealthcare also offers guidance on coping with a new diabetes diagnosis and on controlling diabetes with exercise.
qs: How can I prevent type 2 diabetes?
Does exercise help control diabetes?

atoms.title: What coronary heart disease is
atoms.q: What is coronary heart disease?
atoms.text: The most common type of heart disease is coronary heart disease (CHD). CHD means the arteries in the heart cannot deliver enough oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle, typically because of narrowing of the arteries from a buildup of plaque. UnitedHealthcare notes it may be possible to prevent heart disease, and small changes may stabilize or improve some of its causes.
qs: What is coronary heart disease?
What causes heart disease?

atoms.title: Heart disease can be silent
atoms.q: What are the symptoms of heart disease?
atoms.text: Coronary heart disease is sometimes silent, meaning you might not notice symptoms until a heart attack or other problem. It usually takes years to develop. As plaque narrows the arteries, it can cause chest pain, shortness of breath and neck pain when active. These often go away with rest and return with movement or stress, and any chest pain should be checked by a doctor.
qs: Can you have heart disease without symptoms?
Should I see a doctor for chest pain?

atoms.title: Common heart attack signs and when to call 911
atoms.q: What are the most common signs of a heart attack?
atoms.text: The most common sign of a heart attack for both women and men is pain or discomfort in the center of the chest. It can be mild or strong and may last several minutes, or stop and come back. The more signs you have, the more likely a heart attack is. If you think you might be having one, call 911 right away, even if you are not sure.
qs: What does a heart attack feel like?
When should I call 911 for chest pain?

atoms.title: Heart attack signs in men vs women
atoms.q: How do heart attack signs differ in men and women?
atoms.text: In men, signs include chest pain in the center or left side, pain in the arms, back, shoulders, neck, jaw or above the belly button, shortness of breath, unexplained sweating, nausea, dizziness and a rapid or irregular heartbeat. Women may not always feel chest pain and may instead have back, neck, jaw or throat pain, heartburn or indigestion, nausea, vomiting, extreme tiredness or trouble breathing. Women often have silent heart attacks.
qs: Do women have different heart attack symptoms?
What are heart attack symptoms in men?

atoms.title: Types of heart disease
atoms.q: What are the different types of heart disease?
atoms.text: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is an umbrella term for different conditions. Coronary heart disease (CHD, or coronary artery disease) is the most common and can cause narrowed arteries, blood clots and blockages that lead to heart attack or stroke. Heart failure means the heart is not pumping blood as well as it should. Arrhythmia is a problem with the rate or rhythm of the heartbeat. The page also describes heart valve problems that can affect circulation.
qs: What is heart failure?
What is an arrhythmia?
What is cardiovascular disease?

atoms.title: Health-related risk factors for heart disease
atoms.q: What increases the risk of heart disease?
atoms.text: Risk factors include age (higher risk for women over 55 and men over 45), family history of early heart disease, history of preeclampsia, high cholesterol or high blood pressure, kidney disease, diabetes, HIV/AIDS, sleep disorders, depression, anxiety and PTSD, and lifestyle habits such as heavy drinking, smoking, inactivity or unhealthy eating. Some racial and ethnic groups are more likely to get heart disease.
qs: What are the risk factors for heart disease?
Does age affect heart disease risk?

atoms.title: Social and workplace risk factors for heart disease
atoms.q: Can work and environment affect heart disease risk?
atoms.text: Social, environmental and workplace factors can raise heart disease risk. These include stressors from social drivers of health such as education, economic instability and limited access to health care; indoor or outdoor air pollution, including wildfire smoke; working long hours or night shifts; exposure to toxins, radiation or secondhand smoke at work; and experiencing racism, violence or harassment on the job.
qs: Does shift work raise heart disease risk?
How do social factors affect heart health?

atoms.title: Heart disease facts
atoms.q: How common and deadly is heart disease?
atoms.text: Heart diseases are the leading cause of death for both women and men. Heart disease claims an estimated 17.9 million lives worldwide each year. It may lead to potentially deadly health problems like a heart attack or stroke.
qs: What is the leading cause of death?
How many people die from heart disease?

atoms.title: Questions to ask your doctor about heart disease
atoms.q: What should I ask my doctor about heart disease?
atoms.text: Sample questions include: What should my blood pressure be and how often should it be checked? What should my cholesterol and triglyceride levels be? What should my blood sugar level be? What other screening tests do I need? What is a healthy weight and waist measurement for me? What lifestyle changes would you suggest? How often should I see you for a wellness checkup?
qs: What should I ask my doctor about my heart?
What heart screening tests do I need?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare heart disease management programs
atoms.q: Does UnitedHealthcare offer heart disease management programs?
atoms.text: For eligible members, UnitedHealthcare provides several heart disease management programs for conditions including coronary artery disease, heart failure disease and congenital heart disease. If you think you might be eligible, call the number on your health plan ID card and talk with a representative.
qs: Is there a heart disease program through my plan?
How do I find out if I'm eligible for a disease management program?

atoms.title: What prenatal care is
atoms.q: What is prenatal care?
atoms.text: Prenatal care is the care you receive while you are pregnant. If you think you could be pregnant, schedule a doctor's appointment for early prenatal care, which is a good way to start on a path to a healthy pregnancy. UnitedHealthcare provides resources for every stage of pregnancy, from prenatal care to postpartum support.
qs: What is prenatal care?
When should I see a doctor if I think I'm pregnant?

atoms.title: Prenatal appointment schedule
atoms.q: How often are prenatal appointments?
atoms.text: Prenatal appointments typically start at 8 weeks. For most pregnancies, you will see your doctor every 4 weeks. UnitedHealthcare offers a video series to give an idea of what to expect at each appointment, and a downloadable Prenatal Visit Checklist with what to bring and helpful questions to ask.
qs: When do prenatal visits start?
How often do you see a doctor when pregnant?

atoms.title: What a doula is
atoms.q: What is a doula?
atoms.text: A doula is a person who has a lot of knowledge and training related to birthing. A doula can help you access trusted information and understand your options to support pregnancy. UnitedHealthcare offers information about the benefits of a doula, standards for doula care and how to find a doula.
qs: What does a doula do?
How do I find a doula?

atoms.title: High-risk pregnancy
atoms.q: What is a high-risk pregnancy?
atoms.text: A high-risk pregnancy means you and/or your baby are at risk of complications. UnitedHealthcare offers resources to help you understand risk factors, learn ways to manage a high-risk pregnancy, and find out what to expect if your baby needs to spend time in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).
qs: What makes a pregnancy high risk?
What happens if my baby needs the NICU?

atoms.title: Nutrition and exercise during pregnancy
atoms.q: How do nutrition and exercise matter during pregnancy?
atoms.text: During pregnancy, healthy choices can make a difference. Eating a balanced diet and keeping up with a steady level of exercise are two ways to help support your baby's growth and development. UnitedHealthcare offers a healthy pregnancy quiz as a quick way to check what you know and pick up new tips.
qs: What should I eat when pregnant?
Can I exercise during pregnancy?

atoms.title: Maternity support for individual and employer members
atoms.q: What maternity support does UnitedHealthcare offer?
atoms.text: Individual and employer members can find resources to support them throughout pregnancy and after they give birth. Members can watch maternity video courses to learn what to expect during each trimester, plus get tips on breastfeeding and more. To find out what a plan covers, sign in to your member account.
qs: Does my plan offer maternity support?
Are there pregnancy classes through UnitedHealthcare?

atoms.title: Healthy First Steps rewards for Community Plan members
atoms.q: What is Healthy First Steps?
atoms.text: Healthy First Steps is a program for UnitedHealthcare Community Plan members. Members may be eligible to earn rewards for prenatal, postpartum and children's wellness appointments. To learn more, call 1-800-599-5985, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. local time, or sign in to your plan account.
qs: How do I earn rewards for prenatal visits?
What is the Healthy First Steps phone number?

atoms.title: Wellhop for Mom & Baby
atoms.q: What is Wellhop for Mom & Baby?
atoms.text: In participating states, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan members can join the Wellhop for Mom & Baby program. Members meet online with other expectant moms for group video conversations every other week.
qs: Is there an online group for expecting moms?
What is Wellhop?

atoms.title: Postpartum care and recovery
atoms.q: What is the postpartum period?
atoms.text: After you give birth, you enter the postpartum period, also called the fourth trimester. Many changes happen during this time for you and your newborn. UnitedHealthcare offers information on common postpartum concerns and conditions, including postpartum depression, and on caring for yourself during recovery.
qs: What is the fourth trimester?
What is postpartum recovery like?

atoms.title: Managing depression and anxiety around pregnancy
atoms.q: When should I seek help for feelings after having a baby?
atoms.text: A new baby brings all kinds of emotions, and it is normal to feel stressed, anxious or experience the baby blues. But when these feelings become constant or overwhelming, it may be time to seek help. UnitedHealthcare offers information on the signs to watch for and how to get support before and after pregnancy.
qs: Is it normal to feel anxious after having a baby?
What are the baby blues?

atoms.title: Federal and state help preparing for baby
atoms.q: Where can I get help with supplies for a new baby?
atoms.text: Expecting moms may feel both excitement and stress when preparing for a baby's arrival. Federal and state programs may be able to help you get the support and supplies you need for your new baby. UnitedHealthcare's pregnancy resources are aimed at women who become moms through pregnancy, and the page also acknowledges motherhood through foster parenting or adoption.
qs: How do I get help for baby supplies?
Are there programs for new moms?

atoms.title: Nearly 35 percent of adults sleep too little
atoms.q: How many adults get less than 7 hours of sleep?
atoms.text: Nearly 35 percent of adults get less than the recommended 7 or more hours of sleep per night. UnitedHealthcare notes that sleep affects every aspect of waking life and is essential to overall well-being, and encourages people to seek help if they are not getting a good night's rest.
qs: How many hours of sleep do adults need?
Is 5 or 6 hours of sleep enough?

atoms.title: Short-term and long-term effects of poor sleep
atoms.q: What happens when you do not get enough sleep?
atoms.text: In the short term, poor sleep may result in loss of attention span, poor decision-making, fatigue and irritability. The long-term implications include an increased risk for obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and stroke, and depression.
qs: What are the health risks of not sleeping enough?
Does lack of sleep cause heart disease?

atoms.title: Why get 7-9 hours of sleep
atoms.q: Why should I get 7 to 9 hours of sleep?
atoms.text: Getting 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night helps maintain brain function, helps reduce your risk for disease, helps improve daytime performance and safety, and helps improve your emotional health.
qs: What are the benefits of 7 to 9 hours of sleep?
How much sleep is recommended?

atoms.title: Power down screens before bed
atoms.q: How do screens affect sleep?
atoms.text: Blue light from screens can disrupt your circadian rhythm and affect your ability to sleep. UnitedHealthcare suggests turning off mobile devices at least 30 minutes before you go to bed to help your body recharge.
qs: Should I stop using my phone before bed?
Does blue light affect sleep?

atoms.title: Keep a regular sleep schedule and bedroom
atoms.q: How can I make my sleep routine and bedroom better?
atoms.text: Try going to bed and waking up around the same time every day, even on weekends. Make your bedroom all about sleep: a comfortable mattress, pillow and bedding help, and the room should be dark, cool and quiet. You might consider using white noise to mask startling sounds.
qs: How do I set up my bedroom for better sleep?
Should I keep the same bedtime on weekends?

atoms.title: Caffeine and alcohol affect sleep
atoms.q: Should I avoid caffeine and alcohol before bed?
atoms.text: Because caffeine is a stimulant, it may disrupt sleep, so UnitedHealthcare advises avoiding caffeine after lunch. Also avoid alcohol before bed: even though alcohol might make you feel sleepy, it can disrupt sleep later in the night.
qs: When should I stop drinking coffee for better sleep?
Does alcohol help you sleep?

atoms.title: What to do if you cannot fall asleep
atoms.q: What should I do if I'm still awake after 20 minutes?
atoms.text: If you do not fall asleep within 20 minutes or so, get up and go into another room. Do something relaxing, such as reading or listening to soft music, until you feel tired.
qs: What should I do when I can't fall asleep?
How long should I lie in bed before getting up?

atoms.title: Questions to ask your doctor about sleep problems
atoms.q: What should I ask my doctor about sleep problems?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare suggests asking: Would it help to keep a sleep diary and what should I track? Are there lifestyle changes that could help me sleep better? What are the benefits and risks of prescription and over-the-counter sleep aids? Would a sleep study in a sleep lab be beneficial? Talk with your doctor before taking any sleep remedy, including herbal or natural products.
qs: Do I need a sleep study?
What should I ask a doctor about insomnia?

atoms.title: What an anxiety disorder is
atoms.q: What is an anxiety disorder?
atoms.text: An anxiety disorder is defined as having racing thoughts or feelings paralyzed by fear, or when thoughts feel out of control. Anxiety may at times be a healthy emotion that alerts you to pay better attention to your mental health, but when intrusive what-if worries start to affect daily life, you may have an anxiety disorder. More than 40 million adults in the United States are affected.
qs: What is an anxiety disorder?
When does anxiety become a disorder?
How common are anxiety disorders?

atoms.title: What causes anxiety
atoms.q: What causes anxiety?
atoms.text: The exact cause of anxiety is unknown, but research points to genetic factors and negative events or stressful life experiences playing a role. Some health conditions or medication side effects may also produce or aggravate symptoms. Anxiety can happen as a reaction to relationships, health, school, work, finances, unexpected changes or big life events.
qs: What triggers anxiety?
Can medications cause anxiety?

atoms.title: Signs and symptoms of an anxiety disorder
atoms.q: What are the symptoms of an anxiety disorder?
atoms.text: Signs and symptoms of an anxiety disorder may include thoughts that won't go away, a hard time focusing, avoiding situations out of worry, using alcohol, drugs or tobacco to cope, eating more or less than usual, a sense of danger or doom, feeling nervous, restless, weak or fatigued, increased heart rate, fast breathing, headaches, muscle pain, trouble sleeping, stomach pain, and dizziness.
qs: What are signs of anxiety?
What does an anxiety disorder feel like?

atoms.title: When to seek professional help for anxiety
atoms.q: When should I seek professional help for anxiety?
atoms.text: If you are experiencing the signs of anxiety listed, it may be time to get help; finding a mental health provider is an important first step. You may also consider mental health virtual therapy with a psychologist, counselor or coach at a time and place that is convenient. If you or a loved one has suicidal thoughts or plans, call 911 right away or call or chat the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
qs: When should I see a therapist for anxiety?
Can I do therapy online for anxiety?

atoms.title: Untreated anxiety can worsen but is treatable
atoms.q: Will anxiety go away on its own?
atoms.text: It is not uncommon for people struggling with anxiety to hope it will go away on its own, but if left untreated, symptoms may get much worse. With the right combination of therapy, stress management and medication, anxiety is considered treatable.
qs: Is anxiety treatable?
What treats anxiety?

atoms.title: Ways to help reduce anxiety
atoms.q: What are some ways to reduce anxiety?
atoms.text: Ways to help reduce anxiety include stopping what you are doing and breathing in and out slowly, eating well-balanced meals, getting enough sleep, focusing on what you can change, exercising, limiting alcohol and caffeine, and reframing negative thoughts. You can also bring yourself back to the moment with something tangible, like holding an ice cube, or redirect your energy by going for a walk.
qs: How can I calm anxiety?
What are quick coping techniques for anxiety?

atoms.title: Types of anxiety disorders
atoms.q: What are the different types of anxiety disorders?
atoms.text: Different types of anxiety disorders exist, and knowing which type you may be dealing with can help you understand how to cope and seek help. UnitedHealthcare lists generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder (social phobia), panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and phobias.
qs: What kinds of anxiety disorders are there?
What is the difference between panic disorder and GAD?

atoms.title: 988 Lifeline for suicidal thoughts
atoms.q: Who do I call if I or a loved one has suicidal thoughts?
atoms.text: If you or a loved one has suicidal thoughts or plans, call 911 right away. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is also available 24/7, providing confidential support and prevention and crisis resources. Call 988 or chat online at 988lifeline.org/chat. TTY users can use their preferred relay service or dial 711 and then 988.
qs: What is the 988 lifeline?
How do I get crisis help?

atoms.title: Opening up about depression
atoms.q: Why is it important to talk openly about depression?
atoms.text: Depression may feel like something you want to hide, but giving your mental health proper care and attention may be a healthy path toward feeling better. Being honest with yourself about how you feel can help you navigate true depression or certain days when you feel down. Open conversations may help decrease the stigma around depression and encourage more people to speak up.
qs: Why is it hard to talk about depression?
How do I start talking about depression?

atoms.title: Major depression vs persistent depressive disorder
atoms.q: What are the two most common forms of depression?
atoms.text: According to the National Institute of Mental Health, the two most common forms are major depression and persistent depressive disorder. Major depression means having symptoms most of the day, every day, for at least 2 weeks, and it can happen once or several times in a lifetime. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) involves symptoms lasting typically at least two years, with less severe symptoms like low energy or poor concentration.
qs: What is major depression?
What is dysthymia?
How long do depression symptoms last?

atoms.title: Depression tied to life events or seasons
atoms.q: What other forms of depression are there?
atoms.text: Other forms of depression develop under specific circumstances. Perinatal depression is major depression during pregnancy or after the baby is born (postpartum depression). Seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, happens when the seasons change, especially when daylight hours are short. Depression with symptoms of psychosis is a severe form in which a person experiences delusions or hallucinations.
qs: What is perinatal depression?
What is seasonal affective disorder?

atoms.title: Signs and symptoms of depression
atoms.q: What are the signs and symptoms of depression?
atoms.text: Common signs include feeling sad, anxious or empty; loss of interest in favorite activities; overeating or not wanting to eat; difficulty sleeping or sleeping too much; feeling very tired; aches, pains, headaches, cramps or digestive problems that do not improve with treatment; and thoughts of death or suicide. Symptoms may need to be present most of the day, every day, for at least 2 weeks. Talk with your doctor or call the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357.
qs: What are the symptoms of depression?
How do I know if I am depressed?

atoms.title: Everyday ideas that may help with depression
atoms.q: What can I do to help with depression?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare suggests being around people you love, staying active because exercise releases endorphins, eating for a better mood, meditating, spending time with animals, and talking to a therapist. Therapy can be a way to proactively manage stress and mental well-being. Apps like Talkspace offer 24/7 access to therapists, and members can check what mental health resources their plan offers.
qs: What helps with depression naturally?
Does exercise help depression?

atoms.title: What kind of doctor to see for depression
atoms.q: What kind of doctor should I see for depression?
atoms.text: Natural remedies may work well for some people, but others may need medical treatment for depression and anxiety. It may help to choose a mental health provider who specializes in depression. You might also consider virtual therapy through Mind Your Health provided by Teladoc Health, which lets you meet at a time and place that is convenient, or use mental health resources offered through your UnitedHealthcare benefit plan.
qs: Who treats depression?
Should I see a therapist or psychiatrist for depression?

atoms.title: Crisis and emergency care hotlines
atoms.q: What hotlines are available for mental health crises?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare lists four hotlines: the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) for emotional distress or suicidal thoughts; emergency services (call 911) for immediate life-threatening needs; the Substance Use Helpline (1-855-780-5955, TTY 711) for alcohol and drug concerns; and the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-SAFE (7233) or text START to 88788).
qs: What is the number for the substance use helpline?
What hotlines help in a mental health crisis?

atoms.title: What preventive care is
atoms.q: What is preventive care?
atoms.text: Preventive care is routine health care that helps you stay on top of your health and catch anything before it becomes serious. UnitedHealthcare compares preventive care appointments to car maintenance, such as regular oil checks and brake inspections. Eating whole, nutritious foods, staying active, limiting alcohol, managing stress and getting routine checkups are all part of preventive care.
qs: What is preventive care?
Why do I need routine checkups?

atoms.title: How preventive care is covered
atoms.q: How is preventive care covered by health insurance?
atoms.text: Most health plans cover eligible preventive care services at 100% with $0 out-of-pocket costs when you see a network provider. Certain preventive items and services, including immunizations, are provided with no cost-sharing as specified by applicable law, including the Affordable Care Act and state law. Some plans may require copayments, coinsurance or deductibles for other routine services, so review your plan documents.
ents: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
qs: Is preventive care free with insurance?
Do I pay anything for an annual physical?
Does the ACA cover preventive services?

atoms.title: What counts as preventive care
atoms.q: What services are considered preventive care?
atoms.text: Preventive care includes the services you get as part of a routine well exam: your annual physical exam, vaccines, well-baby and well-child care, and recommended tests and screenings at certain ages for breast cancer (mammogram), colon cancer, prostate cancer, lung cancer and cervical cancer (pelvic exam and Pap smear). It also covers other screenings, such as for osteoporosis and diabetes, and preventive OB/GYN care.
qs: Which screenings are preventive?
Are vaccines preventive care?

atoms.title: What is not considered preventive care
atoms.q: What is not considered preventive care?
atoms.text: Certain tests and screenings are not always considered preventive care. Diagnostic care, bloodwork and sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing may or may not be considered preventive, and specialist visits are listed separately. Ask your doctor which tests are considered preventive, such as cholesterol and blood glucose, and which you may have to pay for out of pocket, such as a thyroid panel.
qs: Is bloodwork covered as preventive care?
What is the difference between preventive and diagnostic care?

atoms.title: Why annual wellness visits matter
atoms.q: Why is a yearly preventive care visit important?
atoms.text: During an annual exam, a primary care provider (PCP) can focus on keeping you healthy and catching illnesses earlier, before they become larger problems. A PCP may ask about your medicines and other providers, order tests based on family or health history, check whether you are up to date on shots, and talk about diet and physical activity, which help prevent chronic conditions like diabetes and heart disease.
qs: Why see a doctor every year?
What does a PCP check during a yearly visit?

atoms.title: What to expect at a preventive care exam
atoms.q: What happens during a physical exam?
atoms.text: Each visit looks a little different, but a typical preventive exam includes: 1) height, weight and body mass index (BMI) assessment; 2) heart rate check and heart exam; 3) blood pressure test; 4) lab work; 5) lung exam; 6) cancer screenings based on age and risk factors; and 7) vaccines, with some, like the flu shot, recommended annually.
qs: What is in a physical exam?
What tests are done at an annual checkup?

atoms.title: Key health numbers: heart rate and blood pressure
atoms.q: What is a healthy resting heart rate and normal blood pressure?
atoms.text: A healthy resting heart rate for adults is typically between 60 and 100 beats per minute (bpm). Normal blood pressure is considered 120/80 mm Hg or less. UnitedHealthcare notes it is important to know your numbers, including body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose, so you can keep them in check.
qs: What is a normal blood pressure?
What is a healthy resting heart rate?

atoms.title: How to prepare for a preventive care visit
atoms.q: What should I bring to my annual checkup?
atoms.text: To make the most of your checkup, bring: a list of your medications, including over-the-counter products, prescriptions, vitamins and supplements; your personal and family health history; your questions, concerns and any symptoms; and, if helpful, a family member or friend to help catch the details. Jot down important information and ask your doctor for a copy of your appointment notes.
qs: What do I bring to a physical?
How do I prepare for my doctor's appointment?

atoms.title: Questions to ask your PCP about screenings
atoms.q: What screening questions should I ask my doctor?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare suggests asking your PCP when to be screened for cervical cancer and colorectal cancer, including the benefits and risks of different tests; whether to be tested for sexually transmitted infections or screened for prostate cancer; how often to check cholesterol and blood pressure and what your numbers should be; how often to screen for diabetes; whether you need a bone density test; and what other screenings are recommended.
qs: What screenings should I ask my doctor about?
When should I get a colon cancer screening?

atoms.title: Where to get a preventive exam
atoms.q: Where can I get a physical exam?
atoms.text: Typically you see your primary care provider (PCP) for your annual checkup. You can see any provider you would like as long as they are in your plan's network; otherwise you may pay out of pocket for the preventive care visit. Members can use UnitedHealthcare's provider search to find a doctor and make an appointment.
qs: Where can I go for my annual physical?
Can I see any doctor for a preventive visit?

atoms.title: Preventive care checklist by age and gender
atoms.q: Is there a checklist of screenings for my age?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers an online preventive care checklist. You enter your age (in years or months), gender identity, sex assigned at birth and pregnancy status to see a checklist of common tests and screenings for your age and gender. It can help you know what to expect at your appointment.
qs: Where can I get a list of screenings by age?
What tests do I need at my age?

atoms.title: Plans for every stage of life
atoms.q: What types of plans does UnitedHealthcare offer?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare's homepage invites visitors to shop plans for every stage of life in four categories: Medicare, Medicaid, Individual & family, and Employers. Visitors can use the Shop for a plan option to find a plan, or sign in as a member to view their benefits. UnitedHealthcare describes its plans as made to deliver what matters, from quality coverage to caring support.
qs: What kinds of health plans does UnitedHealthcare sell?
Where do I shop for a UnitedHealthcare plan?

atoms.title: Four categories of UnitedHealthcare plans
atoms.q: How do UnitedHealthcare's plan categories differ?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare groups its coverage into four categories. Health insurance plans are individual and family options, including ACA Marketplace plans. Medicare plans offer coverage that goes beyond Original Medicare, including Medicare Advantage plans. Medicaid plans are for people with low income or who qualify due to a special circumstance. Dental, vision and supplemental plans can help with medical costs not covered by a medical plan.
qs: What is the difference between individual, Medicare and Medicaid plans?
What do supplemental plans cover?
Which UnitedHealthcare plan is for people with low income?

atoms.title: Members can sign in or use the app
atoms.q: How can UnitedHealthcare members manage their plan online?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare members can sign in to their account to view plan benefits. The UnitedHealthcare app gives members instant access to manage health plan details, request member ID cards, find care and more.
qs: How do I get my UnitedHealthcare member ID card?
What can I do in the UnitedHealthcare app?

atoms.title: Wellness and rewards programs
atoms.q: Does UnitedHealthcare offer wellness or rewards programs?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers wellness and rewards programs for people who want to invest in their health and find motivation and support. The homepage says members may earn rewards for meeting health goals, and it links to a page where visitors can explore these wellness and rewards programs.
qs: Can I earn rewards for healthy habits with my health plan?
What wellness programs does UnitedHealthcare have?

atoms.title: Where to learn health insurance basics
atoms.q: Where can I learn the basics of health insurance?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare's homepage answers common health insurance questions by linking to dedicated guides: what health insurance is, how it works, how to get it through open enrollment, the different types of health insurance, how much it costs, and what it covers, starting with how to review a Summary of Benefits and Coverage. It also links to a broader health insurance learning hub and to an article on how the health system works.
qs: What is health insurance and how does it work?
How do I get health insurance?
How much does health insurance cost?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare's care-first approach
atoms.q: What does UnitedHealthcare say it stands for?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says it puts care at the heart of health insurance, guided by empathy, transparency and human connection. It states that better care comes from understanding what people need and making quality care more personal, and it describes itself as a healthcare partner people can rely on.
qs: What is UnitedHealthcare's mission?
What values guide UnitedHealthcare?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare individual and family plan options
atoms.q: What individual and family health insurance plans does UnitedHealthcare offer?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers individual and family health insurance plans for people under age 65, including short term plans and Individual and Family ACA Marketplace plans. The page also points to coverage for self-employed people, students and people who get plans through work, and lets shoppers enter a ZIP code to see plans available near them.
qs: What health insurance plans can I buy for myself and my family?
Does UnitedHealthcare sell individual health insurance?

atoms.title: What are UnitedHealthcare short term plans?
atoms.q: What is a short term limited duration health plan?
atoms.text: Short term limited duration insurance plans are a way to get fast, flexible coverage if you temporarily don't have coverage and want to assure you have benefits you need. TriTerm Medical plans, a type of short term insurance, offer coverage for nearly 3 years in select states.
qs: What is short term health insurance?
How long does TriTerm Medical coverage last?

atoms.title: Short term plan limitations and underwriting
atoms.q: Do short term plans have to follow Affordable Care Act rules?
atoms.text: Short term plans are medically underwritten and are not required to comply with certain federal market requirements for health insurance, principally those in the Affordable Care Act. A policy may have exclusions or limitations for preexisting conditions or benefits such as hospitalization, emergency services, maternity care, preventive care, prescription drugs, and mental health and substance use disorder services, and may have lifetime or annual dollar limits. Short term coverage is not Minimum Essential coverage as defined in the ACA.
qs: Are short term health plans ACA compliant?
Do short term plans cover preexisting conditions?
Is short term insurance minimum essential coverage?

atoms.title: Short term plans versus ACA Marketplace plans
atoms.q: What is the difference between short term plans and ACA plans?
atoms.text: Short term plans can help bridge a gap in coverage, such as between jobs or while waiting for other coverage to start, and offer limited coverage from one month up to nearly 1 year depending on state. TriTerm Medical offers limited coverage for nearly 3 years in select states. ACA plans are sold on the health care Marketplace (also called the Exchange), may qualify for government subsidies depending on income, and offer comprehensive coverage for a full calendar year as long as you pay your premium.
qs: Short term vs ACA plan: which is better?
How long do short term and ACA plans last?
Can I get a subsidy for a short term plan?

atoms.title: Who should consider short term or ACA plans
atoms.q: Should I choose a short term plan or an ACA plan?
atoms.text: Consider a short term plan if you missed open enrollment and don't qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, have a gap until your ACA plan starts, want coverage until you join Medicare, turned 26 and are coming off a parent's plan, are in between jobs or waiting for benefits to start, or are healthy and under 65. Consider an ACA plan if you can't get health insurance through work, need long-term coverage for you and your family, want comprehensive benefits, or qualify for a premium tax credit.
qs: When should I pick a short term plan instead of an ACA plan?
What do I do if I missed open enrollment?
I turned 26 and lost my parent's coverage, what are my options?

atoms.title: Help choosing a plan and contact numbers
atoms.q: How can I get help finding an individual or family plan?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare lists 1-844-635-2495 for questions about short term plans and 1-877-853-1760, TTY 711 for questions about Individual and Family ACA Marketplace plans. A 'Find my plan' tool asks a few questions to show which insurance options may be available for you, and a ZIP code search shows plans in your state.
qs: What number do I call about ACA plans?
How do I find a plan available in my area?

atoms.title: Other individual and family coverage paths
atoms.q: What coverage is available for self-employed people, students or workers?
atoms.text: Beyond short term and ACA plans, UnitedHealthcare lists self-employed plans for people with no employees, student plans designed for students while they're in school, and plans offered by employers. Current members can sign in and find member resources.
qs: Does UnitedHealthcare have plans for the self-employed?
Is there health insurance for college students?

atoms.title: Supplemental plans to boost coverage
atoms.q: What supplemental plans can I add to my health insurance?
atoms.text: Supplemental plans can help you get coverage for care and services not included with your medical insurance plan. UnitedHealthcare lists dental plans for screenings and preventive care, vision plans for routine eye exams, prescription glasses and contact lenses, fixed benefit health plans, and add-on cash-benefit coverage such as Accident or Critical illness. Combining plans may boost coverage and potentially save money compared to buying plans individually.
qs: What extra coverage can I add to my medical plan?
Can I bundle dental and vision with health insurance?

atoms.title: What are fixed benefit health plans?
atoms.q: What is a fixed benefit health plan?
atoms.text: Fixed benefit health plans are plans that pay you or your provider a preset amount for specific, covered medical services. UnitedHealthcare lists them among its supplemental options for individuals and families.
qs: What does a fixed benefit plan pay?
How are fixed benefit plans different from major medical insurance?

atoms.title: Medicare, Medicaid and employer plan alternatives
atoms.q: Where do I go if I am 65 or older or need Medicaid?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare points people to other coverage areas from the individual and family page. Medicare offers plans for people 65 or older, or under 65 who may qualify because of a disability or special condition. Medicaid offers low cost or no-cost plans or Dual Special Needs plans (D-SNP).
