atoms.title: Choosing between Bronze, Silver and Gold
atoms.q: Which metal level is right for me?
atoms.text: Bronze plans suit people who rarely see a doctor: low monthly premium, typically the highest annual deductible, and help with worst-case scenarios like serious illness or injury. Silver plans suit people who typically see their provider for routine preventive care: a slightly higher premium than Bronze, more coverage, and possible cost-sharing reduction savings. Gold plans suit people who see their doctor often: a higher monthly premium but lower costs when you get care.
tags: how often you see a doctor
qs: Should I pick Bronze or Silver?
Which metal level is best if I see my doctor often?

atoms.title: Who an ACA Marketplace plan may fit
atoms.q: Is an ACA Marketplace plan a good fit for me?
atoms.text: A UnitedHealthcare Individual & Family ACA Marketplace plan could be a good fit if you're new to buying your own health insurance, don't get or don't want insurance through your employer, are self-employed, aren't eligible for Medicare or Medicaid, or have an employer that offers reimbursement to help cover the cost of a health plan you purchase.
qs: Who should buy an ACA plan?
Can self-employed people use the Marketplace?

atoms.title: What is the premium tax credit?
atoms.q: How does the ACA premium tax credit work?
atoms.text: The premium tax credit is a subsidy that lowers your monthly premium. Generally, the lower your household income, the larger your tax credit. If you qualify, you can use some or all of it to help pay your premium, which can result in a low or $0 monthly cost. It is available for Bronze, Silver and Gold plans, and the credit is sent directly to your insurance company.
qs: How is my ACA tax credit calculated?
Does the tax credit work on Bronze plans?

atoms.title: What is a cost-sharing reduction (CSR)?
atoms.q: What is a cost-sharing reduction on an ACA plan?
atoms.text: A cost-sharing reduction (CSR) is extra savings on top of the premium tax credit, if you qualify. With a CSR you pay less than you normally would for covered health benefits. Available only on Silver plans, the discounts lower out-of-pocket costs like copays, coinsurance and deductibles, and you qualify based on your income level.
qs: What is CSR in health insurance?
Which plans offer cost-sharing reductions?

atoms.title: ICHRA and QSEHRA employer reimbursement
atoms.q: What are ICHRA and QSEHRA employer reimbursements?
atoms.text: Some employers offer reimbursement arrangements so employees can buy coverage on their own through the ACA Marketplace instead of employer group health insurance. There are 2 types: Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement (ICHRA) and Qualified Small Employer Health Reimbursement Arrangement (QSEHRA). Employers reimburse some or all of the premiums employees pay for health insurance they purchase on their own.
qs: What is an ICHRA?
What is the difference between ICHRA and QSEHRA?

atoms.title: Reimbursement arrangements and subsidy eligibility
atoms.q: Can I get subsidies if my employer offers ICHRA or QSEHRA?
atoms.text: Typically, if you get an ACA Marketplace health plan with a reimbursement arrangement like ICHRA or QSEHRA, you won't qualify for subsidies. Because you won't qualify for subsidies, you'll need to shop for an off-exchange ACA plan.
qs: Do I need an off-exchange plan with an ICHRA?
Can I get a premium tax credit and an ICHRA?

atoms.title: What is a CHOICE Arrangement?
atoms.q: What is a CHOICE Arrangement for health insurance?
atoms.text: CHOICE Arrangement stands for Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense Arrangement, formerly known as ICHRA. It is a health benefit some employers offer that helps pay for some or all of an individual health insurance plan. The employee enrolls in an individual health plan that fits their needs, and the employer sets a monthly allowance to pay or reimburse the employee's plan premium.
qs: What does CHOICE Arrangement stand for?
Is a CHOICE Arrangement the same as an ICHRA?

atoms.title: Benefits of a CHOICE Arrangement
atoms.q: What are the benefits of a CHOICE Arrangement?
atoms.text: A CHOICE Arrangement gives you the flexibility to choose a plan that fits your coverage needs and budget, and many plans offer broad provider networks that may cover the doctors and specialists you prefer. Other benefits include tax-advantaged contributions (you don't pay income tax on contributions from your employer) and a policy that stays with you, so you can keep your plan even if you leave your job.
qs: Can I keep my plan if I leave my job with a CHOICE Arrangement?
Are employer contributions to a CHOICE Arrangement taxable?

atoms.title: How a CHOICE Arrangement works in five steps
atoms.q: How does a CHOICE Arrangement work?
atoms.text: 1) Your employer sets a monthly allowance amount toward your individual plan. 2) You consider the type of ACA plan you want, shopping and enrolling in an off-exchange ACA individual plan. 3) You shop for an individual health plan. 4) You enroll in coverage, which must be a qualified ACA-compliant plan. 5) Your employer reimburses you; the allowance may be applied through payroll deductions, or you may pay premiums directly and submit qualified expenses for reimbursement.
qs: What are the steps to use a CHOICE Arrangement?
How do I get reimbursed under a CHOICE Arrangement?

atoms.title: Why CHOICE Arrangement shoppers use off-exchange plans
atoms.q: Can I use federal subsidies with a CHOICE Arrangement?
atoms.text: You'll shop and enroll in an off-exchange ACA individual plan because if your employer provides a CHOICE Arrangement contribution toward your health plan, you can't also receive federal premium subsidies for the same coverage.
qs: Why is an off-exchange plan required with a CHOICE Arrangement?
Do I qualify for a premium tax credit with an employer allowance?

atoms.title: Where to shop with a CHOICE Arrangement
atoms.q: Where can I shop for a plan with a CHOICE Arrangement?
atoms.text: Depending on your employer, you may be able to shop for a health care plan through a private enrollment experience through a CHOICE Arrangement administrator, a licensed insurance broker, or directly with an insurance carrier like UnitedHealthcare. Whichever route you take, your coverage must be a qualified ACA-compliant plan.
qs: Can I buy a CHOICE Arrangement plan directly from UnitedHealthcare?
Do I need a broker for a CHOICE Arrangement?

atoms.title: Cost of a plan with a CHOICE Arrangement
atoms.q: How much does a plan with a CHOICE Arrangement cost?
atoms.text: If your plan's premium is less than your employer's monthly allowance, your employer may reimburse the full cost. If the premium is more than your allowance, you typically pay the difference. Keeping this in mind can help you pick a plan that balances your coverage and budget needs.
qs: What if my premium is higher than my employer allowance?
Will my employer pay my whole premium?

atoms.title: How CHOICE Arrangement reimbursement is paid
atoms.q: How do I pay premiums with a CHOICE Arrangement?
atoms.text: After you've enrolled, your employer allowance helps pay for the cost of the plan. This may happen through payroll deductions, or you may have to pay premiums directly to your insurance company. If you pay your insurance company directly, you'll need to submit qualified expenses to your employer or CHOICE Arrangement administrator for reimbursement.
qs: Do I pay my premium myself with a CHOICE Arrangement?
How do I submit expenses for reimbursement?

atoms.title: How many Americans get coverage through work
atoms.q: How many Americans get health insurance through their employer?
atoms.text: Around 49% of Americans get health insurance coverage through their employers, which is nearly 157 million people, according to a January 2021 figure cited on the page. Employer-sponsored health plans play a big role in benefits packages.
qs: What percent of people have employer health insurance?
How many people get insurance from their job?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare network of providers and hospitals
atoms.q: How large is the UnitedHealthcare provider network?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says its network includes 1M+ providers and 6,000+ hospitals, giving greater access to the care you need. Members with pharmacy benefits can access a large, nationwide network of pharmacies that offer greater discounts, convenience and choice.
qs: How many doctors are in the UnitedHealthcare network?
Does UnitedHealthcare have a nationwide pharmacy network?

atoms.title: Virtual Visits for nonemergency care
atoms.q: What are UnitedHealthcare Virtual Visits through work plans?
atoms.text: Services like Virtual Visits connect you with a doctor who can treat a wide range of nonemergency medical conditions and even provide prescriptions if needed, 24/7, anytime, anywhere. Certain prescriptions may not be available. Virtual Visits are not intended for emergency or life-threatening conditions, and benefits are available only through a Designated Virtual Network Provider.
qs: Can I see a doctor by video through my employer plan?
Are Virtual Visits for emergencies?

atoms.title: Member site and UnitedHealthcare app tools
atoms.q: What digital tools come with UnitedHealthcare employer plans?
atoms.text: A personalized member site helps manage your plan 24/7: search for a doctor, find and price network care, view claims details, refill prescriptions and manage financial accounts. The UnitedHealthcare app helps you find in-network care options, see claim details, view progress toward your deductible, share your digital health plan ID card, log in with Touch ID and talk to a doctor by video 24/7.
qs: Can I see my deductible progress in the app?
What can I do on the UnitedHealthcare member site?

atoms.title: Personalized support for members
atoms.q: What personal support does UnitedHealthcare offer members?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says it connects members to support led by trained, caring experts who help with questions and guide you every step of the way, whether you're looking for medical care or ways to manage stress and anxiety. Members can sign in to their account to find the support available through their benefits.
qs: Who do I call for help with my employer health plan?
Does my plan offer help with stress or anxiety?

atoms.title: Wellness programs at no additional cost
atoms.q: Do UnitedHealthcare employer plans include wellness programs?
atoms.text: Depending on your plan, UnitedHealthcare offers a number of wellness programs and services at no additional cost to you, from losing weight and quitting smoking to fitness rewards and more. Members can sign in to their account to find out what's included in their benefits.
qs: Are weight loss or quit smoking programs included in my plan?
Where do I find my wellness benefits?

atoms.title: When is open enrollment for employer health plans?
atoms.q: When can I choose my health plan through my employer?
atoms.text: Open enrollment is when you can select your health insurance plan for the upcoming year. Your employer sets the open enrollment period, but it may typically be in the fall. UnitedHealthcare suggests taking time to explore your options to learn what type of coverage may best fit your needs.
qs: When is open enrollment for work insurance?
Who decides my open enrollment dates?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare employer plan types
atoms.q: What UnitedHealthcare plan types are offered through employers?
atoms.text: The page lists these UnitedHealthcare plans and coverage options for people with insurance through work: Choice plans, Navigate plans, Options PPO plans, Choice Plus plans, Navigate Plus plans, and lost job coverage with COBRA and other insurance options.
qs: What types of employer health plans does UnitedHealthcare have?
What is the difference between Choice and Navigate plans?

atoms.title: What are Choice Plus plans?
atoms.q: What is a UnitedHealthcare Choice Plus plan?
atoms.text: With UnitedHealthcare Choice Plus health plans, you have the freedom to choose a network physician or specialist from the UnitedHealthcare Choice Plus network without visiting a primary care provider (PCP) for a referral. You save money when you use the national network.
qs: Do I need a referral on a Choice Plus plan?
What is a Choice Plus health plan?

atoms.title: Out-of-network coverage on Choice Plus
atoms.q: Does Choice Plus cover out-of-network providers?
atoms.text: With UnitedHealthcare Choice Plus health plans, you also have coverage if you use out-of-network providers, while you save money when you use the national network. You can choose a network physician or specialist from the Choice Plus network without visiting a primary care provider (PCP) for a referral.
qs: Can I go out of network with Choice Plus?
Is out-of-network care covered on Choice Plus plans?

atoms.title: Services covered by Choice Plus plans
atoms.q: What services do Choice Plus plans cover?
atoms.text: Choice Plus plans provide well-rounded coverage for many services, including preventive care (100% at network facility), physician and specialist office visits, lab, X-ray and diagnostic services, urgent care and emergency services, inpatient hospital services, rehabilitation and skilled nursing facility services, and mental health services.
qs: Is preventive care free on Choice Plus?
Does Choice Plus cover mental health services?

atoms.title: Health and wellness resources with Choice Plus
atoms.q: What wellness resources are included with Choice Plus?
atoms.text: An array of health and wellness resources is included with UnitedHealthcare Choice Plus plans, alongside covered services such as preventive care, physician and specialist office visits and mental health services. The resources named on the page are the Online Health Assessment, Personal Health Record and Online Health Coaching modules.
qs: What is the Online Health Assessment?
Does Choice Plus include health coaching?

atoms.title: Managing Choice Plus benefits in the app
atoms.q: How do Choice Plus members manage their benefits?
atoms.text: Choice Plus members can use the UnitedHealthcare app on a mobile device for instant access to see benefits, manage health plan details, find network providers and more. Members can also sign in to their member account or use a mobile browser.
qs: Is there an app for Choice Plus members?
How do I sign in to my Choice Plus account?

atoms.title: Three health coverage options when unemployed
atoms.q: What are my health insurance options if I lose my job?
atoms.text: If you are unemployed or underemployed, you have three main options: enroll in a plan through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace, sign up for continuation of health coverage under the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA), or opt for short term medical insurance. The page quotes Adria Gross, CEO and founder of MedWise Insurance Advocacy, saying you have health insurance options.
qs: What health insurance can I get after losing my job?
Should I choose COBRA, Marketplace or short term insurance?

atoms.title: Does job loss qualify for a Special Enrollment Period?
atoms.q: How soon do I need to apply for Marketplace coverage after losing my job?
atoms.text: Yes. Losing your job qualifies you for a special enrollment period so you can get coverage for the rest of the year, according to the page. You need to apply for Marketplace coverage within 60 days of losing your employment. Your coverage can start the first day of the month after you lose your job-based coverage, and your employer coverage stays in effect until the end of the month.
qs: How long do I have to enroll after losing employer coverage?
When does Marketplace coverage start after a job loss?

atoms.title: What ACA Marketplace plans guarantee
atoms.q: What do ACA Marketplace plans cover if I'm between jobs?
atoms.text: All plans offered in the Marketplace comply with the Affordable Care Act, meaning they meet federal standards. The plans cover essential health benefits and preexisting conditions without annual or lifetime benefit caps. You may also receive income-based subsidies to make coverage and care more affordable.
qs: Do Marketplace plans cover preexisting conditions?
Are there benefit caps on ACA plans?

atoms.title: Savings on Marketplace plans after job loss
atoms.q: What savings can I get on a Marketplace plan after losing my job?
atoms.text: Premium tax credits lower your monthly premium, and the amount depends on your estimated household income for the year. You apply the credit to your monthly premium, which is sent directly to your insurance carrier. If you qualify, you may also qualify for cost-sharing reductions: a lower deductible, lower copayments or coinsurance, and a lower out-of-pocket maximum. You must pick a moderately priced plan to get these; they aren't available with the lowest cost plan.
qs: Can I get a tax credit after losing employer coverage?
Do cost-sharing reductions work with the cheapest plan?

atoms.title: Check networks and drug lists on new plans
atoms.q: What should I check before switching to a Marketplace plan?
atoms.text: You may need to prove that you lost health insurance through your job, and when you apply the Marketplace will tell you if documents are needed. The page also advises checking that all your medical providers are still in network and confirming that all your prescriptions are covered under the new plan's drug formulary to avoid steep out-of-pocket costs, which is especially important with a chronic condition.
qs: Do I need proof that I lost my job coverage?
How do I make sure my doctors are covered on a new plan?

atoms.title: What is COBRA coverage?
atoms.q: What is COBRA health insurance?
atoms.text: COBRA is insurance under federal law that allows you, your spouse and your dependents to stay on your former company's group health plan when your job ends. It applies to employers that have health coverage for at least 20 employees. Some states also have their own mini-COBRA laws for companies with fewer than 20 employees.
qs: What is COBRA?
Does COBRA apply to small employers?

atoms.title: COBRA costs, doctors and duration
atoms.q: How much does COBRA cost and how long does it last?
atoms.text: With COBRA you continue with the same health plan, keep your same doctors, and your prescriptions should still be covered under the existing formulary. But you pay 100% of the costs of the plan, including costs your employer previously paid: monthly premiums and possibly an additional 2% administrative fee. COBRA coverage can last from 18 to 36 months, depending on the qualifying event. If you've already met your deductible, you'll probably have fewer out-of-pocket costs.
qs: Why is COBRA so expensive?
How many months can I stay on COBRA?

atoms.title: Short term and TriTerm options between jobs
atoms.q: How do short term and TriTerm plans work between jobs?
atoms.text: Short term insurance can fill gaps until you choose a long-term solution. Standard short term plans cover 1 month up to nearly 1 year, while TriTerm plans extend to nearly 3 years, with term lengths varying by state. If you qualify, you may get covered as soon as the day after application for standard short term, or as soon as 5 days for TriTerm Medical, choose your deductible, and drop coverage with no penalty if a permanent option comes along.
qs: How fast can short term coverage start?
Can I cancel short term insurance without a penalty?

atoms.title: Short term network size
atoms.q: How large is the network for short term and TriTerm plans?
atoms.text: With short term and TriTerm Medical insurance, you can access an extensive network of health care professionals, with 1.8 million physicians and other health care professionals and approximately 7,200 hospitals and other facilities. Depending on your state, you can apply for another short term plan when the first one finishes, if needed.
qs: How many doctors are in the short term insurance network?
Can I get another short term plan after the first ends?

atoms.title: Short term versus Marketplace and COBRA requirements
atoms.q: How is short term insurance different from COBRA or Marketplace plans?
atoms.text: Unlike COBRA or Marketplace plans, short term insurance requires medical underwriting: plans generally do not cover preexisting conditions and you must answer a series of medical questions, with all covered family members needing to meet the medical requirements. Marketplace plans must cover 10 essential health benefits, including maternity and newborn care and mental health and substance abuse disorder services, while short term plans have no coverage requirements and may have limited prescription or preventive coverage.
qs: Does short term insurance cover preexisting conditions?
Do short term plans cover maternity care?

atoms.title: Who short term insurance may suit best
atoms.q: Who is short term insurance a better option for?
atoms.text: You may save money by choosing short term health insurance, but it needs to be the right choice for you. Given the underwriting and coverage limits, short term insurance is sometimes a better option for someone who's younger, in good health and doesn't anticipate needing frequent medical care.
qs: Is short term insurance a good idea if I'm healthy?
Will short term insurance save me money?

atoms.title: Coverage can change at the next open enrollment
atoms.q: Can I change my coverage after choosing a temporary option?
atoms.text: The page's bottom line is that if you are unemployed or underemployed, you have options and one of them will likely meet your current needs. When the next Open Enrollment Period comes around you can always change, and if you land a new job you may have new options through your employer.
qs: Can I switch plans later after losing my job?
What happens when I get a new job with benefits?

atoms.title: What are Navigate plans?
atoms.q: What is a UnitedHealthcare Navigate plan?
atoms.text: With UnitedHealthcare Navigate health plans, you access your coverage and benefits with the guidance of a primary care provider (PCP). Your coverage requires a referral from your PCP before you see another physician or specialist in the network, and no coverage is provided without a referral.
qs: Do I need a referral on a Navigate plan?
What is a Navigate health plan?

atoms.title: Out-of-network coverage on Navigate plans
atoms.q: Does a Navigate plan cover out-of-network care?
atoms.text: Under UnitedHealthcare Navigate plans, out-of-network coverage is available only in the case of emergency care. Your coverage also requires a referral from your primary care provider (PCP) before you see another physician or specialist in the network, and no coverage is provided without a referral.
qs: Is out-of-network care covered on Navigate?
What happens if I skip my PCP referral?

atoms.title: The role of the PCP in Navigate plans
atoms.q: How does a PCP help on a Navigate plan?
atoms.text: With Navigate plans, PCPs get to know you and your medical history. They help coordinate care across a wide spectrum of health services and make sure you're getting the care you need when you need it.
qs: What does a primary care provider do in a Navigate plan?
Why do Navigate plans use a PCP?

atoms.title: Services covered by Navigate plans
atoms.q: What services do Navigate plans cover?
atoms.text: Navigate plans provide well-rounded coverage for many services, including preventive care, PCP and specialty office visits, lab, X-ray and diagnostic services, urgent care, emergency services, inpatient hospital services, rehabilitation and skilled nursing facility services, and mental health services. Online Health Assessment, Personal Health Record and Online Health Coaching modules are also included.
qs: Does Navigate cover urgent care?
What wellness tools come with Navigate plans?

atoms.title: Managing Navigate benefits in the app
atoms.q: How do Navigate members manage their benefits?
atoms.text: Navigate plan members can use the UnitedHealthcare app for instant access to see benefits, manage health plan details, find network providers and more. Members can also sign in to their member account or use a mobile browser.
qs: Is there a mobile app for Navigate plan members?
How do I find providers on my Navigate plan?

atoms.title: What are Options PPO plans?
atoms.q: What is a UnitedHealthcare Options PPO plan?
atoms.text: With UnitedHealthcare Options PPO health plans, you can use any doctor, clinic, hospital or health care facility in the national network. A network is a group of health care providers and facilities that have a contract with UnitedHealthcare, and staying in the network saves you money.
qs: What is an Options PPO plan?
Can I use any doctor on Options PPO?

atoms.title: No PCP or referrals with Options PPO
atoms.q: Do I need a PCP or referral on Options PPO?
atoms.text: With UnitedHealthcare Options PPO, there's no need to select a primary care provider (PCP) or get referrals to see a specialist. You can receive care and services from anyone in the network.
qs: Can I see a specialist without a referral on a PPO?
Do I have to pick a PCP with Options PPO?

atoms.title: Costs and responsibilities outside the network
atoms.q: What happens if I use out-of-network providers on Options PPO?
atoms.text: With Options PPO, if you don't use the network your costs will be higher and it is your responsibility to submit claims. It's also your responsibility to obtain approvals for both network and non-network services.
qs: Do I file my own claims out of network on Options PPO?
Who gets approvals for services on Options PPO?

atoms.title: Services covered by Options PPO plans
atoms.q: What services do Options PPO plans cover?
atoms.text: Options PPO plans provide well-rounded coverage for many services, including preventive care (100% at network facility), physician and specialist office visits, lab, X-ray and diagnostic services, urgent care and emergency services, outpatient care services, pregnancy and newborn care, prescription drugs, rehabilitation and skilled nursing facility services and devices, mental health and substance use disorder services, and wellness services.
qs: Does Options PPO cover prescription drugs?
Is maternity care covered on Options PPO?

atoms.title: Managing Options PPO benefits in the app
atoms.q: How do Options PPO members manage their benefits?
atoms.text: Options PPO members can use the UnitedHealthcare app for instant access to see benefits, manage health plan details, find network providers and more. Members can also sign in to their member account or use a mobile browser.
qs: Can I use the UnitedHealthcare app with an Options PPO plan?
How do I sign in to my Options PPO account?

atoms.title: Health insurance options for the self-employed
atoms.q: What health insurance options do self-employed people have?
atoms.text: Self-employed people may not get coverage through an employer, but they have options: the Health Insurance Marketplace (ACA plans), short-term health insurance plans and TriTerm Medical health insurance. They can also consider supplemental plans like vision, dental and term life insurance.
qs: How do I get health insurance if I'm self-employed?
What are my options as a freelancer?

atoms.title: ACA Marketplace plans for the self-employed
atoms.q: Can self-employed people buy ACA Marketplace plans?
atoms.text: The Affordable Care Act gives self-employed people options to buy health insurance for themselves and their family through the ACA Marketplace, and UnitedHealthcare offers Individual & Family ACA plans there. Depending on your situation, you may qualify for tax breaks, premium tax credits and other savings. Marketplace plans are only available during open enrollment (November 1 to January 15 in most states) or if you've had a qualifying life event.
qs: Can I get a premium tax credit if I'm self-employed?
When can a freelancer sign up for an ACA plan?

atoms.title: Short term plans for the self-employed
atoms.q: Are short term plans an option if I'm self-employed with no employees?
atoms.text: Short term health insurance can fill in when you might have a gap in coverage. Traditional short term plans can last between one and 12 months while TriTerm Medical plans last nearly three years. UnitedHealthcare-branded short term plans, underwritten by Golden Rule Insurance Company, include a large network of health care professionals, and some plans can start the day after your application. Term lengths vary by state.
qs: How long can a short term plan last for a freelancer?
Who underwrites UnitedHealthcare short term plans?

atoms.title: Short term and TriTerm coverage limitations
atoms.q: What limitations apply to short term and TriTerm plans?
atoms.text: Short term health insurance plans are medically underwritten and do not provide coverage for preexisting conditions, though TriTerm Medical plans cover eligible expenses for preexisting conditions after 12 months on the plan. The TriTerm coverage term is one day less than 3 years (in IN, three 364-day terms). The coverage does not qualify as Minimum Essential Coverage and may not cover all Essential Health Benefits; some states may impose a tax penalty if you lack MEC coverage.
qs: Does TriTerm Medical cover preexisting conditions?
Could I owe a state tax penalty with short term insurance?

atoms.title: Small business health insurance options
atoms.q: What health plans does UnitedHealthcare offer small businesses?
atoms.text: If you have between one and 99 employees working for you, your organization is considered a small business, and UnitedHealthcare offers many options for small businesses. All UnitedHealthcare small business plans come with benefits such as 24/7 access to telehealth, incentives for healthy behaviors, and the vital medication program.
qs: How many employees make a small business for health insurance?
What benefits do small business plans include?

atoms.title: Options by employee count in the self-employed video
atoms.q: What coverage fits a self-employed person with or without employees?
atoms.text: The page's video says that if you're self-employed with no employees, ACA Marketplace plans offer reliable coverage options designed to fit your needs and budget, and you may qualify for subsidies that lower monthly premiums. If you're self-employed with up to 50 employees, it suggests looking into the Small Business Health Options Program (SHOP). To buy, go to the Health Insurance Marketplace or a private insurance company like UnitedHealthcare.
qs: What is SHOP for small businesses?
Where do I buy health insurance as a sole proprietor?

atoms.title: Qualifying life events shown in the video
atoms.q: What life events let me enroll in an ACA plan outside open enrollment?
atoms.text: The self-employed video lists events that can qualify someone to enroll in an ACA plan outside open enrollment: getting married, getting divorced, having or adopting a baby, loss of someone on your health plan, moving to a new state, earning U.S. citizenship, turning 26 or 65, and a change in employment status.
qs: Does turning 65 count as a qualifying life event?
Can a change in employment status qualify me for enrollment?

atoms.title: Supplemental insurance for the self-employed
atoms.q: What supplemental insurance can the self-employed add?
atoms.text: Even the best medical insurance plans don't cover everything. Supplemental plans offer additional coverage for specific needs: vision plans can cover eye exams, glasses and contacts, and dental insurance can help with many common preventive, basic and major dental services. Other supplemental plans pay lump sums to help cover unexpected expenses related to accidents, serious illness and more.
qs: Do I need dental or vision insurance if I'm self-employed?
What plans pay a lump sum for accidents or illness?

atoms.title: What are short term limited duration plans?
atoms.q: What is short term health insurance?
atoms.text: Short term limited duration health plans help bridge gaps in coverage. With options lasting from 1 month to nearly 3 years, short term plans underwritten by Golden Rule Insurance Company can provide a temporary solution to get the benefits you want for the time you need. Short term insurance is also called temporary health insurance or term health insurance.
qs: What is temporary health insurance?
Who underwrites UnitedHealthcare short term plans?

atoms.title: Short Term Medical versus TriTerm Medical
atoms.q: What is the difference between Short Term Medical and TriTerm Medical?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers two kinds of short term plans. Short Term Medical plans last 1 month up to nearly 12 months. TriTerm Medical plans last nearly 3 years. The page describes these short term plans as underwritten by Golden Rule Insurance Company.
qs: How long does TriTerm last compared with short term?
What are the two types of short term plans?

atoms.title: Situations where short term insurance may fit
atoms.q: When is short term insurance the right choice?
atoms.text: Short term insurance may be right if you're waiting for open enrollment to apply for an ACA plan; don't have a qualifying life event or Special Enrollment Period to apply for an ACA plan; are waiting for ACA coverage to start; need coverage to bridge you to Medicare; are turning 26 and coming off a parent's insurance; are between jobs or waiting for benefits at a new job; or are healthy and under 65.
qs: Can I use short term insurance until Medicare starts?
What if I missed open enrollment?

atoms.title: Short term plan coverage details
atoms.q: What do short term plans cover?
atoms.text: Preexisting conditions are not covered with most short term plans, so check your state's definition of preexisting conditions; Short Term Medical plans are medically underwritten. Limited preventive care can sometimes be covered. Prescription coverage may be available with some plans. Coverage for some telehealth (virtual visits) services may be included.
qs: Do short term plans cover prescriptions?
Is telehealth covered under short term insurance?

atoms.title: ACA plans versus short term plans
atoms.q: How are short term insurance plans different from ACA plans?
atoms.text: ACA plans cover preexisting conditions and you cannot be denied coverage based on them. Short term plans do not: you must answer a series of medical questions to apply, and Short Term Medical plans are medically underwritten. ACA plans are required to cover 10 essential health benefits, including maternity and newborn care and mental health and substance abuse disorder services. Short term plans have no specific coverage requirements and vary in what they cover.
qs: Can I be denied a short term plan for health reasons?
Do short term plans cover essential health benefits?

atoms.title: Short term insurance can save money but needs review
atoms.q: Is short term insurance a good way to save money?
atoms.text: You may save money by choosing short term health insurance, but you should know what you are buying and make sure it's a good choice for you. For the right situation, short term insurance plans can provide fast, flexible, temporary health insurance coverage that fits your needs.
qs: Is short term health insurance cheaper?
What should I check before buying a short term plan?

atoms.q: How long has Golden Rule offered short term insurance?

atoms.title: Why consider a student health plan
atoms.q: Why would a college student choose a student health plan?
atoms.text: Student health plans can be a valuable solution for college students and their families. UnitedHealthcare says they can cost less than other plans, even less than staying on an employer-sponsored family plan, and can also provide better benefits.
qs: Is a student health plan cheaper than my parents' plan?
Why get a college student health plan?

atoms.title: Features of UnitedHealthcare student plans
atoms.q: What features do student health plans offer?
atoms.text: Reasons to consider a student health plan include lower cost deductibles and premiums; comprehensive benefits, including added services not always found with other plans; greater access to national and local networks of physicians and behavioral health specialists; and better coverage for school-sponsored, on-site health clinics and virtual visit services.
qs: Do student plans cover campus health clinics?
Do student plans include behavioral health specialists?

atoms.title: Why student plan rates can be lower
atoms.q: Why are student health plans less expensive?
atoms.text: Student plans come with added benefits because they're designed with students in mind. Lower rates are possible partly because they're based on a younger, healthier population and provide coverage for a limited time, just while students are in school. Families and students can save money and get high-quality coverage at the same time.
qs: How can student insurance cost less?
Do student plans only cover me while I'm in school?

atoms.title: Coverage options for college students
atoms.q: What health coverage options do college students have?
atoms.text: Students can consider student insurance plans; parents' employer plans (up to age 26 if dependent coverage is available); employer plans for eligible employed students; and individual plans through the State or Federal Exchange. Depending on your state, you may qualify for Medicaid. Looking at all options may help find the solution that works best for the student and family.
qs: Can I stay on my parents' insurance in college?
What are my health insurance options as a student?

atoms.title: Catastrophic health plan for students under 30
atoms.q: Can a student buy a catastrophic health plan?
atoms.text: If you're under the age of 30, or qualify for a hardship exemption, you can purchase a catastrophic health plan through an Exchange. UnitedHealthcare lists this among the options students can consider when choosing a health plan.

Is there an age limit for catastrophic coverage?

atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare directs students to a student plan site to find a student plan and learn how to get started. Existing members can sign in or register for a student account to access their benefits, and a student plans FAQ page offers more help understanding the options.

atoms.text: Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans offer all the benefits of Original Medicare (Part A and Part B), with extras like dental, vision, hearing, and prescription drug coverage. UnitedHealthcare lists Medicare Advantage as one of the main plan types it offers to people shopping for Medicare coverage.

atoms.text: Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plans help pay some of the out-of-pocket costs that Original Medicare doesn't pay. They are sold by private insurers as a companion to Original Medicare rather than as a replacement for it.

atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare organizes its Medicare coverage into four plan families: Medicare Advantage plans, which bundle Part A and Part B benefits with extras; Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plans, which help with Original Medicare out-of-pocket costs; Part D prescription drug plans; and Dual Special Needs plans for people eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid.

atoms.title: Premiums and cost sharing in Medicare
atoms.q: What costs do I pay with Medicare?
atoms.text: Medicare isn't free. The amount you pay depends on the coverage you choose, the services you use during the year, and whether your plan has in-network and out-of-network rules. Medicare Part B and most Part C, Part D and Medigap plans charge monthly premiums, and in some cases there is a Part A premium. A premium is a fixed amount you pay for coverage to Medicare, a private insurance company, or both. You also pay a share of care costs through deductibles, copays and coinsurance.
qs: How much does Medicare cost?
Which Medicare parts charge a monthly premium?
What is cost sharing in Medicare?

atoms.title: Deductible, copay and coinsurance defined
atoms.q: What are a deductible, copay and coinsurance?
atoms.text: A deductible is a set amount you pay out of pocket for covered services before Medicare or your plan begins to pay. A copay is a fixed amount you pay at the time you receive a covered service, such as $20 for a doctor visit or $12 for a prescription. Coinsurance is your share of the total cost as a percentage; for example, with 25% coinsurance on a $100 service you would pay $25 and your insurance would pay $75.
qs: What is coinsurance?
What's the difference between a copay and a deductible?
How is 25% coinsurance calculated?

atoms.title: Costs of Original Medicare Part A and Part B
atoms.q: How much does Medicare Part A and Part B cost?
atoms.text: With Medicare Part A, most people don't pay a premium, though you may if you or your spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes for less than 10 years. Medicare Part B has a monthly premium you pay directly to Medicare, and the amount can vary based on your income level. Other costs with Part A and Part B include deductibles, coinsurance and copays.

Does the Part B premium depend on income?
What other costs come with Original Medicare?

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage costs and out-of-pocket maximum
atoms.q: What are my costs with a Medicare Advantage plan?
atoms.text: Each Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan sets its own specific costs, but the types of costs you may pay include premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance. Not all plans will have deductibles, copays or coinsurance, so check each plan's cost-sharing rules carefully. Medicare Advantage plans also limit how much you'll pay out of pocket every year, called the out-of-pocket maximum, and each year the limit is set by Medicare.
qs: Does Medicare Advantage have an out-of-pocket maximum?
Who sets the Medicare Advantage out-of-pocket limit?
What costs do Medicare Advantage plans have?

atoms.title: Medigap costs and predictability
atoms.q: What are my costs with a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: Medicare Supplement plans are designed to help limit out-of-pocket costs by helping to pay for some of the costs Original Medicare doesn't pay. There are Medigap plan options available with low to no copays, and the plans offer predictable out-of-pocket costs. Benefits and costs vary depending on the plan you choose. Different plan options are available in Massachusetts, Minnesota and Wisconsin.

Are Medigap plans different in Massachusetts?

atoms.title: 2026 Part D out-of-pocket maximum is $2,100
atoms.q: What is the Part D out-of-pocket maximum for 2026?
atoms.text: Standalone Part D plans (PDP) and Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage (MAPD) set their own costs, but the types of costs they can include are similar: premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance. For 2026, the annual out-of-pocket maximum is $2,100. The amount you pay depends on the drug payment stage you're in and the tier a drug is in, if your plan has a tiered formulary. Part D plan costs can vary widely, even for similar coverage.
qs: What is the Part D out-of-pocket cap in 2026?
How much will I pay for prescriptions at most in 2026?
Do Part D costs vary between plans?

atoms.title: The three Part D drug payment stages
atoms.q: What are the Part D drug payment stages?
atoms.text: 1) Annual Deductible: for plans with a deductible, you pay the full cost of drugs until you reach it, then move to Initial Coverage; plans without a deductible start at Initial Coverage with your first prescription. 2) Initial Coverage: the plan pays its share and you pay your copay or coinsurance, until total drug costs reach $2,100 in 2026. 3) Catastrophic Coverage: once you or others on your behalf reach $2,100 in out-of-pocket drug costs, you pay $0 for Medicare-covered Part D drugs for the rest of the plan year.

What happens after I spend $2,100 on drugs?
What are the stages of Part D coverage?

atoms.title: Programs that help pay Medicare costs
atoms.q: What programs can help me pay Medicare costs?
atoms.text: If you have limited income and assets, you may qualify for help with Medicare costs, and many people who could qualify never sign up. Extra Help from Medicare helps pay some or all Part D premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance. Medicare savings programs help pay Part A and Part B premiums, deductibles and coinsurance, and qualifying for one automatically qualifies you for Extra Help. Medicaid covers individuals and families with limited incomes and may include services Medicare does not, like prescription drugs, eye care or long-term care.

What is a Medicare Savings Program?
Does a Medicare Savings Program qualify me for Extra Help?

atoms.title: PACE and state pharmaceutical assistance
atoms.q: What is PACE and what other help programs exist?
atoms.text: Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) combine medical, social and long-term care services for people over the age of 55 who qualify, and the program is not available in all states. Other programs may be available in your state, such as State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs. Each program has its own rules for qualifying, so read about each carefully. If you have both Medicaid and Medicare, you may be eligible for a Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP).

atoms.title: Look beyond premiums when comparing plans
atoms.q: Should I only compare Medicare premiums?
atoms.text: It's easy to focus on just premiums, but it's a better idea to look at all of your Medicare costs together, including premiums and all out-of-pocket costs. A plan may look like a good choice with a low premium but actually cost more with a high deductible or high copayments for doctor visits or prescriptions. The reverse can also be true: a high premium but low out-of-pocket costs. You may reduce costs by understanding cost sharing, using services wisely and adopting healthy lifestyle behaviors.

Can a low-premium plan cost more overall?

atoms.title: Medicare late enrollment penalties by part
atoms.q: What are the Medicare late enrollment penalties for Parts A, B and D?
atoms.text: Part A, Part B and Part D may charge premium penalties if you miss your initial enrollment dates, unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. Part A: if you must pay a premium, the late penalty is 10%, charged for twice the number of years you delayed. Part B: an additional 10% for each 12-month period you delay, usually paid every month for as long as you have Part B. Part D: 1% of the average Part D premium for each month you delay, paid for as long as you have Part D.
qs: How much is the Part B late penalty?
How long do I pay the Part A late penalty?
What is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

atoms.title: Part B penalty ends at 65 for disabled enrollees
atoms.q: Does the Part B late penalty ever end?
atoms.text: In most cases, you have to pay the Part B late enrollment penalty every month for as long as you have Part B. However, if you're under 65 and disabled, any Part B penalty ends once you turn 65, because you'll have another Initial Enrollment Period based on your age. For Part A, you won't pay a premium if you or your spouse worked and paid taxes for at least 10 years, and the Part A penalty applies no matter how long you delay enrollment.

atoms.title: Who becomes eligible for Medicare
atoms.q: Am I eligible for Medicare?
atoms.text: Most people become eligible for Medicare when they turn 65. You can also become eligible if you have a qualifying disability at any age (eligibility begins after 24 months of receiving Social Security Disability Insurance benefits), or if you have a diagnosis of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease) at any age.

atoms.title: Automatic versus self-enrollment in Original Medicare
atoms.q: Will I be enrolled in Original Medicare automatically?
atoms.text: You will be enrolled in Original Medicare automatically if you are receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits when you turn 65, or if you are eligible because of a disability or medical condition. You must enroll yourself in Medicare Part A and Part B if you are not receiving Social Security benefits when you become eligible, online at www.ssa.gov, in person at your local Social Security office or by phone at 1-800-772-1213 / TTY 1-800-325-0778.
qs: When am I automatically enrolled in Medicare?
How do I sign up for Medicare if I don't get Social Security?
How can I enroll in Part A and B?

atoms.title: Age 65 is what matters for eligibility
atoms.q: Will I be eligible for Medicare at age 65?
atoms.text: You are eligible for Medicare when you turn 65, whether you are working, not working or retired, and whether or not you receive Social Security or other retirement benefits. Your age is what matters. If you receive Social Security Disability Insurance payments, you will be eligible for Medicare the month you receive your 25th benefit payment, while ESRD or ALS qualifies you immediately or within a few months depending on your diagnosis.

atoms.title: Eligibility if you work past 65
atoms.q: Will I still be eligible for Medicare if I work past age 65?
atoms.text: Yes. If you plan to keep working or you have employer health coverage through a spouse, you may be able to delay enrolling in Medicare. Depending on your situation you may not be able to delay; for example, if your employer has fewer than 20 employees, you may be required to enroll in Medicare.

atoms.title: Eligibility rules for each private Medicare plan
atoms.q: How do I qualify for a private Medicare plan?
atoms.text: Once you are enrolled in Original Medicare (Part A and Part B), you can choose coverage from a private insurance company. To be eligible for a Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan, you must have Original Medicare and live in the plan service area. A Chronic Special Needs plan (C-SNP) requires Original Medicare and a qualifying chronic condition. A Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP) requires that you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. A Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plan requires Original Medicare. A Part D plan requires Part A or Part B. All Special Needs plans are Medicare Advantage plans.

atoms.title: Citizenship and residency requirements
atoms.q: Do I need to be a U.S. citizen to be eligible for Medicare?
atoms.text: Yes, or a qualified legal resident. To qualify as a legal resident, you must have lived in the United States for at least 5 years in a row before applying for Medicare coverage.

atoms.title: Premium-free Part A if you never worked
atoms.q: Can I get Medicare coverage if I never worked?
atoms.text: Maybe. Citizens or permanent residents age 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability or medical condition, are eligible for Medicare. You can enroll in Medicare Part A at no cost if your spouse (living or deceased, including a divorced spouse) receives or is eligible to receive Social Security or RRB benefits, if you or your spouse worked long enough in a government job through which you paid Medicare taxes, or if you are the dependent parent of a fully insured deceased child.

atoms.title: Medicare for veterans with VA or TRICARE
atoms.q: What if I qualify for veterans' benefits?
atoms.text: If you're a U.S. veteran, you may have other insurance, such as TRICARE or Veterans Affairs (VA) benefits, but you may still want to enroll in a Medicare plan, and the VA recommends it. Care through the VA covers services at VA facilities or others authorized by the VA, while Medicare can cover care at private hospitals and doctors outside the VA system. Having both means you can get care in more places.

atoms.title: Disability and Medicare timing
atoms.q: I'm on disability. When will I be eligible for Medicare?
atoms.text: It depends on your disability. If you have been receiving Social Security Disability Insurance benefits for at least 24 months, you should be eligible for Medicare coverage.

atoms.title: Next steps once you're eligible
atoms.q: I'm eligible for Medicare. What do I do next?
atoms.text: If you first become eligible because you are turning 65, you will have an Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) that begins three months before the month of your 65th birthday and ends three months afterward. During your IEP, you can enroll in Original Medicare (Part A and/or Part B). Then you can choose to enroll in a Medicare Advantage (Part C) or Medicare Part D prescription drug plan, or apply for a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) insurance plan.

In what order do I enroll in Medicare plans?
When can I pick a Medicare Advantage or Part D plan?

atoms.title: What Original Medicare is
atoms.q: What is Original Medicare?
atoms.text: Original Medicare consists of Medicare Part A (hospital coverage) and Medicare Part B (medical coverage). It's a federal health insurance program for individuals 65 or older; under 65 who have a qualifying disability; and of any age with a diagnosis of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease).
qs: What is Original Medicare?
Who qualifies for Original Medicare?
What is the difference between Part A and Part B?

atoms.title: What Medicare Part A covers
atoms.q: What does Medicare Part A cover?
atoms.text: Medicare Part A covers hospital charges and most associated services while you are admitted as an inpatient. Coverage includes a semi-private room, hospital meals, skilled nursing services, care on special units such as intensive care, drugs, supplies and equipment used during your stay, lab tests and X-rays, operating and recovery room services, some blood transfusions, rehab through home health care, skilled care in your home if you are homebound and need only part-time care, and hospice care. Part B covers doctor visits, even in the hospital, and outpatient services.
qs: Does Medicare Part A cover hospice?
What hospital services are covered by Part A?
What does Part B cover?

atoms.title: Medicare versus Medicaid
atoms.q: Is Medicare the same as Medicaid?
atoms.text: No. Medicare and Medicaid are both government programs that help people pay for health care, but they are not the same. Medicare is a federal program that provides coverage for people who are 65 or older or have certain qualifying disabilities. Medicaid is a joint state and federal program that provides coverage for individuals and families with limited incomes. Dual eligibility means you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid.
qs: What's the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
What does dual eligible mean?
Can I have both Medicare and Medicaid?

atoms.title: Whether Medicare is mandatory
atoms.q: Is Medicare mandatory?
atoms.text: No. Medicare is not mandatory. But if you do decide to enroll after your Initial Enrollment Period and don't qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you could face late enrollment penalties for Medicare Part A, Part B, Part C or Part D.
qs: Do I have to sign up for Medicare?
What happens if I don't enroll in Medicare at 65?
Are there late penalties for Medicare?

atoms.title: Prescription drugs under Original Medicare
atoms.q: Can I get my prescription drugs covered under Original Medicare?
atoms.text: No. Original Medicare doesn't generally cover prescription drugs, though Part A may cover some drugs you get as an inpatient. Part D coverage is available separately through private insurers approved by Medicare, either as a standalone plan or in a Medicare Advantage plan with drug benefits. All Part D plans have a drug list (formulary) showing which drugs are covered; the formulary can change, and your plan will let you know ahead of time.
qs: Does Original Medicare cover my medications?
How do I know if my drug is covered?
What is a Part D formulary?

atoms.title: Choosing doctors and referrals under Medicare
atoms.q: Can I choose my doctor? Does Medicare require referrals?
atoms.text: Your choice of doctor depends on what Medicare coverage you have. With Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) you can see any doctor that accepts Medicare. Most Medicare Advantage plans have provider networks, and some plans may require referrals to specialists. Both Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage plans cover most emergency care when and where it's needed.
qs: Can I see any doctor with Medicare?
Do Medicare Advantage plans need referrals?
Is emergency care covered by Medicare?

atoms.title: Dental, vision and hearing under Original Medicare
atoms.q: Does Original Medicare cover vision, dental, or hearing care?
atoms.text: Generally, no. Original Medicare doesn't cover routine vision or dental care, eyeglasses or hearing aids. Part B may cover some dental or vision services if you meet certain conditions and they are considered medically necessary, but check with your provider and Medicare first. Many Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans do offer these benefits, including routine eye exams with eyeglasses and corrective lenses, dental exams, and hearing tests and hearing aids.
qs: Does Medicare cover dental?
Does Medicare pay for hearing aids?
Which Medicare plans include eye exams?

atoms.title: Nursing home stays under Original Medicare
atoms.q: Does Original Medicare pay for a nursing home stay?
atoms.text: Original Medicare Part A pays for some skilled nursing services, but doesn't cover long-term or custodial care for daily life activities like eating and bathing. You would also still be responsible for a portion of the costs, such as deductibles, copays and coinsurance.
qs: Will Medicare pay for a nursing home?
Does Medicare cover custodial care?
What nursing care does Part A cover?

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage HMO versus PPO
atoms.q: What's the difference between a Medicare Advantage HMO and PPO?
atoms.text: A Medicare Advantage HMO plan usually helps pay only for care you receive from providers in the plan network. A PPO plan will generally help pay for care received outside the plan network, but it may pay less than for the same care received within the network.
qs: HMO or PPO for Medicare Advantage?
Does a Medicare PPO cover out-of-network doctors?
Do HMO plans cover care outside the network?

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage versus Medicare Supplement
atoms.q: What's the difference between a Medicare Advantage plan and a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: A Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan combines Part A, Part B, and often Part D drug coverage in one plan, may include benefits like hearing, vision, dental and fitness, and has an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs on covered services. A Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plan helps with some out-of-pocket costs that Original Medicare doesn't pay, like coinsurance and copayments. You can have either a Medicare Advantage plan or a Medicare Supplement plan, but not both at the same time.
qs: Should I choose Medicare Advantage or Medigap?
Can I have Medicare Advantage and Medigap together?
Does Medicare Advantage have an out-of-pocket limit?

atoms.title: Medigap open enrollment and guaranteed issue
atoms.q: When can I apply for Medicare Supplement insurance?
atoms.text: The best time to enroll in a Medicare Supplement plan is during your Medicare Supplement Open Enrollment period because acceptance is guaranteed. It starts on the first day of the month in which you are both age 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. Some states have additional Open Enrollment periods and Guaranteed Issue requirements. If you apply outside these periods, you may be denied coverage or charged more based on your health history, except in Connecticut and New York, where open enrollment and guaranteed issue is ongoing.
qs: Can I be denied a Medigap plan?
When is Medigap acceptance guaranteed?
Is Medigap guaranteed in New York?

atoms.title: Special Enrollment Period for life events
atoms.q: What is a Medicare Special Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: Medicare grants a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) when you are working past 65 with creditable coverage from your employer and for certain qualifying life events. The SEP for working past 65 gives eight months to enroll in Part A and Part B, but only the first two months to get a Medicare Advantage (Part C) and Part D plan without penalty. A separate 2-month SEP exists for people who already have Medicare and have a qualifying life event, such as moving to a state where their Medicare Advantage plan is not offered.
qs: What qualifies me for a Medicare SEP?
Can I switch plans if I move?
How long is a Special Enrollment Period?

atoms.title: Automatic renewal and the Annual Notice of Change
atoms.q: Do I have to change plans every year or can I keep the same one?
atoms.text: If there are no changes to the contract or coverage area associated with your provider, your Medicare coverage should renew automatically, although plan benefits and costs may change even if a plan renews. You don't have to change plans, but you should always check your options. Review the Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) your insurer sends each fall, which lists any changes in plan coverage, costs, or service areas, and review choices during the Annual Enrollment Period from October 15 to December 7.
qs: Does my Medicare plan renew automatically?
What is the Annual Notice of Change?
Should I review my plan every year?

atoms.title: Costs of Original Medicare
atoms.q: How much does Original Medicare Part A and Part B cost?
atoms.text: Most people pay no premium for Medicare Part A. The premium for Medicare Part B depends on your income and may change each year. For both Part A and Part B there are also deductibles and coinsurance. With Original Medicare you will pay 20% coinsurance based on the Medicare-approved amount, including for inpatient care and durable medical equipment like a wheelchair or CPAP machine. Many Medicare Advantage plans also have a 20% coinsurance payment for certain services.
qs: How much is the Part B premium?
Is Medicare Part A free?
What is the 20% Medicare coinsurance?

atoms.title: Financial help paying for Medicare
atoms.q: Can I get financial help to pay for Medicare?
atoms.text: Financial assistance programs for people with limited income and assets include Extra Help for prescription drugs, Medicare Savings Programs and Medicaid. Program requirements and levels of support will vary. Extra Help is also called Low Income Subsidy (LIS), and a Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP) is a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage for people who have both Medicare and Medicaid.
qs: What is Extra Help?
How can I get help paying Medicare premiums?
What assistance is there for Medicare costs?

atoms.title: Where to compare plans and get free help
atoms.q: Where else can I compare Medicare plans, and what if I get overwhelmed?
atoms.text: The plan comparison page at Medicare.gov shows options from all providers, and you can compare 2027 plans available where you live, with results for premiums, projected drug spend, out-of-pocket costs and added benefits. You can also create a My Medicare account. For help, you can get answers from Medicare.gov or from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), which provides free Medicare help from trained counselors.
qs: Where can I compare all Medicare plans?
What is SHIP?
Where can I get free Medicare counseling?

atoms.title: What the Initial Enrollment Period is
atoms.q: What is the Medicare Initial Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: Your Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) is the first time you can sign up for Medicare due to age, disability or medical condition. During your IEP, you can enroll in Original Medicare (Part A and Part B), a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan, and/or a Medicare Advantage plan, also called Part C.
qs: What is IEP in Medicare?
When can I first sign up for Medicare?
What plans can I enroll in during my IEP?

atoms.title: IEP dates by eligibility reason
atoms.q: When does my Initial Enrollment Period begin and end?
atoms.text: If you become eligible for Medicare by turning 65, your IEP begins three months before the month of your 65th birthday and ends three months after your 65th birthday month. If you become eligible due to disability, your IEP begins three months before the month of your 25th Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) benefit payment and ends three months after that month. If you become eligible due to a medical condition, your IEP happens much sooner: within a few months for end stage renal disease (ESRD), or right away for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
qs: When does my Medicare IEP start if I'm on disability?
How soon can I get Medicare with ALS?
When can I sign up before my 65th birthday?

atoms.title: Automatic enrollment versus signing up yourself
atoms.q: Will I be enrolled in Medicare automatically at 65?
atoms.text: If you start receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits before you turn 65, you should be enrolled in Medicare automatically. If not, you will need to sign up by yourself, online at www.ssa.gov, in person at your local Social Security office or by phone at 1-800-772-1213 / TTY 1-800-325-0778. You may not be notified when you become eligible, so find your Initial Enrollment Period dates and put them in your calendar.
qs: Do I need to apply for Medicare myself?
How do I sign up for Original Medicare?
Will Social Security enroll me in Medicare?

atoms.title: Working past 65 and the IEP
atoms.q: Do I need Medicare if I work past age 65?
atoms.text: If you expect to continue working past age 65, you may want to delay enrolling in Medicare. If you have health coverage from your employer or are covered under a spouse's employer plan, you may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period and be able to delay enrolling without penalty. In some situations, such as working for an employer with fewer than 20 employees, you may still be required to take full Medicare benefits at age 65. If you plan to work past 65, you will need to compare your employer health insurance with what you would get through Medicare.
qs: Can I skip Medicare while still working?
What if my employer has fewer than 20 employees?
Should I compare my job insurance to Medicare?

atoms.title: What happens if you miss your IEP
atoms.q: What if I miss my Initial Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: You can enroll in Original Medicare during the General Enrollment Period (GEP) between January 1 and March 31. Medicare Part A, Part B and Part D may charge premium penalties if you miss your initial enrollment dates, unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period (SEP). If you enroll in Original Medicare during the GEP, you may be able to add a Medicare Advantage plan or Part D plan between April 1 and June 30 of the same year.
qs: What do I do if I missed Medicare enrollment?
Can I add Part D after the General Enrollment Period?
Will I pay a penalty for signing up late?

atoms.title: Medigap requires Parts A and B first
atoms.q: When can I apply for a Medigap plan?
atoms.text: Once you are enrolled in both Medicare Part A and Part B, you can apply for a Medicare Supplement insurance (Medigap) plan.
qs: Do I need Part B to buy Medigap?
When can I apply for a Medicare Supplement plan?
What do I need before applying for Medigap?

atoms.title: When Medicare coverage starts after enrolling
atoms.q: When will my Medicare coverage start once I enroll?
atoms.text: After you complete your Initial Enrollment Period sign-up, your coverage begins on the first day of the following month; for example, completing enrollment on June 25 means coverage starts July 1. If you qualify for premium-free Part A, coverage begins on the first day of the month you turn 65 (or the month before, if your birthday is on the first). For Part B and premium Part A, signing up before you turn 65 starts coverage the first day of your birthday month; signing up in your birthday month or the three months after starts coverage the first day of the following month.
qs: When does Medicare Part B start?
If I enroll in June, when does coverage begin?
When does premium-free Part A start?

atoms.title: What Medicare is
atoms.q: What is Medicare?
atoms.text: Medicare is health insurance for people 65 or older who meet citizenship or residency requirements. You may be eligible sooner if you have a disability or qualifying medical condition. Original Medicare is provided by the federal government, while other Medicare plans are offered by private insurance companies.
qs: What is Medicare?
Who provides Medicare coverage?
Who is eligible for Medicare?

atoms.title: Original Medicare: Part A and Part B
atoms.q: What is Original Medicare?
atoms.text: Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) is health insurance provided by the federal government. Part A helps pay for hospital stays and inpatient care. Part B helps pay for doctor visits and outpatient care.
qs: What do Part A and Part B cover?
What is Original Medicare?
What is the difference between Part A and Part B?

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans
atoms.q: What are Medicare Advantage plans?
atoms.text: Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans offer all the benefits of Original Medicare, many with extras like dental, vision, and hearing benefits. Most include prescription drug coverage. These plans are offered by private insurance companies.
qs: What is Part C?
What extra benefits does Medicare Advantage have?
Does Medicare Advantage include Part D?

atoms.title: Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap)
atoms.q: What are Medicare Supplement Insurance plans?
atoms.text: Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) plans help pay for some of the out-of-pocket costs not covered by Original Medicare, such as medical copayments, coinsurance and deductibles.
qs: What does Medigap cover?
How do I pay for costs Original Medicare doesn't cover?
What is a Medicare Supplement plan?

atoms.title: Medicare Part D plans: PDP and MAPD
atoms.q: What are Medicare Part D plans?
atoms.text: Medicare Part D plans help cover the costs of prescription drugs. You can enroll in a standalone plan (PDP) or choose a Medicare Advantage plan that includes prescription drug coverage (MAPD).
qs: What does PDP mean?
What does MAPD mean?
How do I get prescription coverage with Medicare?

atoms.title: What a Special Needs plan (SNP) is
atoms.q: What is a Medicare Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: A Special Needs plan (SNP) is a Medicare Advantage plan with benefits designed to meet specific health care or financial needs. You may be eligible for a SNP if you meet certain conditions. There are three kinds of Special Needs plans: Dual, Chronic, and Institutional.
qs: What is a SNP?
What kinds of Special Needs plans exist?
Is a Special Needs plan a Medicare Advantage plan?

atoms.title: Dual Special Needs plans (D-SNPs)
atoms.q: What is a Dual Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: Dual Special Needs plans (D-SNPs) are Medicare Advantage plans for people who have both Medicare and Medicaid coverage. They combine Original Medicare benefits, prescription drug coverage and support to help coordinate benefits with Medicaid.
qs: What is a D-SNP?
Which Medicare plan coordinates with Medicaid?
Do D-SNPs include drug coverage?

atoms.title: Chronic Special Needs plans (C-SNPs)
atoms.q: What is a Chronic Special Needs plan?
atoms.text: Chronic Special Needs plans (C-SNPs) are Medicare Advantage plans designed for people living with specific chronic or disabling long term health conditions, such as diabetes, chronic heart failure or cardiovascular disorders.
qs: What is a C-SNP?
Is there a Medicare plan for diabetes?
What conditions does a Chronic Special Needs plan serve?

atoms.title: I-SNPs versus IE-SNPs
atoms.q: What is the difference between an I-SNP and an IE-SNP?
atoms.text: Institutional Special Needs plans (I-SNPs) are specialized Medicare Advantage plans designed for people who live in a long term care setting such as a nursing home. Institutional Equivalent Special Needs plans (IE-SNPs) are specialized Medicare Advantage plans for individuals who need nursing home-level care and live in assisted living, independent living or memory care communities.

Is there a Medicare plan for assisted living?
What is an IE-SNP?

atoms.title: Getting ready if you plan to work past 65
atoms.q: I plan to work past age 65. What do I need to do about Medicare?
atoms.text: Start researching your Medicare options at least 6 months before your 65th birthday, looking for coverage that meets your needs. Find out the dates for your Initial Enrollment Period (IEP), a 7-month period surrounding your 65th birthday. You may not need to enroll in both Part A and Part B right away, but knowing your IEP dates will help you plan.
qs: When should I start researching Medicare if I'm still working?
How long is my IEP?
Do I have to enroll in Part A and B at 65 if I work?

atoms.title: Employer size and your Medicare options
atoms.q: Do I have to get Medicare if I have employer coverage?
atoms.text: If you are still working and have health coverage through your employer or union, including federal or state employment, active-duty military service, or a spouse's work, you may want to delay Medicare. If your employer has fewer than 20 employees, you may need to enroll in Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period. If your employer has 20 or more employees, you may delay Medicare enrollment, drop your employer coverage for Medicare, or have both. For a spouse's employer, review the employer's rules.

Can I have both Medicare and employer insurance?
Does a small employer change when I must enroll?

atoms.title: Questions for your benefits administrator
atoms.q: What should I ask my benefits administrator before enrolling in Medicare?
atoms.text: The main question to ask your benefits administrator is whether you should keep your existing coverage. Ask if Medicare can work with your employer plan and if retiree coverage is available. Also ask how changing your insurance would affect your spouse and any dependents, and find out whether they will be eligible for COBRA if you drop employer coverage.
qs: What should I ask HR about Medicare?
Will my spouse lose coverage if I drop my employer plan?
Can Medicare work alongside my employer plan?

atoms.title: Delaying both Part A and Part B
atoms.q: Can I delay Medicare Part A and Part B without penalty?
atoms.text: If you qualify, you can delay both Medicare Part A and Part B without penalty. When you stop working or lose employer coverage, whichever comes first, you will need to enroll during a Special Enrollment Period. To avoid Part D penalties, you will also need to provide written proof of creditable prescription drug coverage, meaning a plan expected to pay, on average, at least as much as Medicare drug coverage does.

What proof of creditable coverage do I need?
When do I need to enroll after I stop working?

atoms.title: Enrolling in Part A only while working
atoms.q: Can I enroll in only Part A while I'm still working?
atoms.text: Medicare Part A is premium-free for most people, so you could enroll in only Part A while still working. If you have a health savings account (HSA), you will have to stop making contributions once you enroll in Part A. You can still use the funds for qualified medical expenses, including some Medicare costs such as premiums, deductibles and copays.
qs: Is Part A free if I'm still working?
Does enrolling in Part A stop my HSA contributions?
Can I use my HSA to pay Medicare costs?

atoms.title: Why some people delay Part B
atoms.q: Why would someone delay enrolling in Part B while working?
atoms.text: Medicare Part B charges a premium. Some people who work past 65 and have employer coverage delay enrolling in Part B and postpone paying the premium, then sign up later during a Special Enrollment Period. In some situations, such as when an employer has fewer than 20 employees, you may need to get Part B during your Initial Enrollment Period to avoid penalties. Most people pay the standard Part B premium, and people with higher incomes may pay more.
qs: Do I have to pay the Part B premium while working?
When must I take Part B if my employer is small?
Do high earners pay more for Part B?

atoms.title: Check for creditable drug coverage before delaying
atoms.q: Why do I need creditable drug coverage before delaying Medicare?
atoms.text: Before you officially delay Medicare, make sure you have creditable drug coverage, meaning your employer provides drug coverage at least as good as standard Medicare Part D coverage. If your employer's drug coverage isn't creditable, you will need to enroll in a Part D plan during your Initial Enrollment Period to avoid the Part D late enrollment penalty. You will also need to get either Part A or Part B in order to get a Part D plan.

Do I need Part B to get a Part D plan?
How do I avoid a Part D penalty while working?

atoms.title: Having both Medicare and employer coverage
atoms.q: Can I have both Medicare and employer coverage?
atoms.text: Yes. Ask your benefits administrator how your employer plan will work with Medicare. Depending on your situation, one will act as your primary coverage and one as secondary.
qs: Which pays first, Medicare or my employer plan?
Can I keep my job insurance and have Medicare?
What is primary vs secondary coverage?

atoms.title: How COBRA and Medicare work together
atoms.q: How do COBRA and Medicare work together?
atoms.text: If you have COBRA before Medicare, you will need to enroll in Medicare when you become eligible; you may delay Part D if COBRA includes creditable drug coverage, otherwise you have 63 days to get Part D without penalty after losing COBRA. If you enroll in Medicare Part A and Part B before COBRA, you can have both, but COBRA is optional, Medicare is primary and COBRA is secondary. If you enroll in Part A only before COBRA, you must enroll in Part B within eight months of your employment ending to avoid penalties.

How long do I have to enroll in Part B after COBRA?
Does Medicare or COBRA pay first?

atoms.title: TRICARE, CHAMPVA and FEHB with Medicare
atoms.q: How do TRICARE, CHAMPVA and FEHB work with Medicare?
atoms.text: If you have TRICARE or CHAMPVA coverage, you will need to see if you qualify for premium-free Part A; if eligible, you may be required to enroll in both Part A and Part B to keep that coverage, and if not eligible, enrollment is optional but late penalties are possible. If you receive Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB), you can delay enrolling in Part A and/or Part B if your insurance is based on employment, or a spouse's employment, with an employer that has 20 or more employees.

Can federal employees delay Medicare?
How does CHAMPVA work with Medicare?

atoms.title: Enrolling in Medicare when you retire
atoms.q: What happens when I retire if I delayed Medicare?
atoms.text: If you qualify for Medicare and delay enrollment past age 65, you will have a Special Enrollment Period once you retire or lose your employer coverage. If you choose a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage or a standalone Part D plan, you have 63 days to enroll without penalty. If you choose Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) only, you have up to 8 months. The 8-month SEP gives up to 8 months for Parts A and/or B, but only the first two months to enroll in Parts C and/or D.

How long is the SEP after I lose employer coverage?
When must I join a Part D plan after leaving my job?

atoms.title: Notify Social Security to delay Part B
atoms.q: What else do I need to do if I delay Medicare enrollment?
atoms.text: If you receive Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits, you should be enrolled in Medicare Part A and Part B automatically when you turn 65. If you receive Social Security benefits and are eligible for Medicare, you should enroll in Part A. If you want to delay enrollment in Part B, you will need to notify the Social Security Administration.
