This article describes four types: Essential, Value, Advantage and Copay Focus, each with its own mix of premium and deductible.
qs: What are the UnitedHealthcare ACA plan types?
How do I choose among ACA plan types?

atoms.title: The Essential plan
atoms.q: What is the UnitedHealthcare Essential ACA plan?
atoms.text: The Essential plan is a high-deductible plan with basic coverage for serious illness or injury, shown as premium $ and deductible $$$$. You pay a lower monthly premium but more when you get care, so it fits people who rarely see a provider but want a low-cost way to protect against worst-case scenarios. Essential plans are available only at the Bronze metal level and only when shopping off-exchange directly from UnitedHealthcare or through a licensed insurance agent.
qs: Is the Essential plan on the Marketplace?
Who is a high-deductible Bronze plan good for?

atoms.title: The Value plan
atoms.q: What is the UnitedHealthcare Value ACA plan?
atoms.text: The Value plan is shown as premium $$ and deductible $$. It offers a low or even $0 monthly premium, a moderate deductible, and a mix of copays and coinsurance when you get care. Some Value plans offer a Health Savings Account (HSA) option. It may fit people who see a provider regularly and want more benefits covered than an Essential plan, and it is available in all markets on all metal levels.
qs: Do Value plans have an HSA option?
Can I get a $0 premium on a Value plan?

atoms.title: The Advantage plan
atoms.q: What is the UnitedHealthcare Advantage ACA plan?
atoms.text: The Advantage plan is shown as premium $$$ and deductible $. You invest in a higher monthly premium to benefit from a lower deductible, pay manageable copays for many services, and reach your low deductible faster. It is a good match if you see your provider often and are willing to pay a little more each month to pay less when you get care. Advantage plans are available in most markets on Silver and Gold metal levels.
qs: Which ACA plan has a low deductible?
Are Advantage plans available in Silver and Gold?

atoms.title: The Copay Focus plan
atoms.q: What is the UnitedHealthcare Copay Focus ACA plan?
atoms.text: Copay Focus plans are shown as premium $$$$ with no deductible. They are designed to help you know what your care may cost before you head to the provider. You pay a moderate premium and have a $0 medical deductible, so the plan begins to pay its portion from day one, and you pay fixed copays when you get care. A deductible may apply for some prescription drug benefits. Copay Focus plans are available in all metal levels.
qs: Which ACA plan has fixed copays?
Does Copay Focus have a deductible for prescriptions?

atoms.title: Qualifying for a $0 monthly premium
atoms.q: What is required to get a $0 monthly premium?
atoms.text: The article notes that to qualify for a $0 monthly premium you must meet household income requirements for Advanced Premium Tax Credits. It mentions a low or even $0 monthly premium in connection with Value plans.
qs: How do I get a $0 premium ACA plan?
Does a $0 premium depend on income?

atoms.title: What are ACA Marketplace plans?
atoms.q: What are ACA Marketplace plans?
atoms.text: ACA Marketplace plans are health care coverage plans that people can buy on their own, rather than through an employer or another government-run program, like Medicare or Medicaid. You may also hear names like Exchange Plans and Individual & Family Plans. The health care Marketplace (also called the Exchange) is where ACA health care plans are sold.
qs: What is an ACA Marketplace plan?
What are Exchange plans?

atoms.title: Premium
atoms.q: What is a premium on an ACA plan?
atoms.text: A premium is the amount you pay for your ACA health insurance plan every month. The premium amount can vary depending on the metal level and plan type you choose. UnitedHealthcare says it can help estimate your premium and find out if you qualify for a $0 monthly premium, which requires meeting household income requirements for Advanced Premium Tax Credits (APTC).
qs: What does premium mean in health insurance?
How do I qualify for a $0 monthly premium?

atoms.title: Deductible
atoms.q: What is a deductible on an ACA plan?
atoms.text: A deductible is the amount you pay for your covered medical services before your ACA health plan starts to kick in. UnitedHealthcare has a variety of plan options, from low or $0 deductibles to high deductible plans. Copay Focus plans offer a $0 medical deductible, though a deductible may apply for some prescription drug benefits.
qs: What is a deductible in health insurance?
Which ACA plans have a $0 deductible?

atoms.title: Copayment
atoms.q: What is a copayment on an ACA plan?
atoms.text: A copayment is the fixed amount you'll pay for a covered medical service at the time of getting care, and the amount can vary depending on the service. If you prefer predictable copays, UnitedHealthcare offers Copay Focus plans with low copays for most covered services, so you can plan your family's medical expenses ahead of time.
qs: What does copay mean?
Which plan has predictable copays?

atoms.title: Coinsurance
atoms.q: What is coinsurance on an ACA plan?
atoms.text: Coinsurance is the portion that you're responsible for paying for a covered medical service. It is one of the cost terms UnitedHealthcare lists for understanding the costs of ACA Marketplace coverage, alongside premium, deductible, copayment and out-of-pocket max.
qs: What is coinsurance in health insurance?
How is coinsurance different from a copay?

atoms.title: Out-of-pocket max
atoms.q: What is an out-of-pocket maximum?
atoms.text: The out-of-pocket max is the maximum amount you'll have to pay during the policy period, usually a calendar year, before your health insurance starts to cover 100% of the covered amount.
qs: What is the most I could pay in a year on an ACA plan?
What happens after I hit my out-of-pocket max?

atoms.title: Subsidy
atoms.q: What is a subsidy for ACA plans?
atoms.text: A subsidy is money granted by the government to offer health coverage at a reduced cost, or even for no cost, to low-income individuals. UnitedHealthcare offers a subsidy calculator to see if you qualify for savings.
qs: What is a health insurance subsidy?
How do I see if I qualify for ACA savings?

atoms.title: Network
atoms.q: What is a network on an ACA plan?
atoms.text: A network includes the facilities, doctors and providers that are contracted to provide care for you when you have ACA Marketplace health insurance coverage. Check the provider network before enrolling in a plan or getting care so you can avoid having to pay out-of-network costs.
qs: What does in-network mean?
How do I avoid out-of-network costs?

atoms.title: Formulary
atoms.q: What is a formulary or drug list?
atoms.text: A formulary, also known as a drug list, is a list of commonly used medications organized into different cost levels called tiers, with costs decided by a health insurer. You can view the Prescription Drug List (PDL) to see what's covered by an Individual & Family plan.
qs: What is a formulary?
Where can I see which drugs my ACA plan covers?

atoms.title: Enrollment status noted in the terms guide
atoms.q: Can I still enroll if open enrollment has ended?
atoms.text: The article notes that open enrollment for 2026 Individual & Family ACA Marketplace plans has ended. It adds that people looking for coverage outside the open enrollment period may qualify for a special enrollment period.
qs: What if I missed ACA open enrollment?
Can I get a special enrollment period?

atoms.title: Act quickly after losing Medicaid or CHIP
atoms.q: How long do I have to enroll in an ACA plan after losing Medicaid?
atoms.text: You have a limited time to enroll in an ACA plan after losing Medicaid eligibility. If you lose Medicaid or Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) coverage, you may qualify for a special enrollment period (SEP). SEPs last for a limited time, so don't wait.
qs: What happens if I lose Medicaid coverage?
Is there a deadline to enroll in an ACA plan after Medicaid ends?

atoms.title: Applying early to avoid a coverage gap
atoms.q: Can I apply for an ACA plan before my Medicaid ends?
atoms.text: You can apply and enroll in an ACA Marketplace plan as early as 60 days before your Medicaid or CHIP coverage ends. Applying early helps prevent a gap in coverage, which can help you avoid unexpected health care costs.
qs: How early can I enroll in a Marketplace plan before Medicaid ends?
How do I avoid a gap in coverage after Medicaid?

atoms.title: Understanding ACA plan options after Medicaid
atoms.q: What do ACA Marketplace plans cover compared to Medicaid?
atoms.text: ACA Marketplace plans cover 10 essential health benefits. Depending on the plan, they can offer a wide range of health benefits, including medical, dental and vision coverage, and even mental health and fitness benefits.
qs: What benefits do ACA plans include?
Do ACA plans cover dental and vision?

atoms.title: Savings available when moving from Medicaid
atoms.q: Can I get financial help for an ACA plan after Medicaid?
atoms.text: Depending on your income, you may be eligible for subsidies, or savings. These come in the form of premium tax credits to lower your monthly premium cost and cost-sharing reductions to help cover your cost for care. You can see an estimate of your savings and apply for subsidies during the enrollment process.
qs: How much will an ACA plan cost after Medicaid?
Can I get a tax credit after losing Medicaid?

atoms.title: Enrolling during open enrollment or with a SEP
atoms.q: When can I enroll after Medicaid, and what documents might I need?
atoms.text: You can enroll in an ACA Marketplace plan during the annual open enrollment period, which typically runs November 1 to January 15 in most states. If you qualify for a SEP due to the loss of Medicaid coverage, you may be asked to provide documentation to confirm your eligibility. SEPs are time-sensitive, so apply before your SEP ends.
qs: Do I need to prove I lost Medicaid to enroll?
When does open enrollment run?

atoms.title: Changes when moving from Medicaid to Marketplace
atoms.q: How is an ACA plan different from Medicaid?
atoms.text: According to the article's video, a new plan may have a monthly premium, which you should pay each month to avoid gaps in coverage. The plan has a network of doctors, specialists and pharmacies, and care out of network means you pay your care expenses out of pocket. You may also need a primary care provider referral approved by UnitedHealthcare before seeing an in-network specialist.
qs: What is a premium for someone coming from Medicaid?
Do I need a referral for a specialist on an ACA plan?

atoms.title: Getting help after losing Medicaid
atoms.q: Where can I get help moving to an ACA plan?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare provides 1-on-1 guidance from a licensed agent at no cost to help you find the plan that fits your needs after Medicaid. Members who need help at any time can call the phone number on the back of their health plan ID card or start a chat through their online account.
qs: Is there free help finding a plan after Medicaid?
How do I contact support for my ACA plan?

atoms.title: What is the No Surprises Act?
atoms.q: What is the No Surprises Act and balance billing?
atoms.text: Until 2022, it was legal for out-of-network providers involved in a patient's care, such as an anesthesiologist or an air ambulance, to bill the patient the difference between the plan's discounted rate and their full fee. That practice is known as balance billing. Thanks to the No Surprises Act, balance billing is now outlawed unless the patient provides consent.
qs: What is the No Surprises Act?
What is balance billing?
Can an out-of-network doctor bill me the difference?

atoms.title: How common surprise bills were
atoms.q: How common were surprise medical bills before the law?
atoms.text: A 2020 study by the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker estimated that 1-in-5 emergency claims and 1-in-6 network hospitalizations included at least 1 surprise bill for out-of-network services. In 13% of cases, those bills amounted to more than $2,000 in expenses for patients.
qs: How often do surprise medical bills happen?
How much are typical surprise bills?

atoms.title: What the No Surprises Act covers in emergencies
atoms.q: What emergency care does the No Surprises Act cover?
atoms.text: The law applies to people with private health insurance and covers most emergency care in an air ambulance, a hospital ER and a freestanding emergency room. Everything that happens until the patient is stabilized is covered. The protections still apply even if the final diagnosis is not something most people would consider an emergency, so a plan cannot deny coverage just because the diagnosis turns out to be gas rather than appendicitis.
qs: Does the No Surprises Act cover emergency room visits?
Is an air ambulance covered?

atoms.title: Nonemergency care at network facilities is protected
atoms.q: Does the No Surprises Act cover planned care?
atoms.text: The No Surprises Act also applies to certain nonemergency care. For a planned procedure at a network hospital or facility, no one who treats the patient there can charge more than the network rates, regardless of whether they are individually part of the patient's plan.
qs: Can an out-of-network doctor at an in-network hospital bill me extra?
Does the No Surprises Act apply to planned surgery?

atoms.title: What the No Surprises Act does not cover
atoms.q: What is not covered by the No Surprises Act?
atoms.text: The No Surprises Act does not cover deductibles, copays and coinsurance, ground ambulances (even in emergencies), out-of-network urgent care centers, birthing centers or nursing homes. If a person thinks there is an error in their situation, they can file a complaint with the federal No Surprises Help Desk at 800-985-3059.
qs: Are ground ambulances covered by the No Surprises Act?
Who do I call to file a No Surprises complaint?

atoms.title: Out-of-network consent rules
atoms.q: Can I decline out-of-network care consent forms?
atoms.text: If an out-of-network specialist will provide care, they need to provide a written consent form along with a cost estimate and a list of other in-network providers within 72 hours of treatment. If asked to consent to out-of-network care, a person can decline. People have a right to information in another language and to accommodations for disabilities.
qs: Do I have to consent to out-of-network care?
What paperwork must out-of-network providers give me?

atoms.title: Three ways to avoid surprise bills
atoms.q: How can I avoid surprise medical bills?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare lists three strategies. 1) Comparison shop by getting cost estimates from local providers; members can see cost and quality information for more than 820 common medical services on myuhc.com or in the app. 2) Stay in-network for non-emergency care. 3) Confirm that screenings are covered, since some advanced screenings may not count as preventive services; a preauthorization form can be completed in advance if needed.
qs: How do I avoid surprise medical bills?
How do I compare costs before getting care?

atoms.title: Out-of-network care costs exceed $40 billion a year
atoms.q: Why is staying in-network important?
atoms.text: For non-emergency care, UnitedHealthcare advises starting with network health care services and facilities, including preventive care, lab work and other tests. Receiving care from an out-of-network provider or facility can lead to a surprise charge, with the total cost of this type of care exceeding $40 billion for Americans each year.
qs: Why should I stay in network?
How much do out-of-network surprise charges cost Americans?

atoms.title: What to do about a billing mistake
atoms.q: What should I do if there is a billing mistake?
atoms.text: Before or around billing, a person receives an explanation of benefits (EOB), which says it is not a bill but lists what the plan paid, what might be owed and deductible status, and can show charges for services not received. If there is an unexpected charge, 1) call the provider's billing office to confirm it or ask for it to be waived or reduced. 2) For a surprise out-of-network bill, call the number on the health plan ID card. 3) For unresolved issues, contact the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059.
qs: What do I do about an unexpected medical bill?
How can I use my EOB to find billing errors?

atoms.title: Members can view bills online
atoms.q: Where can UnitedHealthcare members see their bills?
atoms.text: Many insurers' websites let people view their bills. UnitedHealthcare members can view bills online by signing in to their account or in the My Plan section of the UnitedHealthcare app. This shows everything being billed to the member, everything UnitedHealthcare paid, and requests from providers to UnitedHealthcare.
qs: Where can I see my medical bills online?
What does the My Plan section show?

atoms.title: Naviguard helped a member with an out-of-network balance bill
atoms.q: How can UnitedHealthcare help with out-of-network balance bills?
atoms.text: In a member story featured in the article, a UnitedHealthcare member named Darren received an out-of-network bill from an assistant surgeon he had not known was involved in his surgery. His wife Marva described the original bill as like a $34,000 bill. The UnitedHealthcare Naviguard services team reminded them they were not obligated to pay the balance bill because it is prohibited under the No Surprises Act.
qs: What is Naviguard?
Can UnitedHealthcare help with out-of-network bills?

atoms.title: What are ACA Marketplace plans?
atoms.q: What is an ACA Marketplace plan?
atoms.text: ACA Marketplace plans are health care plans that people can buy on their own, rather than through an employer or another government-run program, like Medicare or Medicaid. The article explains that these plans can be bought either on-exchange or off-exchange.
qs: What is an ACA plan?
Can I buy ACA plans outside the Marketplace?

atoms.title: On-exchange ACA plans
atoms.q: What is an on-exchange ACA plan?
atoms.text: On-exchange plans are plans that you purchase through the health insurance Marketplace. These plans are ACA-compliant, meaning they must cover 10 essential health benefits. If you shop on-exchange you may be eligible for financial help in the form of monthly premium subsidies and cost-sharing reductions, which can significantly lower what you pay each month and your out-of-pocket costs when you receive care.
qs: What does on-exchange mean?
Do on-exchange plans qualify for subsidies?

atoms.title: Off-exchange ACA plans
atoms.q: What is an off-exchange ACA plan?
atoms.text: Off-exchange plans are health insurance plans you buy directly from an insurance company or broker, outside of the health insurance Marketplace. They still fall under ACA compliance, providing minimum coverage and essential health benefits, but may offer more flexibility in coverage options. One of the biggest differences is that you won't be eligible for the premium subsidies and cost-sharing reductions available with on-exchange plans.
qs: What is an off-exchange plan?
Are off-exchange plans ACA compliant?

atoms.title: On-exchange versus off-exchange at a glance
atoms.q: How do on-exchange and off-exchange ACA plans differ?
atoms.text: On-exchange plans are bought through the health insurance Marketplace and may come with premium subsidies and cost-sharing reductions. Off-exchange plans are bought directly from an insurance company or broker and are not eligible for those subsidies, but may offer more flexibility in coverage options. Both are ACA-compliant. The article labels on-exchange as subsidy smart and off-exchange as more options.
qs: On-exchange vs off-exchange: which is better?
Which type of ACA plan gets subsidies?

atoms.title: Off-exchange plans for high earners
atoms.q: When do off-exchange plans make sense for high earners?
atoms.text: If your income disqualifies you from Marketplace subsidies, off-exchange plans could offer comparable coverage, without the subsidy factored in, at a potentially lower premium. UnitedHealthcare lists being a high earner as one situation where an off-exchange plan might be a good fit.
qs: Should I buy off-exchange if I earn too much for subsidies?
Can an off-exchange plan have a lower premium?

atoms.title: Off-exchange plans with employer reimbursement
atoms.q: Why do ICHRA and QSEHRA users shop off-exchange?
atoms.text: Individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements (ICHRA) and qualified small employer health reimbursement arrangements (QSEHRA) allow employers to reimburse employees for some or all of the premiums for health insurance they purchase on their own. Most people who are offered an ICHRA or QSEHRA will not qualify for subsidies and will likely need to shop off-exchange plans.
qs: Do I need an off-exchange plan if my employer offers an ICHRA?
Can I get subsidies with a QSEHRA?

atoms.title: Off-exchange plans for specific coverage needs
atoms.q: Can off-exchange plans offer a wider variety of options?
atoms.text: Shopping off-exchange plans can offer a wider variety of options for those looking for different plans, one of three situations the article lists where off-exchange may be a good fit; the others are being a high earner or having employer reimbursement. UnitedHealthcare advises considering factors like network coverage, premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket costs.
qs: What should I compare when shopping off-exchange?
Do off-exchange plans have more plan options?

atoms.title: No-cost help choosing an ACA plan
atoms.q: Does UnitedHealthcare offer help choosing between on- and off-exchange plans?
atoms.text: Whether you're looking for a subsidy-eligible on-exchange plan or an ICHRA-eligible off-exchange plan, UnitedHealthcare says it can help guide you through your choices. With an easy online enrollment process, UnitedHealthcare offers no-cost 1-on-1 help finding a plan to fit your needs.
qs: Is there free help choosing an ACA plan?
Can I get one-on-one help enrolling?

atoms.title: The ACA premium tax credit
atoms.q: What is the premium tax credit on an ACA plan?
atoms.text: When you start shopping for an ACA Marketplace plan, you'll find out if you qualify for a premium tax credit that lowers your monthly premium. It's already part of the UnitedHealthcare plan application, so you don't have to do any additional work to see if you qualify. Premium tax credits reduce monthly payments (premiums) paid to your insurance plan and cap the amount an individual or family must pay for health insurance.
qs: How do I find out if I qualify for a premium tax credit?
What does the premium tax credit do?

atoms.title: Premium tax credit size follows a sliding income scale
atoms.q: How is the size of the premium tax credit determined?
atoms.text: The size of the premium tax credit is based on a sliding income scale. People who have a lower income will get a larger credit to help cover the cost of their insurance.
qs: Do lower incomes get bigger ACA tax credits?
Is the ACA tax credit based on income?

atoms.title: What is cost-sharing?
atoms.q: What does cost-sharing mean in health insurance?
atoms.text: Cost sharing is literally sharing medical costs with your insurance company: you pay some costs out-of-pocket and your insurer pays some. Sometimes your insurer pays everything, for example you pay $0 for preventive care because your plan covers it at 100%. Sometimes you might be responsible for the full amount, like if a service isn't covered or you choose an out-of-network provider.
qs: What is cost sharing?
When do I pay the full cost of care?

atoms.title: Deductible, copay and coinsurance examples
atoms.q: What are examples of cost-sharing?
atoms.text: Examples of cost-sharing include a deductible, the amount you must spend on care covered by your health plan before they begin to pay; a copay, a set dollar amount you have to pay when you get care covered by your plan; and coinsurance, the percentage of the costs of a covered health care service you pay after you've paid your deductible.
qs: What is the difference between a deductible, copay and coinsurance?
What are the types of cost sharing?

atoms.title: What are cost-sharing reductions?
atoms.q: What are cost-sharing reductions on ACA plans?
atoms.text: Cost-sharing reductions, also called decreased cost-sharing or extra savings, are part of the Affordable Care Act and help people save on out-of-pocket costs when they get care. People who qualify may have a lower out-of-pocket maximum, and may also have lower copays and deductibles.
qs: What are extra savings on ACA plans?
Do cost-sharing reductions lower my deductible?

atoms.title: 2027 open enrollment start date
atoms.q: When does open enrollment for 2027 ACA plans start?
atoms.text: According to a note on the article page, open enrollment for 2027 Individual & Family ACA Marketplace plans starts November 1, 2026. The page also offers a link to get started for people looking for a 2026 plan.
qs: When can I sign up for 2027 ACA coverage?
What is the 2027 open enrollment start date?

atoms.title: Most adults 50+ rate their health good to excellent
atoms.q: How do older Americans rate their health?
atoms.text: More than three-quarters of Americans ages 50 and older rated their health as good to excellent, even if they have chronic conditions, according to a survey by AARP and National Geographic. More than 60% are taking steps to stay healthy, such as getting good sleep and maintaining a healthy weight.
qs: How healthy are older Americans?
What do people over 50 do to stay healthy?

atoms.title: What healthy aging means
atoms.q: What is healthy aging?
atoms.text: Healthy aging is not just about preventing disease, but also about fostering resilience, maintaining independence and ensuring a high quality of life, according to Dr. Kien Vuu quoted in the article. It also means having the energy and physical ability to go about day-to-day activities well. The article notes aging begins in our 30s and 40s, and it is never too late to improve the aging process.
qs: What does healthy aging mean?
When should I start thinking about healthy aging?

atoms.title: Eat more heart-healthy foods
atoms.q: What should older adults eat to protect their hearts?
atoms.text: To help lower cholesterol, aim for a diet with plenty of vegetables, fruits and fiber, and healthy sources of protein such as poultry, seafood, beans and other legumes. Limit sodium, refined carbohydrates, processed foods and red meats, cut back on saturated fats, and swap in mono- and polyunsaturated fats from fish, olive oil, nuts and seeds. Eating well and being active may also help maintain a healthy weight.
qs: What diet lowers cholesterol?
What foods are heart healthy as you age?

atoms.title: Strengthen your muscles as you age
atoms.q: How much exercise do older adults need?
atoms.text: Staying active is key as people get older. That includes at least 150 minutes per week of activities that get your heart pumping, such as brisk walking, dancing or swimming laps, plus a few muscle-building sessions per week, such as push-ups, squats, lifting weights or digging in the garden. Strength training helps mobility and range of motion, which helps people move well and avoid injuries or falls.
qs: How many minutes of exercise per week do seniors need?
Does strength training prevent falls?

atoms.title: Added sugar intake versus American Heart Association limits
atoms.q: How much added sugar should I have?
atoms.text: Americans typically consume 17 teaspoons of added sugar a day, while the American Heart Association recommends 9 teaspoons for men and 6 teaspoons for women. Older adults are especially vulnerable to the effects of a high-sugar diet, as processed sugars can increase joint inflammation, cause metabolic issues and raise the risk of diabetes and heart disease.
qs: How many teaspoons of sugar a day is healthy?
What is the AHA sugar limit?

atoms.title: Mindfulness to manage stress
atoms.q: How can mindfulness help with aging?
atoms.text: Chronic stress may harm health, and the American Institute of Stress notes it speeds up the effects of aging by increasing inflammation and may even make vaccines less effective. A mindfulness practice, where you focus on your breath or sounds to stay in the present moment, may reduce stress and help you recognize negative thought patterns. Your primary care provider or a therapist can suggest strategies.
qs: Does stress make you age faster?
How do I start mindfulness?

atoms.title: Stay hydrated as you age
atoms.q: Why is hydration important for older adults?
atoms.text: A National Institutes of Health study found that not drinking enough fluids speeds up the effects of aging and raises the risk of chronic diseases such as heart failure, stroke and dementia, along with consuming too much salt. Water is not the only source of hydration, since foods with high water content include avocados, bananas, eggs and cucumbers.
qs: How much water should seniors drink?
What foods help with hydration?

atoms.title: Reach out to others to reduce isolation
atoms.q: How does social connection affect health?
atoms.text: Being socially isolated and lonely is a risk factor for heart disease and other chronic diseases. Regular social interactions, such as talking with neighbors, getting together with family and friends or joining organizations, can ward off loneliness and even boost immunity. Volunteering provides both regular social interaction and a sense of purpose, another habit that is helpful to aging well.
qs: Is loneliness bad for your health?
How can seniors stay socially connected?

atoms.title: Prioritize sleep for healthy aging
atoms.q: How much sleep do older adults need?
atoms.text: Getting at least 7 hours of high-quality sleep lets your body repair itself and has a powerful impact on metabolism, sugar and insulin control and the immune system. Sleep is essential for regulating mood, weight, stress and emotions. To sleep better, go outdoors for a while every day, especially early, block street light in the bedroom, and keep electronic devices in another room.
qs: How many hours of sleep do seniors need?
How can I sleep better as I age?

atoms.title: What electrolytes are and do
atoms.q: What are electrolytes and what do they do?
atoms.text: Electrolytes are chemicals and essential minerals in blood, sweat and urine. When they dissolve in the blood or other body fluids, they develop electric charges that send signals to nerves and muscles. Electrolytes help your body stay hydrated, regulate pH levels, support muscle and nerve function, and help regulate blood pressure, blood sugar and heart rate.
qs: What are electrolytes?
What do electrolytes do in the body?

atoms.title: Main electrolytes in the body
atoms.q: Which minerals are electrolytes?
atoms.text: Main electrolytes include bicarbonate, which balances pH and moves carbon dioxide through the bloodstream; calcium, which supports bones and teeth; chloride, which regulates fluids; magnesium, which supports heart, muscle and nerve function and helps regulate blood sugar; phosphate, which works with calcium; potassium, which helps cells, heart and muscles function; and sodium, which helps maintain fluid balance.
qs: What does potassium do?
What is the role of magnesium in the body?

atoms.title: How to get enough electrolytes
atoms.q: How do I get electrolytes?
atoms.text: You are likely getting all the electrolytes you need if you eat a healthy diet and drink an adequate amount of water. About 20% of an adult's water intake comes from food. UnitedHealthcare advises prioritizing healthy, whole foods with naturally occurring electrolytes.
qs: Do I need electrolyte drinks?
How much water comes from food?

atoms.title: Electrolytes, fluid balance and fluid loss
atoms.q: Why do electrolytes matter for hydration?
atoms.text: The balance of electrolytes and water in your body is closely linked. If your sodium levels are high, the body signals thirst to increase water intake, and your kidneys help balance electrolytes. Your body loses electrolytes when you sweat, vomit or have diarrhea, and you can replace them with food or fluids that contain electrolytes. Water does not contain electrolytes.
qs: Does water have electrolytes?
How do you replace electrolytes after vomiting?

atoms.title: Drinks that contain electrolytes
atoms.q: What drinks have electrolytes?
atoms.text: Fresh fruit or vegetable juice, bone broth and coconut water all contain electrolytes. Electrolyte drinks may benefit people with prolonged vomiting or diarrhea, especially children, people who work outside in hot climates and people who do prolonged, high-intensity exercise. Energy drinks, sports drinks and hydration powders usually contain electrolytes but may also have added sugar and artificial flavors, so check the label.
qs: Which drinks have electrolytes?
Are sports drinks good for hydration?

atoms.title: Foods that contain electrolytes
atoms.q: What foods have electrolytes?
atoms.text: Healthy, whole foods with naturally occurring electrolytes include tofu, low-fat dairy and some plant-based milks for calcium; fiber-rich foods such as leafy greens, beans, nuts and whole grains for magnesium; coconut water for potassium; lemon juice and raw honey for sodium, potassium and magnesium; and table salt for sodium and chloride.
qs: What foods are high in magnesium?
Which foods are good sources of potassium?

atoms.title: What causes an electrolyte imbalance
atoms.q: What causes an electrolyte imbalance?
atoms.text: Activity level, age, climate and altitude determine how many electrolytes your body needs, and that can change each day. Certain medications, vomiting or diarrhea, sweating and low water intake can throw levels off. Dehydration is a common condition that can lead to an electrolyte imbalance, such as after forgetting to drink water, an intense workout or a stomach flu.
qs: What causes low electrolytes?
Can medications cause an electrolyte imbalance?

atoms.title: Symptoms of electrolyte imbalance and dehydration
atoms.q: What are the symptoms of an electrolyte imbalance?
atoms.text: Symptoms of an electrolyte imbalance may include nausea and vomiting, muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat, numbness and tingling, constipation and confusion, although some people feel no signs. Signs of mild dehydration may include dry mouth, thirst, dark urine, headache, muscle cramps and not peeing much. Your provider may order blood tests to measure your electrolyte levels.
qs: What are signs of low electrolytes?
How are electrolyte levels tested?

atoms.title: Insurance coverage for electrolyte supplements
atoms.q: Does insurance cover electrolyte supplements?
atoms.text: Most health plans do not cover over-the-counter (OTC) supplements, but may cover those prescribed by a provider. You may be able to use your health savings account, if you have one, to pay for some supplements.
qs: Is Pedialyte covered by insurance?
Can I use my HSA for electrolyte supplements?

atoms.title: When an electrolyte imbalance needs medical attention
atoms.q: When should I seek medical attention for an electrolyte imbalance?
atoms.text: Electrolyte imbalances can become serious if left untreated. Depending on the electrolytes involved, a severe imbalance could make you feel dizzy or confused, cause a rapid or irregular heartbeat, or cause seizures. In those cases, you may need emergency treatment.
qs: When is low electrolytes an emergency?
Can an electrolyte imbalance cause seizures?

atoms.title: Many older adults take several prescriptions
atoms.q: How many prescriptions do older adults take?
atoms.text: According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data, in a given month 68% of older adults have three or more prescription drugs to manage, and 41% have five or more medications. With that many pills to remember, it can be easy to miss a dose or accidentally double up on one.
ents: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
qs: How many medications do seniors take?
Why is it hard to remember medications?

atoms.title: Risks of missed or incorrect doses
atoms.q: What happens if I miss or double my medication?
atoms.text: Missed or incorrect doses can lead to worsening of symptoms, trips to the emergency room and poor health over time. Skipping blood pressure medication can increase the risk of heart disease and stroke, according to the American Heart Association. Not taking diabetes medications as directed can lead to high blood sugar and risk of diabetic coma, or low blood sugar, which raises the risk of falls.
qs: What happens if I skip my blood pressure pill?
Why is taking medicine on time important?

atoms.title: Strategy 1: Make a medication list
atoms.q: How do I make a medication list?
atoms.text: Make a list with your doctor's help or review it together. Tell your doctor all medications you take, including prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins and supplements, and any concerns such as cost or side effects. For each medication ask: What is it for? How much do I take and how often? Are there side effects? Share the list with all your doctors and keep a copy in your wallet or purse.
qs: What should be on my medication list?
What should I ask my doctor about each medicine?

atoms.title: Strategy 2: Ask about easy ways to fill prescriptions
atoms.q: What are easier ways to fill prescriptions?
atoms.text: If getting to the pharmacy is difficult, check with your doctor, pharmacy or health plan for more convenient options, such as ordering a 90-day supply through home delivery by mail. Many pharmacies offer refill reminders by phone, text or email, can coordinate refills so you pick up multiple medications on the same day, or offer presorted packs of each day's medication.
qs: Can I get a 90-day supply by mail?
Do pharmacies offer refill reminders?

atoms.title: Strategy 3: Use a pill organizer
atoms.q: Does a pill organizer help?
atoms.text: An old-fashioned pillbox with separate tabs for each day of the week is still one of the simplest and most effective ways to organize your medications. There are many variations to shop around for, and you can upgrade to an electronic pillbox that will blink, beep or alert you with medication reminders.
qs: What is the best way to organize pills?
Are there electronic pillboxes?

atoms.title: Strategy 4: Store medication sensibly
atoms.q: Where should I store my medications?
atoms.text: Keep medications in a safe but easily accessible spot. The National Institutes of Health recommends a cool, dry place, like a kitchen shelf away from the stove or sink. If young children live with you or visit often, keep both prescription and over-the-counter medications out of their reach.
qs: How should I store prescription drugs?
Where should medicines be kept around kids?

atoms.title: Strategies 5 and 6: Routine and calendar
atoms.q: What daily routines help me remember medications?
atoms.text: Taking medications at the same time and place each day makes them easier to remember; set a phone alarm or sync doses with habits like eating breakfast or brushing your teeth. A large, easy-to-read calendar posted in a visible spot, such as the kitchen fridge, can help you track medications each day. Mark the calendar when you have taken your medicine.
qs: How do I build a medication routine?
Should I use a calendar for my medicines?

atoms.title: Strategy 7: Use a medication reminder app
atoms.q: Are there apps that remind me to take medications?
atoms.text: Several smartphone apps offer medication reminders and drug interaction information. Some help you set a medication schedule, and others prompt you to track healthy habits, such as drinking more water or checking your blood pressure. UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage members with prescription drug coverage can also download the UnitedHealthcare app to view drug coverage details.
qs: What app helps me take my pills on time?
Can I see my drug coverage in the UHC app?

atoms.title: Enrolling in any Medicare part ends HSA contributions
atoms.q: Can I contribute to an HSA after I enroll in Medicare?
atoms.text: Once you enroll in any part of Medicare, you're no longer eligible to make HSA contributions. This includes Medicare Part A or Medicare Part B; either one will prevent you from contributing further to your HSA. HSAs are built up with pre-tax contributions and used for qualified health expenses.
qs: Does Medicare stop HSA contributions?
Can I keep funding my HSA with Medicare Part A?
Why can't I contribute to an HSA on Medicare?

atoms.title: Part A is premium-free but ends HSA contributions
atoms.q: If I keep working, should I enroll in premium-free Part A and keep my HSA?
atoms.text: Many people turning 65 who continue to work consider getting Medicare Part A since it's premium-free, but once you enroll in Part A you can't make any more pre-tax contributions to your HSA. If you plan to keep working and want to continue building your HSA, check whether you're eligible to delay Medicare enrollment. However, if you're receiving Social Security benefits, Medicare Part A is mandatory.
qs: Should I delay Part A to keep contributing to my HSA?
Is Part A mandatory if I get Social Security?
How do I keep contributing to an HSA at 65?

atoms.title: Stop HSA contributions about 6 months early
atoms.q: When should I stop contributing to my HSA before enrolling in Medicare?
atoms.text: If you enroll in Medicare Part A, the coverage is retroactive for up to 6 months, but no earlier than your eligibility date. Because of this, you should plan to stop HSA contributions around 6 months before enrolling in Medicare. You can contribute to your HSA for the months that you were eligible for Medicare and were not yet enrolled.
qs: How far back does Part A coverage go?
When do I need to stop HSA contributions?
Can I contribute while eligible but not enrolled?

atoms.title: You can still spend HSA funds on Medicare costs
atoms.q: Can I still use my HSA funds after enrolling in Medicare?
atoms.text: Even after you enroll in Medicare and stop HSA contributions, you can still withdraw funds tax-free for qualified medical expenses. You can even use your HSA to pay for some Medicare expenses, including your Medicare Part B, Part D and Medicare Advantage plan premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance.
qs: Can I pay Medicare premiums with my HSA?
Are HSA withdrawals still tax-free on Medicare?
What Medicare expenses can an HSA cover?

atoms.title: HSA funds can cover items Medicare does not
atoms.q: What non-Medicare expenses can I use my HSA for?
atoms.text: In addition to traditional Medicare expenses, your HSA may also be used to cover a number of items and services that may not be covered by your Medicare plan. This may include long-term health care coverage, expenses associated with dental, hearing or vision, and other costs that the IRS considers qualified medical expenses.
qs: Can I use my HSA for dental and hearing on Medicare?
Can an HSA pay for long-term care?
What qualified expenses does the IRS allow for HSAs?

atoms.title: Social Security and using an HSA with Medicare
atoms.q: Will receiving Social Security benefits affect my ability to use an HSA with Medicare?
atoms.text: If you are receiving Social Security benefits and are 65 or older, you may have been automatically enrolled in Original Medicare (Part A and Part B). If you are enrolled in Medicare, you are no longer eligible to contribute to an HSA but can continue to use your HSA funds to help cover qualified medical expenses.
qs: Does Social Security auto-enrollment stop my HSA contributions?
Can I still spend my HSA if I'm on Social Security and Medicare?
Will I be enrolled in Medicare automatically if I collect Social Security?

atoms.title: Definition of creditable drug coverage
atoms.q: What is creditable drug coverage?
atoms.text: Medicare defines creditable coverage as coverage that is at least as good as what Medicare provides. Therefore, creditable drug coverage is drug coverage that is as good as or better than Medicare Part D.
qs: What does creditable coverage mean in Medicare?
Is my employer drug plan as good as Part D?
What is creditable prescription drug coverage?

atoms.title: Why creditable coverage matters
atoms.q: Why does creditable drug coverage matter?
atoms.text: Creditable drug coverage matters because it may allow you to delay enrolling in Medicare and avoid the Part D late enrollment penalty. The penalty is charged if you enroll in a Medicare Part D plan after your Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) ends and don't qualify for an exception.
qs: How can I avoid the Part D penalty?
Why is creditable coverage important?
When is the Part D late penalty charged?

atoms.title: Steps to delay Part D without penalty
atoms.q: What do I need to do to delay Part D enrollment without a penalty?
atoms.text: To delay Part D enrollment without penalty: 1) make sure you can qualify for a Medicare Special Enrollment Period; 2) get a written notification of creditable coverage from your previous plan; and 3) enroll in a Part D plan within 63 days of losing or leaving your former plan and/or the former creditable drug coverage.
qs: How many days do I have to join Part D after losing employer coverage?
What proof of creditable coverage do I need?
How do I avoid a Part D penalty when I retire?

atoms.title: Ask your benefits administrator if still working
atoms.q: How do I find out if my employer plan has creditable drug coverage?
atoms.text: Delaying Part D while keeping other drug coverage is typically seen most for people who plan to keep working past 65. If you are working past age 65 and plan to delay Medicare enrollment, talk with your employee benefits administrator, who can tell you if your employer plan provides creditable drug coverage.
qs: Who tells me if my work drug plan is creditable?
Should I enroll in Part D if I work past 65?
How do I know if my employer coverage counts?

atoms.title: Part D late penalty is 1% per month
atoms.q: How much is the Medicare Part D late enrollment penalty?
atoms.text: The late penalty for Medicare Part D is an additional 1 percent of the premium amount for each month you're late, and you pay the penalty for as long as you have Part D. For example, if you enroll in a Part D plan that starts on November 1 but your IEP ended on June 30, you are four months late and your penalty would be 4 percent of the premium.
qs: How is the Part D penalty calculated?
Does the Part D penalty ever go away?
What is the cost of enrolling late in Part D?

atoms.title: How to get Part D coverage
atoms.q: How do I get Medicare prescription drug coverage?
atoms.text: You can get Medicare prescription drug coverage in a stand-alone Part D plan or as part of a Medicare Advantage plan (Part C). Private insurance companies offer the plans under contract with Medicare. You will need to have Part A and/or Part B to get a stand-alone Part D plan, and you will need both Parts A and B to get a Medicare Advantage plan.
qs: How do I add drug coverage to Medicare?
Do I need both Part A and B for Medicare Advantage?
Who sells Medicare Part D plans?

atoms.title: What Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment is
atoms.q: What is the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: The Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period is when Medicare Advantage plan members can make changes to their existing plan or disenroll from their current plan and return to Original Medicare. It runs from January 1 to March 31.
qs: When is Medicare Advantage open enrollment?
Can I leave my Medicare Advantage plan after January 1?
What can I change during MA OEP?

atoms.title: MA open enrollment mirrors annual enrollment changes
atoms.q: What changes can I make during Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment?
atoms.text: The changes you can make during Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment are similar to those you can make during the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period. It basically gives you another opportunity to get the coverage you want and need.
qs: Can I switch plans after annual enrollment ends?
Is MA open enrollment like AEP?
What can I do between January and March?

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment vs Annual Enrollment
atoms.q: How is Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment different from Medicare Annual Enrollment?
atoms.text: The main difference is who can use each one. Medicare Annual Enrollment is when anyone who has Medicare can make coverage changes for the upcoming year, while Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment is only for people who are currently enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan. Timing also differs: Annual Enrollment is October 15 to December 7, while Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment is January 1 to March 31. Both happen every year.
qs: What's the difference between AEP and MA OEP?
Who can use Medicare Advantage open enrollment?
Can someone on Original Medicare use MA OEP?

atoms.title: How to review your plan before changing
atoms.q: How do I get ready for Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment?
atoms.text: Whether you recently enrolled or have had your plan for years, use this period to confirm or change your plan choice. Review how your plan stacks up: 1) your doctors and other providers are in the plan network; 2) your prescription drugs are on the plan formulary; 3) you are comfortable with your costs, including premiums, deductibles, copays and coinsurance; 4) you have the additional dental, vision and hearing coverage you want; and 5) you are happy with additional benefits such as fitness programs, mail-order pharmacy, nurse line and other wellness services.
qs: How do I know if my Medicare Advantage plan is still right?
What should I check before switching plans?
Are my doctors and drugs covered by my plan?

atoms.title: New plan benefits last the rest of the year
atoms.q: If I change plans during MA OEP, when do the new benefits take effect?
atoms.text: If you decide to make a change during the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, you have from January 1 to March 31 to do it. You can explore other plan options, and your new plan benefits will be in effect for the rest of the year.
qs: How long do I have to switch Medicare Advantage plans?
When does my new plan take effect?
Is the March 31 deadline firm?

atoms.title: What the Annual Enrollment Period is
atoms.q: What is the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: The Medicare Annual Enrollment Period, or AEP, is a set time each year for changing your Medicare coverage choices if you choose to. AEP runs from October 15 to December 7, and new coverage choices go into effect on January 1.
qs: When is Medicare open enrollment?
When do AEP changes take effect?
What does AEP stand for in Medicare?

atoms.title: AEP options with Original Medicare only
atoms.q: What can I do during AEP if I only have Original Medicare?
atoms.text: If you currently have just Original Medicare (Parts A and B), you can join a Medicare Advantage plan (Part C) with or without built-in drug coverage, or join a stand-alone Part D prescription drug plan. A penalty may apply if you do not currently have other creditable drug coverage. You can also make no changes, and your current coverage will renew as is.
qs: Can I join Medicare Advantage during AEP if I have Original Medicare?
Can I add Part D at annual enrollment?
Will I be penalized for adding drug coverage at AEP?

atoms.title: AEP options with Original Medicare and a Part D plan
atoms.q: What can I do during AEP if I have Original Medicare and a stand-alone Part D plan?
atoms.text: If you currently have Original Medicare and a stand-alone Part D plan, you can join a Medicare Advantage plan with or without built-in drug coverage, switch to another Part D plan, or drop Medicare prescription drug coverage completely. You may be charged a penalty if you later decide you want drug coverage again. You can also make no changes and your coverage will renew as is.
qs: Can I switch Part D plans in October?
What happens if I drop Part D coverage?
Can I move from a Part D plan to Medicare Advantage?

atoms.title: AEP options with a Medicare Advantage plan
atoms.q: What can I do during AEP if I have a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage?
atoms.text: If you currently have a Medicare Advantage plan with built-in drug coverage, you can switch to another Medicare Advantage plan with or without built-in drug coverage, or drop your plan and go back to Original Medicare. You can join a stand-alone Part D plan if you return to Original Medicare or switch to a plan without drug coverage, drop drug coverage completely (a penalty may apply if you want it later), or make no changes.
qs: Can I leave Medicare Advantage during open enrollment?
Can I switch Medicare Advantage plans in the fall?
How do I go back to Original Medicare?

atoms.title: AEP options with Medicare Advantage and a separate Part D plan
atoms.q: What can I do during AEP if I have both a Medicare Advantage plan and a stand-alone Part D plan?
atoms.text: If you currently have a Medicare Advantage plan and a stand-alone Part D plan, you can switch to another Medicare Advantage plan with or without built-in drug coverage, switch to another prescription drug plan, drop your Medicare Advantage plan and go back to Original Medicare, or drop prescription drug coverage completely. A penalty may apply if you later want drug coverage again. You can also make no changes.
qs: What can I change if I have two Medicare plans?
Can I switch my Part D plan without changing Medicare Advantage?
How do I drop my Medicare Advantage plan at AEP?

atoms.title: Use AEP to review your plan each year
atoms.q: Should I review my Medicare plan every year?
atoms.text: AEP is a good reminder to review your Medicare plan each year so you can make sure you have the coverage you need going forward. The specific actions you can take during AEP depend on your current coverage, and making no changes means your current coverage will renew as is.
qs: Why should I review my Medicare plan every year?
What happens if I don't change my plan at AEP?
How do I get ready for annual enrollment?

atoms.title: The two kinds of Special Enrollment Periods
atoms.q: What is a Medicare Special Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: A Medicare Special Enrollment Period allows you to switch plans or sign up for Medicare outside of the standard Medicare enrollment periods. There are two kinds: a 2-month Special Enrollment Period for qualifying life events, and an 8-month Special Enrollment Period for people working past 65.
qs: What is a Medicare SEP?
How many kinds of Special Enrollment Periods are there?
Can I enroll in Medicare outside of the usual periods?

atoms.title: 2-month versus 8-month Special Enrollment Period
atoms.q: Who uses the 2-month SEP and who uses the 8-month SEP?
atoms.text: For people who already have Medicare and experience a qualifying life event, there is a two-month Special Enrollment Period for switching a Medicare Advantage or Part D plan. For people who qualified to delay Medicare because they had creditable coverage, usually from an employer, there is an 8-month Special Enrollment Period for enrolling in Medicare Parts A, B, C and D.
qs: How long is the Medicare SEP?
Which SEP applies when I leave my employer plan?
Which SEP lets me switch Medicare Advantage plans?

atoms.title: Life events that trigger the 2-month SEP
atoms.q: What qualifies for a Medicare Special Enrollment Period to switch plans?
atoms.text: You may qualify for a 2-month Special Enrollment Period if you move out of your plan's service area; your plan closes, stops serving your area, significantly reduces its provider network or consistently receives low star ratings; you want to enroll in a 5-star plan at any time or drop your first Medicare Advantage plan within 12 months of enrolling; or you move into or out of an institutional facility like a nursing home.
qs: Can I switch plans if my plan leaves my area?
Can I join a 5-star plan any time?
Can I drop my first Medicare Advantage plan within a year?

atoms.title: Assistance and program changes that trigger an SEP
atoms.q: Do financial assistance programs trigger a Special Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: You may also qualify for a 2-month Special Enrollment Period if you are enrolled in or lose eligibility for a qualified State Pharmaceutical Assistance Program; you have Medicare financial assistance such as Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program or Extra Help, or gain or lose eligibility for any of these; you enroll in or leave the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE); or you gain or lose eligibility for a Special Needs Plan. Some other situations may qualify as well, and your State Health Insurance Assistance Program can help.
qs: Does gaining Medicaid let me change Medicare plans?
What is PACE and does it trigger an SEP?
Who can I call about whether I qualify for an SEP?

atoms.title: The 8-month SEP when working past 65
atoms.q: How does the 8-month Special Enrollment Period work when working past 65?
atoms.text: For people who work past 65 and qualify to delay Medicare with creditable employer coverage, there is an 8-month Special Enrollment Period that allows you to enroll in Part A (if you haven't yet), Part B, Part C and Part D without late penalties. To qualify for the Part B SEP, you must have creditable employer or union health coverage based on current employment. Your SEP begins eight months after your employer coverage ends or you leave your job, whichever happens first.
qs: How long do I have to sign up for Part B after my job coverage ends?
What coverage qualifies me for the working-past-65 SEP?
Do I need creditable coverage for the 8-month SEP?

atoms.title: Only 2 months for Part C or D in the 8-month SEP
atoms.q: How long do I have to enroll in Part C or Part D during the 8-month SEP?
atoms.text: The working-past-65 Special Enrollment Period is tricky: while you have the whole 8 months to get Parts A and B, you only get the first 2 months to enroll in Part C or Part D without penalty. If you enroll after the two-month mark, you'll face late enrollment penalties for Part D, regardless of whether you end up with a stand-alone Part D plan or a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage.
qs: When do I have to join Part D after leaving my employer plan?
Will I get a Part D penalty if I wait three months?
Is the Part C deadline the same as the Part B deadline?

atoms.title: AI to simplify benefits and coverage
atoms.q: How is UnitedHealthcare using AI to improve the member experience?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says it works with its partners at Optum to use artificial intelligence (AI) to take some of the complexity out of health care when consumers need to know about their benefits and coverage. It describes five ways: Smart Choice provider search, Members Like You cost estimates, Conversational AI, a claims assistant and advocate tools.
qs: What AI tools does UnitedHealthcare offer members?
How does UnitedHealthcare use AI for benefits?

atoms.title: Smart Choice personalized search preferences
atoms.q: What preferences can I set in Smart Choice provider search?
atoms.text: Smart Choice, available on the UHC app, uses Optum's AI capabilities to show results that reflect personalized search preferences. Members can set criteria such as distance, language spoken, virtual or in-person appointments, gender preference, and availability for evening and weekend appointments.
qs: Can I search for a doctor who speaks my language?
How does Smart Choice personalize doctor search?

atoms.title: Four Smart Choice matching standards
atoms.q: How does Smart Choice match members with providers?
atoms.text: Four key standards are used to match members with a provider. Quality covers factors such as credentialing and whether physicians meet UnitedHealth Premium care criteria. Benefits covers the member's health plan benefits. Convenience covers where providers have appointments available, virtual or in-person, and their proximity. Personal fit covers how a provider matches personal preferences.
qs: What criteria does Smart Choice use?
What is UnitedHealth Premium in provider search?

atoms.title: Members Like You cost estimates
atoms.q: What is the Members Like You feature?
atoms.text: In the UnitedHealthcare app, the Members Like You cost estimates feature shows general and anonymous demographic information, like gender and age, to suggest the types of services commonly used by other members on a similar care journey. The insights come with cost estimates meant to help members understand potential out-of-pocket costs and avoid surprises.
qs: How does UnitedHealthcare estimate costs based on similar members?
What are AI-driven care path suggestions?

atoms.title: Conversational AI voice assistant
atoms.q: How does UnitedHealthcare's conversational AI voice assistant work?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare's conversational voice assistant converses in natural language to understand the reason for a call. It decides how best to support the caller by routing them to provider, enrollment or benefit information, either through self-service or by transferring to a live advocate. The article states the AI does not give verbal answers to member questions.
qs: Does the UnitedHealthcare phone AI answer my questions?
How does the phone system route my call?

atoms.title: Claims assistant cuts submission time
atoms.q: How does the Claims Assistant AI tool help with out-of-network claims?
atoms.text: The Claims Assistant AI tool supports out-of-network claim submissions by simplifying the process and helping to populate the medical field values. It cuts the time to complete an out-of-network claim submission from 12-15 minutes down to 3 minutes, and completion rates have nearly doubled as a result.
qs: How fast is the Claims Assistant for out-of-network claims?
Can AI help me fill out a claim?

atoms.title: AI tools that support advocates
atoms.q: How does AI support UnitedHealthcare advocates on calls?
atoms.text: AI tools help advocates answer questions about health benefit navigation, coverage information or costs. The Welcome experience provides member insights based on claims activity or previous calls before the call. In-call assist uses voice analytics to understand needs and provide benefits, coverage and cost answers. In-call summarization summarizes the conversation for the member's file so callbacks go faster.
qs: Why does the advocate already know my history?
What AI do advocates use during calls?

atoms.title: Why out-of-network bills can be high
atoms.q: Why do out-of-network doctors send high bills?
atoms.text: Bills from out-of-network doctors can be shockingly high, so it almost always makes more sense to explore in-network options and find a suitable alternative. A provider that is out of network does not have a contract with the health insurer and has not agreed to negotiated payment rates.
qs: Why is my out-of-network bill so high?
What does out-of-network mean?

atoms.title: Bill from an out-of-network provider you chose
atoms.q: I chose an out-of-network provider and got a bill. What should I do?
atoms.text: The insurer either paid the provider an out-of-network rate, and the provider is now billing the balance, or paid nothing if the plan has no out-of-network benefits. In that case the provider can bill the full amount only if the member signed a consent form in advance. Members can check with their health plan for support, or ask the provider about monthly payment plans.
qs: What do I do if I get a bill from an out-of-network doctor?
Can I set up a payment plan for a medical bill?

atoms.title: Programs that negotiate out-of-network bills
atoms.q: Can my health plan help negotiate an out-of-network bill?
atoms.text: If a person gets insurance through work, they may be eligible for a program that helps employees facing large bills from out-of-network providers. For example, some employers have opted into a UnitedHealthcare program that negotiates with out-of-network providers on members' behalf, helping reduce what they owe. The first step is to check with the health plan.
qs: Does UnitedHealthcare negotiate medical bills for me?
What support exists for large out-of-network bills?

atoms.title: Size of the UnitedHealthcare network
atoms.q: How large is UnitedHealthcare's care provider network?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says it has developed one of the largest care provider networks in the country, with more than 1.7 million physicians and care professionals and over 7,000 hospitals and care facilities nationwide. The figures are attributed to UnitedHealthcare internal data from 2026.
qs: How many doctors are in the UnitedHealthcare network?
How many hospitals does UnitedHealthcare cover?

atoms.title: Out-of-network doctor at an in-network hospital
atoms.q: I had care at an in-network hospital but one doctor was out of network. Do I owe the bill?
atoms.text: Thanks to the No Surprises Act, a patient is not responsible for the bill in this situation. The law protects people who unknowingly receive care from an out-of-network provider while being treated at an in-network hospital. If the care qualifies, the member will not be responsible for paying anything more than their cost-share. A health plan can confirm eligibility.
qs: What is a surprise medical bill?
Do I have to pay an out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network hospital?

atoms.title: No Surprises Act protections
atoms.q: What does the No Surprises Act do?
atoms.text: The No Surprises Act was passed in 2020 in large part because of out-of-network physician groups billing patients who had no way of knowing the physicians were out of network. The law prohibits out-of-network providers from billing patients in these situations for anything more than the cost-share owed under their benefit plan, meaning their copay, coinsurance or deductible. It has protected patients since it went into effect in 2022.
qs: When did the No Surprises Act start?
What can an out-of-network provider legally bill me?

atoms.title: Ground ambulances are not covered by the No Surprises Act
atoms.q: Does the No Surprises Act protect me from ambulance bills?
atoms.text: No. The No Surprises Act does not apply to ground ambulances, so companies that operate ambulance services can still legally bill patients for rides to the hospital, even in a medical emergency. The article says ambulance bills typically range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars.
qs: Are ambulance rides covered by the No Surprises Act?
Why did I get a big ambulance bill?

atoms.title: Out-of-network ambulance charges versus Medicare
atoms.q: How do out-of-network ambulance charges compare with Medicare rates?
atoms.text: In many cases, out-of-network ambulance companies' charges are three to four times higher than the Medicare rate for an ambulance ride. If they joined insurers' networks, the in-network payment rate would typically be closer to the Medicare rate, and they would lose the ability to bill patients for more than the copay or coinsurance owed under their plan.
qs: Why are ambulance bills so high?
Why don't ambulance companies join insurance networks?

atoms.title: State protections and self-insured plans
atoms.q: Do state laws protect me from surprise ambulance bills?
atoms.text: The article says 24 states have passed legislation protecting residents from surprise ambulance bills. Those protections should apply to people in fully insured employer-sponsored plans in those states, because fully insured plans are governed by state laws. Most people who get insurance through work are in a self-insured plan, which is subject to federal rather than state laws. Members can ask their HR department which type they have.
qs: Does my state protect me from ambulance bills?
What is the difference between fully insured and self-insured plans?

atoms.title: Steps for an ambulance bill and emergencies
atoms.q: What should I do if I get a large ambulance bill?
atoms.text: 1) Check whether your state has surprise ambulance bill protections. 2) If in a self-insured employer plan, ask the health plan for support, since the insurer may be able to negotiate a lower payment. 3) Contact the ambulance operator to ask about a lower payment or a monthly payment plan. In a true emergency, never hesitate to call 911 and go to the nearest hospital, where care is processed at the in-network rate.
qs: How do I dispute an ambulance bill?
Is emergency care at an out-of-network hospital paid at the in-network rate?

atoms.title: What is health insurance?
atoms.q: What is health insurance?
atoms.text: Health insurance is a plan, or policy, that covers a percentage of doctors' visits and hospital bills. It exists to help offset the costs of medical events, whether they are planned or happen unexpectedly. Health insurance may also protect people when they are feeling good, and may help keep them feeling that way, through wellness programs and preventive care.
qs: What is health insurance?
What does a health insurance policy do?
Why do people need health insurance?

atoms.title: Going without insurance risks health and finances
atoms.q: Why is not having health insurance a risk?
atoms.text: Even someone in good health right now cannot know when they will need health insurance. A car accident, an injury or a cancer diagnosis does not come with warning. According to UnitedHealthcare, not having health insurance is a risk both for the preservation of a person's health and for their financial security.
qs: Do I need health insurance if I'm healthy?
What happens if I don't have health insurance?

atoms.title: How does health insurance work?
atoms.q: How does health insurance work?
atoms.text: Health insurance is a contract between a person and their insurance company, or insurer. When someone purchases a plan, they become a member of that plan. The plan may be a Medicare plan, a Medicaid plan, a plan through an employer, or an individual policy such as an Affordable Care Act (ACA) plan. Knowing how health insurance works can help when deciding which plan is right.
qs: How does health insurance work?
Is health insurance a contract?
What does it mean to be a plan member?

atoms.title: Supplemental plans and memberships add options
atoms.q: What do supplemental plans and memberships do?
atoms.text: Supplemental plans, like accident insurance or travel insurance, can help boost coverage for a variety of scenarios. Memberships, like dental savings memberships, are an alternative to insurance that helps people save on qualified services from participating service providers. Both are described by UnitedHealthcare as options alongside traditional health insurance.
qs: What is supplemental insurance?
Is a dental savings membership the same as insurance?

atoms.title: What are the different types of health insurance?
atoms.q: What are the different types of health insurance?
atoms.text: There are different types of health insurance plans to fit different needs. Some types include government plans, such as Affordable Care Act (ACA) plans, which can also be called Marketplace or Exchange plans, Medicare plans and Medicaid plans. Before choosing a plan during open enrollment, it may help to review the various plan types to see which may work best.
qs: What kinds of health insurance are there?
What is a Marketplace or Exchange plan?

atoms.title: What is health insurance open enrollment?
atoms.q: What is open enrollment?
atoms.text: Open enrollment is a special period of time when a person gets to start, stop or change their health insurance plan. It most often happens once a year, unless the person experiences a qualifying life event. There are different enrollment periods depending on whether a person has insurance through an employer, Medicare or an ACA plan.
qs: What is open enrollment?
How often can I change my health plan?

atoms.title: Insurance does not make health care free
atoms.q: Does having insurance mean health care is free?
atoms.text: Having insurance does not mean health care will be free. Members still pay a monthly rate, or premium. Members may also pay copayments or other out-of-pocket fees, or have to meet deductibles every year before insurance coverage kicks in. Different factors can affect health insurance costs, so it is important to understand them before selecting a plan.
qs: Is health care free with insurance?
What do I still pay if I have health insurance?
What costs come with a health plan?

atoms.title: Medicaid renewal is also called redetermination
atoms.q: What is Medicaid renewal and how do I stay covered?
atoms.text: A person asked to renew their Medicaid eligibility may wonder what to do next. Medicaid redetermination is also called Medicaid renewal or recertification. UnitedHealthcare offers information on how to stay covered if Medicaid coverage is changing.
qs: What is Medicaid redetermination?
What should I do if I'm asked to renew Medicaid?

atoms.title: Common insurance terms have plain-language definitions
atoms.q: Where can I find definitions of health insurance terms?
atoms.text: Terms such as deductibles, premiums, network, claims and benefits can make health insurance seem like it has a language of its own. UnitedHealthcare provides a list of common health insurance terms with quick definitions that explain what they mean in everyday language.
qs: What do health insurance terms mean?
Where is a health insurance glossary?

atoms.title: Why do I need health insurance?
atoms.q: Why do I need health insurance?
atoms.text: Health insurance is designed to help prepare for unexpected moments in life, like accidents or illnesses. Without it, a person could be faced with paying medical bills themselves, and health care can be expensive. Health insurance can also keep people on track with preventive care, which may be covered by insurance at 100% in many cases. Regular doctor visits may help people stay healthier over time.
qs: Why do I need health insurance if I'm healthy?
Is preventive care covered at 100%?

atoms.title: How do I get health insurance?
atoms.q: How do I get health insurance?
atoms.text: Options depend on a person's situation. Federal and state programs include Medicaid, for people with a lower income, and Medicare, for people over 65 or who may qualify due to a disability or special situation. Short term coverage can fill coverage gaps for a period of time. A person may also be able to purchase a plan from an employer, or buy an individual plan such as an Affordable Care Act (ACA) plan.
qs: How can I get health insurance?
What are my options for buying health insurance?

atoms.title: What is TriTerm Medical short term coverage?
atoms.q: What is TriTerm Medical health insurance?
atoms.text: TriTerm Medical health insurance is a type of short term coverage that can last nearly 3 years. UnitedHealthcare describes short term coverage in general as a way to help fill coverage gaps for a period of time.
qs: What is TriTerm Medical?
How long can short term insurance last?

atoms.title: What is fixed benefit health insurance?
atoms.q: What is fixed benefit health insurance?
atoms.text: Fixed benefit health insurance is a type of fixed indemnity insurance. It allows a person to apply for coverage year round and to be paid a preset amount when they receive qualified medical services.
qs: What is fixed benefit insurance?
Can I apply for fixed indemnity coverage any time of year?

atoms.title: What are qualifying life events?
atoms.q: What counts as a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: A life-changing event at any point in the year may be considered a qualifying life event, which may mean a person qualifies for a special enrollment period. Examples include getting married or divorced, having a baby, gaining a dependent, moving, losing a job or landing a new job, and turning 65 years old.
qs: What is a qualifying life event?
Can I change my health plan after a major life change?

atoms.title: How much does health insurance cost?
atoms.q: How much does health insurance cost?
atoms.text: Many variables affect the cost of health insurance. These can include a person's age, where they live, whether or not they use tobacco, how many people are covered by the plan and the type of plan. Choosing the best health plan for a budget depends on a person's unique circumstances.
qs: What affects the cost of health insurance?
Why does my premium depend on where I live?

atoms.title: What does health insurance cover?
atoms.q: What does health insurance cover?
atoms.text: Every health plan is different, so coverage should be checked before receiving care. Plans may cover preventive services (when delivered by a network doctor or provider), pre-existing conditions, mental and behavioral health services, prescription drugs, some medical devices (like breast pumps), maternity care and some costs of cancer treatment. Coverage can range from big, unexpected events such as hospital stays to routine checkups.
qs: What does health insurance cover?
Does health insurance cover pre-existing conditions?
Are prescription drugs covered by insurance?

atoms.title: How to check what your plan covers
atoms.q: How do I find out what my plan covers?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare says to check coverage before receiving care. 1) Call the number on your member ID card, or sign in to your account and go to Benefits & Coverage to review what is covered. 2) Look at your health plan documents to learn your exact coverage.
qs: How do I check what my health plan covers?
Where do I find my benefits?

atoms.title: What is prior authorization in health insurance?
atoms.q: What is prior authorization?
atoms.text: Some types of care or prescription drugs may need approval from a health plan before a person gets them. This is called prior authorization. UnitedHealthcare provides a separate page explaining what it is, why it may be required, how the process works, how long it may take and what to do if a request is denied.
qs: What is prior authorization?
Do I need approval before care?

atoms.title: How does prescription drug coverage work?
atoms.q: How does prescription drug coverage work?
atoms.text: The best way to learn about pharmacy benefits is to understand the health plan's Prescription Drug List (PDL), also called a formulary. Drug tiers, which group prescription drugs into price categories, also matter, as does how brand, generic and biosimilar drugs are covered. This matters most for people who take medications regularly.
qs: How does prescription coverage work?
What is a formulary?
What are drug tiers?

atoms.title: EOB vs. bill vs. SBC
atoms.q: What is the difference between an EOB, a bill and an SBC?
atoms.text: An explanation of benefits (EOB) is an insurance company's statement describing the costs involved for visits to a doctor or clinic, sent to let a person know a claim has been filed. It is different from a bill, which tells how much a person needs to pay. It is also different from a Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC), which describes coverage rather than giving a breakdown of a health care visit.
qs: What is the difference between an EOB and a bill?
Is an EOB the same as an SBC?

atoms.title: What is an explanation of benefits (EOB)?
atoms.q: What is an explanation of benefits?
atoms.text: An explanation of benefits (EOB) is an insurance company's statement that describes the costs involved for visits to a doctor or clinic. In short, it is a statement to let a person know a claim has been filed, along with details of the costs.
qs: What is an EOB?
What does explanation of benefits mean?

atoms.title: An EOB is not a bill
atoms.q: Is an EOB a bill?
