atoms.text: An EOB is different from a bill. Its purpose is to tell a person which costs their insurance has paid for and what the patient must pay. The medical provider sends a separate bill for the patient's amount, which should match what is on the EOB.
qs: Do I have to pay my EOB?
What is the difference between an EOB and a medical bill?

atoms.title: How do you read an EOB?
atoms.q: What information is on an EOB?
atoms.text: An EOB typically includes the patient's name; plan information, including name and member ID; the doctor, health professional or facility that provided services; a claim number and status; the service description and date; total cost of services; how much the health plan paid; costs the plan did not cover; any amount paid from an HRA; and what the patient owes. Some EOBs also show out-of-pocket expenses that count toward the deductible.
qs: How do I read an EOB?
What does an EOB show?
What is a claim number on an EOB?

atoms.title: Why an EOB is important
atoms.q: Why is an EOB important?
atoms.text: An EOB is a tool that can help a person better understand how their insurance works and feel confident making decisions about their plan and care. EOBs can be useful to track health care costs, find billing errors, understand what a plan covers and for tax documentation. Over time, patterns in EOBs may help a person decide if their insurance plan is right for their needs.
qs: Why should I keep my EOBs?
Can an EOB help me find billing errors?

atoms.title: Common reasons an EOB and bill do not match
atoms.q: Why might my EOB and my provider's bill not match?
atoms.text: If an EOB and a provider's bill do not match, a few possibilities should be checked first. A previous balance may have been carried over. A payment may have been made between the time the EOB and bill were sent, so the EOB does not show real costs. Or the bill may have been sent before the insurance company paid, in which case waiting for the claim to be processed may produce an updated bill.
qs: Why is my bill different from my EOB?
What should I check if my EOB and bill disagree?

atoms.title: Fixing an error on your EOB
atoms.q: What should I do if I find an error on my EOB?
atoms.text: After ruling out common errors: 1) Call the doctor or clinic to see if there is an explanation and request an itemized bill. 2) Call the insurance company to ask about the error. 3) If needed, ask about filing an appeal. Throughout, save a file of EOBs, the medical bill and details of calls.
qs: How do I dispute an EOB error?
Can I get an itemized bill?
How do I appeal a claim?

atoms.title: No Surprises Act may protect against out-of-network bills
atoms.q: Can the No Surprises Act protect me from an out-of-network bill?
atoms.text: Sometimes seeing an out-of-network provider is out of a person's control, such as in emergency care or when an out-of-network provider is involved in care without the person's choice. In this case, the federal No Surprises Act or state surprise billing law may protect the person from paying more than their copayment, coinsurance or deductible.
qs: What is the No Surprises Act?
Do I have to pay an out-of-network emergency bill?

atoms.title: How long should I keep my EOB?
atoms.q: How long should I keep my EOB?
atoms.text: Since EOBs can provide both short- and long-term value, it is a good idea to save an EOB at least until the final bill from the doctor or clinic arrives. Keeping paper copies for future reference might be useful, especially for someone facing a chronic illness or serious condition.
qs: How long do I keep EOBs?
Should I save my explanation of benefits?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare members can view claims online
atoms.q: How can UnitedHealthcare members see their claims?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare members can sign in to their member account or use the UnitedHealthcare app to see their claims. Regularly reviewing EOBs can help a person stay an active participant in their health care and potentially avoid wasting money due to errors.
qs: Where can I see my claims?
How do I find my EOB online?

atoms.title: What is a Summary of Benefits and Coverage?
atoms.q: What is a Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC)?
atoms.text: A Summary of Benefits and Coverage, also called an SBC, is a document that outlines what is covered, and not covered, under a health plan. It is often discussed when choosing health plans and learning about costs. When making decisions about buying a plan or using benefits, an SBC can be a useful tool to help compare costs and understand coverage options.
qs: What is an SBC?
What is a summary of benefits and coverage?

atoms.title: Health plans must provide an SBC for each plan
atoms.q: Are insurers required to provide an SBC?
atoms.text: All health plan companies are required to provide a Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC) for each of their different plans. The SBC was created to make it easier to compare and shop for health plans.
qs: Do all health plans have an SBC?
Why was the SBC created?

atoms.title: Standard SBC format enables apples-to-apples comparison
atoms.q: How does an SBC help me compare plans?
atoms.text: Every health plan has to use the same outline to show the costs and coverage for each of the plans it offers. Because every SBC is in the same format, it is easier to make apples-to-apples comparisons. An SBC can be used to compare prices, benefits and other plan options and features that might be important to a shopper.
qs: How do I compare health plans?
Is the SBC format the same for every insurer?

atoms.title: What information is in an SBC?
atoms.q: What information does an SBC include?
atoms.text: An SBC includes an overview of what is covered; what is not covered and any limits on coverage; costs a person might pay such as deductibles, coinsurance and copayments; and coverage examples, including pregnancy and a minor injury. It also points to where to find complete plan documents, a network provider list, prescription drug coverage information and a Uniform Glossary, plus a contact number for questions.
qs: What is in a summary of benefits and coverage?
Does the SBC show coverage examples?

atoms.title: SBC states ACA minimum essential coverage and minimum value
atoms.q: What do SBC statements about MEC and minimum value mean?
atoms.text: An SBC includes a statement on whether the plan meets minimum essential coverage (MEC) for the Affordable Care Act (ACA). It also includes a statement that the plan meets minimum value, meaning the plan covers at least 60 percent of the medical costs of benefits for a population on average.
qs: What is minimum value in health insurance?
Does my plan meet minimum essential coverage?

atoms.title: An SBC is only a summary
atoms.q: Does the SBC show all plan details?
atoms.text: Every SBC is created with four double-sided pages and 12-point type. It includes a reminder that the SBC is only a summary. To get all the details, a person should look at the complete health plan documents, and the SBC says where to go online to review and print copies of them.
qs: How long is an SBC?
Where do I find full plan documents?

atoms.title: Where can I get an SBC?
atoms.q: How do I get a copy of my SBC?
atoms.text: A person can request an SBC anytime by calling the number on their member ID card. People who already have a health plan receive one automatically at certain times: on the first day of open enrollment, when they renew the plan, when changes happen within the plan, and when they make a change or are added to a plan, for example after getting married, having a child or another qualifying life event.
qs: How do I get an SBC?
When do I receive my SBC automatically?

atoms.title: Can I get an SBC in another language?
atoms.q: Can I get an SBC in another language?
atoms.text: Yes. A person can call the number on their member ID card to connect with customer service and ask for a copy of the SBC in the language they need.
qs: Is the SBC available in Spanish?
How do I get plan documents in another language?

atoms.title: Uniform Glossary explains confusing SBC terms
atoms.q: Where can I look up confusing terms in an SBC?
atoms.text: Even though an SBC is made to make health plan information easier to understand, some terms can be confusing. The Glossary of Health Coverage and Medical Terms, also called a Uniform Glossary, gives clear, simple answers about what terms mean.
qs: What is a uniform glossary?
Where do I find definitions of health plan terms?

atoms.title: Brokers can search SBC and COC documents
atoms.q: Where can brokers find SBC and COC documents?
atoms.text: Agents and brokers for UnitedHealthcare ACA Marketplace plans can use a search tool provided by UnitedHealthcare to find and view Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC) and Certificate of Coverage (COC) documents.
qs: How can a broker find an SBC for ACA Marketplace plans?
What is a COC document?

atoms.title: What is a Prescription Drug List (PDL)?
atoms.q: What is a prescription drug list or formulary?
atoms.text: A Prescription Drug List (PDL), sometimes called a formulary, is a list of the most commonly prescribed medications. It includes both brand-name and generic prescription medications approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Medications are listed by common categories or classes and placed in tiers that represent the cost a person pays out-of-pocket.
qs: What is a formulary?
What is a PDL in health insurance?
How do I know if my drug is covered?

atoms.title: What is a drug tier?
atoms.q: What is a drug tier and how does it work?
atoms.text: Prescription Drug Lists often have tiers, or groups of drugs categorized by cost. A person's cost-share or copayment is based on which tier their drug is in. There are typically three or four tiers.
qs: What are drug tiers?
Why does my copay depend on the tier?

atoms.title: Drug tiers 1 through 4 compared
atoms.q: What does each drug tier mean?
atoms.text: Under a typical Prescription Drug List: Tier 1 holds the least expensive drug options, often generic drugs. Tier 2 holds higher-price generic and lower-price brand-name drugs. Tier 3 holds mainly higher-price brand-name drugs. Tier 4 holds the highest-cost prescription drugs.
qs: What is a Tier 1 drug?
Which drug tier is most expensive?
Are generics in the lowest tier?

atoms.title: Does health insurance cover all prescription drugs?
atoms.q: Does health insurance cover all prescription drugs?
atoms.text: Not necessarily. Medications under different names may provide similar clinical benefits yet look different and have different price points. Sometimes only certain types or brands of prescriptions are covered under a plan. A person should know their pharmacy benefits and whether a prescription is covered before heading to the pharmacy counter.
qs: Are all prescriptions covered by my plan?
How do I know if my drug is covered before I get to the pharmacy?

atoms.title: Checking whether a plan covers your prescriptions
atoms.q: How do I know if a plan covers my prescriptions?
atoms.text: A person can sign in to their account to view their Prescription Drug List (PDL) or call the number on their member ID card. Prescription drugs are evaluated on how well they work, how they compare to others in the same class, and total cost.
qs: How can I check if my medicine is covered?
How are drugs chosen for a drug list?

atoms.title: Medicare Part B and Part D drug coverage
atoms.q: How does Medicare cover prescription drugs?
atoms.text: Medicare Part B covers some outpatient prescription drugs. If a drug is not covered under Part B, it may be covered under Part D. Most Medicare Part D drug plans have their own Prescription Drug List, also known as a formulary, with drugs placed into tiers.
qs: Does Medicare Part B cover prescription drugs?
Do Part D plans have formularies?

atoms.title: Medicaid prescription lists vary by state
atoms.q: Does Medicaid cover prescription drugs?
atoms.text: Most Medicaid plans cover some prescription drugs, but the Prescription Drug List and plan benefits can vary from state to state. People enrolled in a UnitedHealthcare Community Plan can sign in to their account to confirm their pharmacy benefits.
qs: Does Medicaid cover prescriptions?
Do Medicaid drug lists differ by state?

atoms.title: How can I understand my prescription label?
atoms.q: What information is on a prescription drug label?
atoms.text: A prescription label typically shows the patient's name, medication name, dosage instructions, expiration or discard-after date, number of refills allowed, prescription (Rx) number, pharmacy phone number, pharmacy name and location, the prescribing doctor's name, and often a warning label on the back. Medication should be taken only as directed. If any information is hard to read, a pharmacist can print it in larger type.
qs: What is on a prescription label?
How do I read my prescription bottle?

atoms.title: Questions to ask your pharmacist
atoms.q: What should I ask my pharmacist about a new medication?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare suggests asking a pharmacist: how to store the medication; whether anything should not be eaten or drunk while taking it, including vitamins, supplements or alcohol; whether it is safe to take with other prescription or over-the-counter drugs; and when it is safe to stop taking it. It adds that people should seek the advice of a medical professional before making health care decisions.
qs: What should I ask my pharmacist?
How do I store my medication safely?

atoms.title: Tips for a smooth prior authorization
atoms.q: How can I make the prior authorization process go smoothly?
atoms.text: To help prior authorization go smoothly: check the policy documents or Prescription Drug List (PDL) to see if prior authorization is needed; work with the doctor to submit a prior authorization; keep careful records to know when it expires; and begin getting a new prior authorization at least one month in advance. To find out if a drug needs one, call the number on the member ID card or sign in to an account.
qs: How do I get prior authorization for a drug?
When should I renew a prior authorization?

atoms.title: What is prior authorization?
atoms.q: What is prior authorization?
atoms.text: Prior authorization is a process that starts before care is delivered. It is also known as preauthorization, prior approval or precertification. It is a decision by a health plan that a health care service, treatment plan, prescription drug or durable medical equipment (DME) is medically necessary. Most care does not need prior authorization.
qs: What is prior authorization?
Is preauthorization the same as precertification?
Does all care need prior authorization?

atoms.title: Why is prior authorization required?
atoms.q: Why is prior authorization required?
atoms.text: Sometimes a doctor may recommend care that needs to be reviewed first, and the doctor asks the health plan to approve it before the patient gets it. This helps the plan check if the care is medically needed, is treatment the patient has not already tried, and is an option that is both effective and lower in cost. Prior authorization can help make sure care is safe, covered and needed.
qs: Why does my insurance need to approve care first?
Why do I need prior authorization?

atoms.title: Prior authorization may help find lower-cost drugs
atoms.q: Can prior authorization save me money?
atoms.text: Prior authorization may help lower health care costs. It may help find lower-cost drugs that can treat the same condition. These options may help lower a person's costs while still giving effective treatment.
qs: Does prior authorization save money?
How does prior authorization lower my costs?

atoms.title: How does prior authorization work?
atoms.q: How does prior authorization work?
atoms.text: A doctor may ask the health plan to approve some care before the patient gets it. The plan reviews the request to see if the care is covered and meets quality and safety standards. Decisions are based on medical evidence. If a request is not approved right away, a qualified clinician, which may include a pharmacist or doctor, reviews it. Clinical review rules are typically based on FDA-approved drug information, safety details, medical and pharmacy research, and treatment guidelines.
qs: How does the prior authorization process work?
Who reviews prior authorization requests?

atoms.title: What to do when prior authorization is required
atoms.q: What should I do if my doctor says prior authorization is required?
atoms.text: If a treatment or service needs prior authorization: 1) The doctor sends a request to the health plan. 2) The patient may need to help by filling out forms or sharing documents. 3) Clinicians at the health plan review the request. 4) The plan then decides how or if it will cover the care.
qs: What happens after my doctor requests prior authorization?
Do I need to fill out forms for prior authorization?

atoms.title: Prior authorization timelines vary by state
atoms.q: How long does prior authorization take?
atoms.text: Rules on how long prior authorizations take vary by state. If care is urgent, many states require the health plan to reply within 1 to 3 days. If care is not urgent, states require the health plan to reply within 2 to 15 days. A person can check state rules or ask the health plan or doctor's office what to expect.
qs: How long does prior authorization take?
How fast must insurance respond to a prior authorization?

atoms.title: What commonly needs prior authorization
atoms.q: Which treatments, services and drugs need prior authorization?
atoms.text: It depends on the health plan, and high-cost care is more likely to need it. Prior authorization is often used when there is more than one treatment option, when care guidelines change, or when care may cost a lot. Commonly included are high-cost and specialty drugs, advanced imaging, mental health and substance use disorder services, elective surgeries and durable medical equipment.
qs: What services need prior authorization?
Do MRIs need prior authorization?

atoms.title: Where to find the prior authorization list
atoms.q: How can I tell if my care or drug needs prior authorization?
atoms.text: A health plan has a list of drugs and services that may need prior authorization. It can typically be found in plan documents or online. A person can also use the Prescription Drug List (PDL), also called a formulary, which is a list of commonly used medications organized into cost levels called tiers. A plan may also ask members to get care at certain hospitals or clinics that have a payment agreement with the plan.
qs: Where do I find the list of services requiring prior authorization?
How do I know if a drug needs prior authorization?

atoms.title: Why do some prescriptions require prior authorization?
atoms.q: Why do some prescription drugs need prior authorization?
atoms.text: Some prescription drugs need prior authorization before a plan helps pay for them, to check that the drug is safe, needed and covered. For example, some long-acting opioids may need it to make sure they are used the right way. Most pharmacy claims are checked right away and do not need prior authorization. Medications that typically do not need it include drugs for high cholesterol, high blood pressure, asthma, depression, substance use disorders and diabetes.
qs: Why does my medication need prior authorization?
Which medications don't need prior authorization?

atoms.title: How prescription prior authorization works
atoms.q: How does prior authorization work at the pharmacy?
atoms.text: The pharmacy typically sends a claim first. The health plan system often checks it right away for eligibility, whether the drug is on the Prescription Drug List, safety limits and prior authorization rules. If prior authorization is needed, the plan tells the pharmacist and the process starts then. The plan may use information it already has to review faster, and some requests can be approved without asking the doctor for more information.
qs: What happens when my pharmacy says prior authorization is needed?
Can a prescription be approved automatically?

atoms.title: What happens if a prior authorization is denied?
atoms.q: What can I do if prior authorization is denied?
atoms.text: If prior authorization is denied, a person can appeal and should talk with their doctor about next steps. The doctor may need to explain why the drug is needed, why other covered options may not work, or why the drug may be safer or more effective, and lab or imaging results may be needed. If the appeal is denied, the doctor may suggest another treatment. About 4 out of 5 appeals end up overturning a prior authorization denial.
qs: What if my prior authorization is denied?
How often are prior authorization appeals successful?
Can I appeal a denial?

atoms.title: Emergency care never requires prior authorization
atoms.q: Do I need prior authorization in an emergency?
atoms.text: If a plan covers emergency care, it cannot require prior authorization for emergency medical care, even if the hospital or provider is out of network. Prior authorization only applies to planned services and is never required for emergencies or urgent care.
qs: Do I need prior authorization for the ER?
Is approval needed for urgent care?

atoms.title: Where can I find prior authorization forms?
atoms.q: Where can I find prior authorization forms?
atoms.text: Prior authorization forms can typically be found in the health plan's member portal. The doctor's office may also be able to submit the request for the patient. A person could also call the number on their member ID card to ask where to send the form. UnitedHealthcare members can sign in to their member account or the UHC app to see plan details and find member forms.
qs: Where do I get a prior authorization form?
Can my doctor submit prior authorization for me?

atoms.title: What open enrollment means
atoms.q: What is open enrollment?
atoms.text: An open enrollment period is a window of time that happens once a year, typically in the fall, when you can sign up for health insurance, adjust your current plan or cancel your plan. It is usually limited to a few weeks. If you miss it, you may have to wait until the next open enrollment period to make any changes.
qs: What is open enrollment for health insurance?
How long does open enrollment last?
What happens if I miss open enrollment?

atoms.title: Which insurance types have open enrollment
atoms.q: What types of insurance use open enrollment?
atoms.text: People who get health insurance through a job, through Medicare or through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace have an open enrollment period. Medicaid programs, including the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), have no open enrollment period.
qs: Does Medicaid have open enrollment?
Which health plans have an open enrollment period?

atoms.title: Open enrollment dates by coverage type
atoms.q: What are the open enrollment dates for each type of coverage?
atoms.text: ACA Marketplace plans for individuals and families: open enrollment is November 1 through January 15 in most states. Health insurance through work: enrollment periods are set by the employer, typically in the fall. Medicare: the Annual Enrollment Period (AEP) is October 15 to December 7 every year, and the Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) is around age 65. Medicaid and Dual Eligible Special Needs Plans (D-SNP): enroll anytime.
qs: When is open enrollment this year?
What are the open enrollment dates for Medicare and the ACA?
When can I enroll in Medicaid?

atoms.title: When ACA open enrollment happens
atoms.q: When is open enrollment for ACA plans?
atoms.text: For UnitedHealthcare Individual & Family ACA Marketplace plans, open enrollment for most states is November 1 through January 15. Some state-based markets may have open enrollment periods that differ from federal-based marketplaces, as well as special enrollment periods.
qs: When does ACA marketplace enrollment start and end?
Do state marketplaces have different enrollment dates?

atoms.title: Open enrollment for job-based coverage
atoms.q: When is open enrollment if I get health insurance through my work?
atoms.text: If you get health insurance through work, your employer sets the open enrollment period. It is typically in the fall so that your benefits can start at the beginning of the calendar year. Choosing a health care plan for the year ahead is an important decision, so take time to explore your options before you enroll.
qs: Who decides my open enrollment dates at work?
Why is employer open enrollment in the fall?

atoms.title: When Medicare enrollment happens
atoms.q: When is Medicare enrollment?
atoms.text: One key Medicare enrollment period for changing coverage is the Annual Enrollment Period (AEP), which runs from October 15 to December 7 every year. During AEP you can join, switch or drop a plan. If you make no changes during AEP, your current plan will automatically renew the next year. The Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) is around age 65.
qs: When is the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period?
What happens if I don't change my Medicare plan during AEP?
Can I drop a Medicare plan in the fall?

atoms.title: Open enrollment for Medicaid
atoms.q: Is there an open enrollment period for Medicaid?
atoms.text: There is no open enrollment period for Medicaid programs, including the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP). In all states Medicaid provides coverage to low-income families and children, pregnant women, the elderly and people with disabilities, and some states cover all low-income adults below a certain income level. To apply, contact your state agency that manages the Medicaid program.
qs: Can I sign up for Medicaid any time of year?
Who does Medicaid cover?
How do I apply for Medicaid?

atoms.title: Open enrollment for Dual Special Needs Plans
atoms.q: When is open enrollment for a Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan?
atoms.text: People who have both Medicaid and Medicare benefits could be eligible for a Dual Special Needs Plan (D-SNP). Those who qualify for this type of Medicare Advantage plan can switch to a new plan at any point during the year, not just during open enrollment.
qs: Can I switch a D-SNP plan any time?
What is a Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan?

atoms.title: Changes outside open enrollment
atoms.q: Can I make changes outside of the open enrollment period?
atoms.text: Typically, once you have made your benefit elections, you have to wait until the next open enrollment period to make changes. Not always, though. Qualifying life events are life events that let you make changes to your benefits outside of the open enrollment period.
qs: Can I change my health plan in the middle of the year?
What is a qualifying life event?

atoms.title: What to do if you missed open enrollment
atoms.q: What if I missed the deadline for open enrollment?
atoms.text: If you need coverage when annual open enrollment is not available and you have not had a qualifying life event, you can buy short term health insurance or a fixed benefit health plan. Short term health insurance can fill needs for 1 month to nearly 1 year, depending on your state. TriTerm Medical can provide coverage for up to 3 years in select states. Fixed benefit plans pay preset amounts for qualified medical services and are a supplement to health insurance, not a substitute for ACA minimum essential coverage.
qs: What can I do if I missed open enrollment?
Can I get health insurance outside open enrollment?
How long does short term health insurance last?

atoms.title: Questions to ask before choosing a plan
atoms.q: What should I think about before choosing a health insurance plan?
atoms.text: Before choosing a plan during open enrollment, consider four questions. How much did you spend on health care last year, including your premium, deductible and out-of-pocket costs? Did what you or your family spent line up with your health care needs? Is your doctor or clinic in network? Are your medications covered?
qs: How do I pick the best health plan at open enrollment?
What should I review before enrolling in a health plan?

atoms.title: What a qualifying life event is
atoms.q: What is a qualifying life event for health insurance?
atoms.text: A qualifying life event is a life-changing situation, sometimes planned and sometimes unexpected, that can affect you and your health insurance. Experiencing a significant life change may allow you to change your health plan outside of the annual enrollment period, also called open enrollment. If you have had one, check your plan materials, contact your employer or call the number on your member ID card.
qs: What counts as a qualifying life event?
Can I change my health insurance after a big life change?

atoms.title: Common qualifying life events
atoms.q: What events count as qualifying life events?
atoms.text: Qualifying life events include, but are not necessarily limited to: getting married, getting divorced, having or adopting a baby, the death of someone who shares your health plan, moving to a new area, earning U.S. citizenship, turning 26, turning 65, experiencing a shift in employment status, and loss of health insurance.
qs: Does getting married let me change my health plan?
Is turning 26 a qualifying life event?
Does losing my job count as a qualifying life event?

atoms.title: How to qualify for a special enrollment period
atoms.q: How do I qualify for a special enrollment period?
atoms.text: If you experience any qualifying life event, you qualify for a special enrollment period (SEP), which means you can enroll in a health plan outside the annual enrollment period. Sometimes SEPs are offered for other qualifying reasons, such as natural disaster relief, pandemic relief or a public health emergency.
qs: What is a special enrollment period?
Can a natural disaster give me a special enrollment period?

atoms.title: Losing Medicaid opens a special enrollment period
atoms.q: Do I get a special enrollment period if I lose Medicaid?
atoms.text: If you are no longer eligible for Medicaid, you qualify for a special enrollment period (SEP). If you are asked to renew or recertify your Medicaid (also called redetermination) and you lose your Medicaid coverage, you may qualify for a special enrollment period.
qs: What if I lose Medicaid coverage?
Can I enroll in a new plan after Medicaid redetermination?

atoms.title: How to enroll after a qualifying life event
atoms.q: How do I enroll in a plan after a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: After a qualifying life event, check your plan materials, contact your employer or call the phone number on your member ID card. Three things to know: timing, because changes can most often be made within either 30 or 60 days after the event; the deadline, because missing it may mean waiting until the next open enrollment period; and documentation, because you may need to submit documents confirming the event.
qs: What do I do after a qualifying life event?
Do I need proof of a life event to change my plan?

atoms.title: 30 or 60 day window to make changes
atoms.q: How long do I have to change my plan after a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: Changes after a qualifying life event can most often be made either 30 or 60 days after the life event happens. If you miss this deadline, you may have to wait until the next open enrollment period, which could be as long as a year.
qs: What is the deadline to enroll after getting married?
How many days after a life event can I change health insurance?

atoms.title: Turning 65 is a qualifying life event
atoms.q: Is turning 65 a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: Turning 65 is a qualifying life event. It gives you a chance to look into your opportunities to choose a Medicare plan. Parts A and B are sometimes called Original Medicare, and they do not cover everything: services like dental work, vision exams and eye care, and out-of-pocket costs such as deductibles are not covered.
qs: What should I do when I turn 65?
Does Original Medicare cover dental and vision?

atoms.title: Medicare Parts C and D
atoms.q: What are Medicare Part C and Part D?
atoms.text: Medicare Part C, also called Medicare Advantage, is a private health plan that combines hospital and medical insurance, plus the potential for additional health benefits. Medicare Part D plans, offered by insurance companies approved by Medicare, add prescription drug coverage to Original Medicare and Medicare Supplement insurance plans.
qs: What is the difference between Medicare Part C and Part D?
What is Medicare Advantage?
Which Medicare part covers prescriptions?

atoms.title: Documents you may need for a life event
atoms.q: What documents do I need for a qualifying life event?
atoms.text: When you experience a qualifying life event, you may be asked for documents confirming it, and the type depends on the event. Events with common documentation lists include marriage, divorce or legal separation, adoption or birth of a child, a dependent passing away, losing or gaining eligibility for other health benefits, turning 26 and aging off a parent's plan, and moving out of or into a plan area. Ask your health insurance provider what is needed for your situation.
qs: What proof do I need to add a spouse to my insurance?
What paperwork do I need after turning 26?

atoms.title: Options without a special enrollment period
atoms.q: What if I don't qualify for a special enrollment period?
atoms.text: If you are between enrollment periods and have not had a qualifying life event, short term insurance can bridge the gap. Standard short term health insurance plans can fill a gap in coverage from 1 month to just under one year, depending on your state. TriTerm Medical is a special type of short term health insurance available in select states that offers coverage for nearly 3 years.
qs: How can I get health insurance if I missed enrollment?
What is TriTerm Medical?
How long does short term insurance last?

atoms.title: Other insurance options to explore
atoms.q: What other types of insurance can I explore?
atoms.text: Beyond a standard health plan, UnitedHealthcare points people to other options to explore: Individual & Family ACA Marketplace plans, student health insurance, fixed benefit health insurance, hospital insurance, term life insurance, critical illness insurance, international travel medical insurance and accident insurance.
qs: What other kinds of insurance does UnitedHealthcare offer?
Is there student health insurance?

atoms.title: Choosing an employer plan at open enrollment
atoms.q: How should I approach choosing a health plan offered by my employer?
atoms.text: Open enrollment is your time to choose your health insurance plan for the year. If your employer offers more than one plan, think about the kind of coverage you will need for the year ahead and compare the options based on your budget and your care needs. Understanding some coverage details first can help you make a decision that may work best for your life situation.
qs: How do I choose between health plans my employer offers?
What should I know before enrolling in a work health plan?

atoms.title: Plans cover network providers differently
atoms.q: Do all health plans cover out-of-network providers?
atoms.text: Each health plan covers care through a network of designated doctors, specialists and facilities. Some plans help cover care only within their own network. Other plans are more flexible and agree to cover part of the cost for out-of-network providers. Learn whether your provider is in the network for the plan you are considering, and check whether there is partial coverage for out-of-network providers.
qs: Will my plan cover an out-of-network doctor?
Do I need to stay in network to have coverage?
How do I check if my doctor is in my plan's network?

atoms.title: What preventive care is
atoms.q: What is preventive care?
atoms.text: Preventive care helps you stay healthier before you have symptoms. Plans often cover preventive care such as routine checkups, immunizations and tests, and one wellness visit per year. Each plan covers preventive care differently, so check each plan's covered preventive services and find out how often you can use them in one plan year.
qs: What counts as preventive care?
Does my plan cover an annual wellness visit?

atoms.title: What diagnostic care is
atoms.q: What is diagnostic care?
atoms.text: Diagnostic care helps you determine what is wrong when you already have symptoms. Plan coverage can vary, and you may have to pay more for diagnostic care services such as services other than routine care and certain tests, procedures, doctors and specialists. Ask which services are considered diagnostic before you receive care, because these services generally cost a lot more.
qs: What is the difference between diagnostic and preventive care?
Why does diagnostic care cost more?

atoms.title: Preventive versus diagnostic care examples
atoms.q: How can I tell if the care I need is preventive or diagnostic?
atoms.text: Coverage can change depending on whether care is preventive or diagnostic. A primary care visit is preventive for a wellness checkup but diagnostic if you have a cough that is not getting better. A mammogram is preventive when it is a routine screen for breast cancer but diagnostic when ordered to learn more about a lump. A colonoscopy is preventive when routine without symptoms but diagnostic when ordered based on symptoms.
qs: Is a colonoscopy preventive or diagnostic?
Will I pay more for a mammogram if I found a lump?

atoms.title: Plan documents to review before enrolling
atoms.q: What plan documents should I read before I enroll?
atoms.text: Before you enroll, review the health plan documents. The Summary of benefits gives an overview of coverage for each plan, including benefits, cost-sharing requirements and coverage limitations and exceptions. The plan coverage document, which you can ask your employer for, offers a deeper dive into the coverage details for each plan.
qs: What is a summary of benefits?
Where do I find the details of what my plan covers?

atoms.title: Preventive care with no cost-sharing
atoms.q: Is preventive care free under my plan?
atoms.text: Certain preventive care items and services, including immunizations, are provided as specified by applicable law, including the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA), with no cost-sharing to you, and may be based on your age and other health factors. Other routine services may be covered under your plan, and some plans may require copayments, coinsurance or deductibles for them. Review your plan documents for specifics.
ents: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
qs: Are immunizations covered at no cost?
Do I pay a copay for preventive care?

atoms.title: Learning plan benefits through video series
atoms.q: Where can I learn more about how plan benefits work?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers a video series to help people learn how plan benefits work and another video series on how specialty benefits work. It also offers a guide with three tips for choosing a health insurance plan through work and a page on the benefits of UnitedHealthcare plans through work.
qs: Are there videos explaining how health plan benefits work?
Where can I find open enrollment help?

atoms.title: Overview of UnitedHealthcare plan benefits through work
atoms.q: What do UnitedHealthcare employer-sponsored plans offer?
atoms.text: With employer-sponsored plans from UnitedHealthcare, members can find easier ways to manage their costs and care throughout the year. These plans include more care options, convenient ways to manage a plan, and a support team that is there for members every step of the way.
qs: What are the benefits of a UnitedHealthcare plan through work?
Why choose a UnitedHealthcare employer plan?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare network size
atoms.q: How big is the UnitedHealthcare provider network?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare's network for employer-sponsored plans includes 1,205,773 doctors and health care professionals, 6,126 hospitals and more than 67,000 pharmacies. The hospital, doctor and health care professional counts are stated as of Q1, 2021. Members can look up network doctors, facilities and more with the provider search tool.
qs: How many doctors are in the UnitedHealthcare network?
How many hospitals does UnitedHealthcare cover?

atoms.title: Nationwide coverage even out of network
atoms.q: Do UnitedHealthcare plans cover care out of network?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers convenient care options and nationwide coverage with most employer-sponsored plans, even when members go out of network. This is presented as part of getting access to a wider provider network, along with a large count of doctors, hospitals and pharmacies.
qs: Is UnitedHealthcare coverage nationwide?
Can I use UnitedHealthcare out of network?

atoms.title: 24/7 nurse line
atoms.q: Can I talk to a nurse anytime with UnitedHealthcare?
atoms.text: With UnitedHealthcare plans through work, a registered nurse is available 24/7 to discuss your symptoms. Members can talk with a nurse anytime as one of the convenient care options offered with these plans.
qs: Is there a 24 hour nurse line?
Can I ask a nurse about my symptoms?

atoms.title: Virtual Visits with a doctor
atoms.q: What are Virtual Visits?
atoms.text: With Virtual Visits, you can talk with a doctor using your mobile device, tablet or computer and get a prescription for minor diagnoses. Certain prescriptions may not be available and other restrictions may apply. Virtual Visits are not an insurance product or a health plan, are not intended for emergency or life-threatening conditions, and benefits are generally available only through a Designated Virtual Network Provider.
qs: Can I see a doctor from my phone with UnitedHealthcare?
Can a virtual visit prescribe medication?
Are Virtual Visits for emergencies?

atoms.title: Quality care physicians marked with a blue heart
atoms.q: How can I find a quality care physician?
atoms.text: Members with UnitedHealthcare plans through work can find a quality care physician, who is indicated with a blue heart. Finding a quality care physician is listed among the convenient care options available with these plans.
qs: What does the blue heart mean on a UnitedHealthcare doctor?
How do I find a high-quality doctor?

atoms.title: Manage your plan online and in the app
atoms.q: How can I manage my UnitedHealthcare plan with ease?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare plans through work give members quick access to plan details on any device. Members can sign in to their member account to manage benefits, see claims and account balances, print a health plan ID card and more. They can also download the UnitedHealthcare app, available for iPhone or Android, to view benefits and the health plan ID card from a mobile device.
qs: Where can I print my health plan ID card?
Can I see my claims in the UnitedHealthcare app?

atoms.title: Help choosing a health plan through work
atoms.q: Where can I get more help choosing my health plan through work?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare directs people who want more help choosing a health plan through work to its open enrollment video series, which explains plan benefits, and to a page with three tips for choosing a health plan through work. The goal is to help people choose a plan that may work best for their needs and budget.
qs: Are there open enrollment videos from UnitedHealthcare?
Where can I find tips for choosing a health plan?

atoms.title: Three tips for choosing a plan through work
atoms.q: What are the tips for choosing a health insurance plan through my employer?
atoms.text: At open enrollment, you can use a three-step checklist to weigh the plans your employer offers. 1) Check to see which providers are in network. 2) Consider your health care needs for the year ahead. 3) Decide how you prefer to manage your costs, for example by keeping your monthly premium low or by paying more each month to pay less when you need care.
qs: How do I choose a health plan at work?
What should I look for when picking a health insurance plan?

atoms.title: Check which providers are in network
atoms.q: Why should I check if my providers are in network?
atoms.text: Finding a doctor or clinic that is in network may help keep costs lower, and many plans will only cover network providers. When reviewing plans, check whether your primary doctor, provider or clinic is in network; check whether your mental health providers, dentists and specialty providers are in network; and find out whether there is partial coverage for out-of-network providers.
qs: Should my doctor be in my plan's network?
What providers should I check before choosing a plan?

atoms.title: Using provider search for a UnitedHealthcare plan
atoms.q: How do I find out which doctors are in a UnitedHealthcare network?
atoms.text: If you are considering a UnitedHealthcare plan, you can search for network providers and clinics using the UnitedHealthcare provider search tool. Knowing which providers are in network may help you narrow your health plan choices. For example, if you prefer a specific doctor, you will likely want to be sure that doctor is in network for the plan you choose.
qs: How can I see if my doctor takes UnitedHealthcare?
Where is the UnitedHealthcare provider search tool?

atoms.title: Consider your care needs for the year ahead
atoms.q: How do my health care needs affect which plan I should pick?
atoms.text: Coverage needs may change from year to year, for example because of different medication needs or a procedure planned for the upcoming year. Before you enroll, think about the care you or your family may need in the year ahead. The checklist suggests asking what you see the doctor for, whether you have a major procedure planned, whether you take medications and who else needs coverage through your plan.
qs: What health needs should I consider before enrolling?
Should a planned surgery change which plan I choose?

atoms.title: Lower premium versus lower copay plans
atoms.q: Should I choose a lower premium plan or a lower copay plan?
atoms.text: Some people prefer to keep their monthly premium low, while others choose to pay higher monthly premiums so they may pay less in copays when they need care. A lower premium plan can save money if you do not have major care needs. A lower copay plan may cost less when you visit a doctor, clinic or urgent care. Compare each plan's deductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket limit as well.
qs: Is it better to have a low premium or low copays?
How do I decide how to manage health costs with my plan?

atoms.title: How a lower premium plan works
atoms.q: What does a lower premium plan mean for my paycheck?
atoms.text: If you do not have any major care needs, you can save money by finding a plan that charges a lower premium each month. This means the plan takes less money out of your paychecks to pay for insurance. Compare your plan options to see which plan's premium amount requires you to pay the least.
qs: How can I pay less each month for health insurance?
Does a lower premium mean less taken from my paycheck?

atoms.title: Compare copays and cost-sharing to avoid surprises
atoms.q: How can I avoid cost surprises with my health plan?
atoms.text: Some plans give you the option to spend less when you pay for care, like visiting the doctor. Consider the cost of copays when you visit a doctor, clinic or urgent care, and compare each plan's deductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket limit to see which plans may help you save more. Researching these costs and understanding how you and your plan share costs together helps you avoid cost surprises later.
qs: What costs should I compare between health plans?
How do I avoid surprise medical costs?

atoms.title: What is the Affordable Care Act (ACA)?
atoms.q: What is the Affordable Care Act?
atoms.text: The Affordable Care Act (ACA), also called Obamacare or Bidencare, was put in place to help make health insurance easier for people to get. Marketplace or ACA plans are sold on the health care Marketplace, or Exchange. They focus on preventive care, cover pre-existing conditions and provide benefits for things like doctor visits, prescriptions and lab tests. Marketplace coverage usually requires enrolling during the established enrollment period.
qs: What is the ACA?
What are Marketplace plans?
Do ACA plans cover pre-existing conditions?

atoms.title: What is Medicare?
atoms.q: What is Medicare?
atoms.text: Medicare is a federally funded and operated health insurance program originally designed for people who are 65 or older. Over the years it has expanded to include disabled people under 65 and those with special circumstances. The program is divided into four parts, A, B, C and D, and is the same nationwide.
qs: What is Medicare?
How many parts does Medicare have?
Who qualifies for Medicare?

atoms.title: What is Medicaid?
atoms.q: What is Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicaid is a federal and state program in place for low income families, seniors and individuals with mental or physical disabilities. People qualify by meeting federal income standards. The program is operated on a state-by-state basis and may be called different names depending on where a person lives. In Minnesota, for example, Medicaid is called Minnesota Medical Assistance.
qs: What is Medicaid?
Who qualifies for Medicaid?
Is Medicaid different in each state?

atoms.title: Medicare vs. Medicaid and dual coverage
atoms.q: What is the difference between Medicaid and Medicare, and can I have both?
atoms.text: Medicare and Medicaid are often mentioned together because both are government programs, but they work differently. A Dual Special Needs Plan (D-SNP) is another type of plan that includes both Medicare and Medicaid benefits. People may qualify for Medicare, Medicaid or both, depending on their situation.
qs: What's the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
Can I have Medicare and Medicaid at the same time?
What is a D-SNP?

atoms.title: About 49% of Americans have employer coverage
atoms.q: How many Americans get health insurance through work?
atoms.text: Around 49% of Americans get health insurance coverage through their employers, which is nearly 157 million people, according to a January 2021 source cited on the page. Employer-sponsored health plans play a big role in benefits packages, and depending on the employer there may be several plans to choose from.
qs: How many people get insurance through their employer?
What percent of Americans have employer health insurance?

atoms.title: What are HMO, PPO, EPO, POS and HDHP plans?
atoms.q: What are HMO, PPO, EPO, POS and HDHP health plans?
atoms.text: HMO, PPO, EPO, POS and HDHP are common types of health plan options, often chosen by people who get insurance through an employer when there is more than one choice. The choice affects access to medical care and may affect out-of-pocket costs. People shopping for Medicare plans may also choose between these same types of options, though not everyone has the same options.
qs: What do HMO, PPO and EPO mean?
Which type of health plan is right for me?

atoms.title: What are dental HMO and dental PPO plans?
atoms.q: What is the difference between PPO and HMO dental insurance?
atoms.text: Dental health maintenance organization (DHMO) and dental preferred provider organization (DPPO) are two common dental insurance plans. Each type has benefits and limitations, and understanding the difference between the two can help a person choose which one would best fit their needs.
qs: Is dental PPO or HMO better?
What are DHMO and DPPO plans?

atoms.title: What is COBRA?
atoms.q: What is COBRA?
atoms.text: COBRA stands for the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985, a program that may help someone who needs coverage between jobs. If a person loses a job, is furloughed or has reduced hours and it changes their health insurance coverage, they may look into COBRA. With COBRA, a person can continue the same coverage they had when employed, including medical, dental and vision plans.
qs: What is COBRA?
Can I keep my health insurance after losing my job?

atoms.title: What is short term health insurance?
atoms.q: What is short term health insurance?
atoms.text: Short term health insurance, also called temporary health insurance or term health insurance, may be right for someone who needs to fill a gap in coverage until a longer-term solution. Examples include being between jobs, waiting for coverage to start, bridging to Medicare, or turning 26 and coming off a parent's insurance. Depending on the state, it offers flexible, fast coverage from 1 month to nearly 3 years.
qs: What is short term health insurance?
How long does short term insurance last?
Can short term insurance bridge me to Medicare?

atoms.title: What is a fixed benefit health plan?
atoms.q: What is a fixed benefit (fixed indemnity) plan?
atoms.text: Fixed benefit health plans, sometimes called fixed indemnity plans, are designed to give traditional health insurance a boost. They pay a preset amount when a person receives any of the qualified medical services specified in the plan. The benefit paid stays the same no matter what the total bill for the service was and no matter what other insurance pays.
qs: What is a fixed indemnity plan?
How does a fixed benefit plan pay?

atoms.title: What is ACA health insurance?
atoms.q: What is ACA health insurance?
atoms.text: ACA insurance plans are sold on the health care Marketplace, also called the Exchange. In most cases they are subsidized by the Federal or State government, which typically leads to a lower monthly premium. They are plans people buy on their own, instead of through an employer or a government-run program like Medicare or Medicaid, and suit those who need coverage for a full calendar year for themselves or their family.
qs: What are ACA plans?
Are ACA plans subsidized?
Who buys ACA insurance?

atoms.title: When an ACA plan fits
atoms.q: When is an ACA plan a good fit?
atoms.text: An ACA plan might be a good fit if a person's job does not offer health insurance, they want long-term coverage for their family, they want comprehensive benefits, or they qualify for a premium tax credit.
qs: Should I choose an ACA plan?
Who should buy a Marketplace plan?

atoms.title: What is short term health insurance?
atoms.q: What is a short term insurance plan?
atoms.text: A short term insurance plan is a good fit for bridging a gap for a short time when someone is uninsured. Depending on the state, typical short term plans offer coverage from one month up to nearly one year. TriTerm Medical insurance is a type of short term plan that offers coverage for nearly 3 years with just one application.
qs: What is a short term plan?
How long does TriTerm Medical last?

atoms.title: When a short term plan fits
atoms.q: When is a short term plan a good fit?
atoms.text: A short term plan might be a good fit if a person missed Open Enrollment and does not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, is waiting for an ACA plan to start, wants coverage until joining Medicare, is turning 26 and coming off a parent's plan, is between jobs or waiting for benefits to start, or is healthy and under 65.
qs: Who should get short term insurance?
What if I missed open enrollment?

atoms.title: Short term plans generally do not cover pre-existing conditions
atoms.q: Do short term plans cover pre-existing conditions?
atoms.text: Unlike ACA plans, short term plans generally do not cover preexisting conditions, and applicants must answer a series of medical questions to apply. Preexisting conditions may be covered only on extended TriTerm Medical plans after the first year. ACA plans cover preexisting conditions.
qs: Are pre-existing conditions covered by short term insurance?
Does ACA cover pre-existing conditions?

atoms.title: ACA vs. short term: enrollment
atoms.q: How does enrollment differ between ACA and short term plans?
atoms.text: ACA plans are available during Open Enrollment or a Special Enrollment Period after a qualified life event; open enrollment is November 1 through January 16 in most states. Short term plans can be applied for any time. ACA plans have no underwriting, so a plan is guaranteed. Short term plans have underwriting, so applicants could be denied depending on health history.
qs: When can I enroll in ACA vs short term?
Can short term insurance deny me?

atoms.title: ACA vs. short term: duration and premium
atoms.q: How long does coverage last under ACA vs. short term plans?
atoms.text: ACA plans cover a person for a full calendar year, or longer if premiums continue to be paid. Short term plans cover 1 to nearly 12 months, varying by state, or up to nearly 3 years in select states with TriTerm Medical. For both plan types, the monthly premium varies based on the plan and personal factors, such as whether a person smokes tobacco.
qs: How long does ACA coverage last?
What affects short term plan premiums?

atoms.title: ACA vs. short term: covered services
atoms.q: What services do ACA and short term plans cover?
atoms.text: ACA plans cover preventive care, doctor visits, emergency care, hospital care, virtual care, prescription drugs and maternity and newborn care. Short term plans vary by plan for doctor visits, emergency care, hospital care, virtual care and maternity and newborn care, and offer limited or no preventive care and prescription drug coverage.
qs: Does short term insurance cover prescriptions?
Is preventive care covered by short term plans?

atoms.title: What is COBRA?
atoms.q: What is COBRA health insurance?
atoms.text: COBRA is a federal law that gives a person the right to continue their employer-sponsored health insurance for a limited time after they lose their job, reduce their work hours or experience another qualifying life event. It can be more expensive, since a person typically pays the full premium plus an administrative fee, but it helps ensure they do not lose access to health care coverage during a transition period.
qs: What is COBRA?
How does COBRA work when you lose your job?

atoms.title: Do I qualify for COBRA?
atoms.q: Who qualifies for COBRA coverage?
atoms.text: A person may qualify for COBRA if their job or life situation has changed. Examples are losing a job, voluntarily or by the company's decision for any reason except gross misconduct, and losing health coverage; having work hours reduced so benefits are lost and health coverage is lost; or a qualifying event such as the death of the covered employee or a divorce or legal separation from the covered employee.
qs: Am I eligible for COBRA?
Can I get COBRA after a divorce?
Does COBRA cover reduced hours?

atoms.title: What is covered under COBRA?
atoms.q: What does COBRA cover?
atoms.text: With COBRA, a person can continue the same coverage they had when employed, including medical, dental and vision plans. They cannot choose new coverage or change to a different plan. For example, someone with a medical plan and a dental plan can keep one or both, but cannot add a vision plan that was not part of their coverage before COBRA.
qs: Does COBRA include dental and vision?
Can I change my plan under COBRA?

atoms.title: How do I pay for COBRA?
atoms.q: How much does COBRA cost?
atoms.text: Under COBRA, a person has to pay the full premium for their coverage, plus an administrative fee. When employed, an employer generally pays some of the cost of health insurance, so a person will likely pay more for COBRA. It may get expensive, depending on the kind of coverage.
qs: Why is COBRA so expensive?
Do I pay the full premium with COBRA?

atoms.title: COBRA time limits and reasons it can end
atoms.q: How long does COBRA last, and when can it end?
atoms.text: COBRA coverage is only a short-term solution, with a general time limit of 18 to 36 months. Coverage can also end if the person does not pay premiums on time, if the former employer stops offering any group health plans, if the person gets comparable coverage through a new job, or if the person becomes eligible for Medicare.
qs: How long can I keep COBRA?
What makes COBRA coverage end?

atoms.title: Other coverage options besides COBRA
atoms.q: What other health insurance options exist besides COBRA?
atoms.text: Because COBRA is only a short-term solution, UnitedHealthcare recommends exploring other options. Two alternatives it points to are Affordable Care Act (ACA) or Exchange plans, and short term health insurance plans. TriTerm Medical is a type of short term plan that can last for nearly 3 years.
qs: What are alternatives to COBRA?
Should I choose ACA or COBRA after losing my job?

atoms.title: Dental HMO and dental PPO plans
atoms.q: What are the two most common types of dental insurance?
atoms.text: Dental health maintenance organization (DHMO) and dental preferred provider organization (DPPO) plans are the two most common dental insurance plans. UnitedHealthcare says one option is not better than the other; each type has its own advantages and limitations.
qs: What are the types of dental insurance?
Is dental PPO or HMO better?

atoms.title: Dental PPO versus dental HMO at a glance
atoms.q: What is the difference between PPO and HMO dental insurance?
atoms.text: A dental PPO is best for more control and flexibility, with higher premiums, a broad network, partial out-of-network reimbursement that likely costs less with a network provider, no primary care dentist or specialist referral required, an annual maximum, and sometimes a copay. A dental HMO is best for affordability, with lower premiums, a smaller network, no out-of-network coverage, a required primary care dentist and referrals, no annual maximum, and copays.
qs: Dental PPO vs HMO comparison
Which dental plan has an annual maximum?
Do dental HMO plans require referrals?

atoms.title: What a dental PPO plan is
atoms.q: What is dental PPO insurance?
atoms.text: A dental preferred provider organization (DPPO) plan is a type of insurance that offers members broad access to pre-selected providers. These dentists and specialists have already agreed to participate in the insurance company's network, which usually makes it cheaper and easier to see providers within that network.
qs: What does PPO mean for dental insurance?
How does a dental PPO work?

atoms.title: Advantages of dental PPO plans
atoms.q: What are the pros of a dental PPO plan?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare lists four pros of dental PPO plans: greater flexibility in choosing a dentist, since members can visit network or out-of-network providers; lower costs for services, with deeper discounts for in-network care; no referral required to see a specialist; and possible partial reimbursement for out-of-network services, depending on the plan.
qs: Can I see any dentist with a PPO?
Do I need a referral to see a dental specialist on a PPO?

atoms.title: Drawbacks of dental PPO plans
atoms.q: What are the cons of a dental PPO plan?
atoms.text: Cons of dental PPO plans include higher monthly premiums than HMO plans, in exchange for flexibility and more options. A PPO plan requires meeting a deductible, a set amount paid for dental care before benefits start to pay, which resets every 12 months. Coinsurance, a percentage of the cost of a procedure, also tends to be higher with PPO dental plans than with HMO plans.
qs: Do dental PPO plans have a deductible?
Are dental PPO premiums higher than HMO?

atoms.title: When a dental PPO may be right for you
atoms.q: Is PPO dental insurance right for me?
atoms.text: A dental PPO plan is a good choice for someone who wants more flexibility in choosing a provider and the ability to see a specialist without a referral. UnitedHealthcare adds that if a person knows they will need more care in the coming year and can budget for higher premiums, a PPO dental plan might be right for them.
qs: Should I choose a PPO dental plan?
Who is a dental PPO best for?

atoms.title: What a dental HMO plan is
atoms.q: What is dental HMO insurance?
atoms.text: A dental health maintenance organization (DHMO) is a budget-oriented plan designed to help lower the cost of care. These plans emphasize preventive care and prioritize regular check-ups with a primary dental facility or provider.
qs: What does HMO mean for dental insurance?
How does a dental HMO work?

atoms.title: Advantages of dental HMO plans
atoms.q: What are the pros of a dental HMO plan?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare lists three pros of dental HMO plans. Lower monthly premiums and out-of-pocket costs, since they work with a network of providers at reduced rates. Usually no deductible or annual maximum, because the plans focus on preventive care and routine procedures. Fixed copays, a predetermined flat rate listed in the benefits for covered services, which makes dental costs easier to budget.
qs: Do dental HMO plans have deductibles?
Are dental HMO plans cheaper?
How do copays work on a dental HMO?

atoms.title: Drawbacks of dental HMO plans
atoms.q: What are the cons of a dental HMO plan?
atoms.text: Cons of dental HMO plans include a restricted network, since a member selects a primary care dentist from a smaller network of covered providers. Care outside the HMO's network is not covered. Seeing a specialist requires a referral from the primary care dentist, and without a referral, dental services may not be covered by the plan.
qs: Does a dental HMO cover out-of-network dentists?
Do I need a referral for a dental specialist on an HMO?

atoms.title: When a dental HMO may be right for you
atoms.q: Is HMO dental insurance right for me?
atoms.text: If flexibility and frequent specialist care are not a top priority, a dental HMO plan could be the best bet, and UnitedHealthcare calls DHMO plans a great option when affordability and low dental costs are the main concerns. The plans work best for people who want to stick with a primary dentist to coordinate care and are comfortable obtaining referrals for specialist care.
qs: Should I choose a dental HMO?
Who is a dental HMO best for?

atoms.title: Medicare vs. Medicaid at a glance
atoms.q: What is the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicare and Medicaid are terms often heard together because both are government programs, but they work differently. Medicare is a national program run by the federal government, while Medicaid is managed by each state. People may qualify for Medicare, Medicaid or both, depending on their situation.
qs: What's the difference between Medicare and Medicaid?
Is Medicaid federal or state?

atoms.title: What is Medicare?
atoms.q: What is Medicare?
atoms.text: Medicare is a national health insurance program run by the federal government. It covers people age 65 and older and some people under age 65 who may qualify due to a disability or another special situation. There are 4 different parts to Medicare, which helps give people more health care choices so they can pick the plan that best meets their needs.
qs: What is Medicare?
Who is covered by Medicare?
How many parts does Medicare have?

atoms.title: What is Medicaid?
atoms.q: What is Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicaid is a way to get health care at a lower cost or sometimes at no cost to the person. It is managed by each state, so the eligibility requirements can change from state to state. A state may even have its own name for its Medicaid program.
qs: What is Medicaid?
Do Medicaid rules differ by state?
Is Medicaid free?

atoms.title: What are Dual Special Needs Plans (D-SNP)?
atoms.q: What is a Dual Special Needs Plan?
atoms.text: Dual Special Needs Plans (D-SNP) are for people who could use some extra help, which may be because of income, disabilities, age and/or health conditions. Dual eligible health plans are a special type of Medicare Part C (Medicare Advantage) plan. Members keep all their Medicaid benefits, could get more benefits than with Original Medicare, and could get it all for a $0 plan premium.
qs: What is a D-SNP?
Can I have Medicare and Medicaid together?
Do dual eligible plans cost anything?

atoms.title: Can I be eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.q: Can I have both Medicare and Medicaid?
atoms.text: Yes, people may qualify for Medicare, Medicaid or both, depending on their situation. Dual Special Needs Plans include both Medicare and Medicaid benefits for those who are eligible for both.
qs: Can I get Medicare and Medicaid at the same time?
What is dual eligibility?

atoms.title: Medicaid is run by each state
atoms.q: Why do Medicaid requirements vary by state?
atoms.text: Medicaid is managed by each state, so the eligibility requirements can change from state to state. A state may also have its own name for its Medicaid program, so a program called something different locally may still be Medicaid.
qs: Why is Medicaid different in each state?
Does my state call Medicaid something else?

atoms.title: Short term insurance can fill a gap
atoms.q: What can fill a coverage gap while I wait for other coverage?
atoms.text: During times of transition, short term health insurance can help fill a gap in coverage from 1 month to just under 1 year, depending on the state. UnitedHealthcare notes that product design and availability vary by state.
qs: How long does short term insurance last?
Is short term insurance available in every state?

atoms.title: What is private health insurance?
atoms.q: What is private health insurance?
atoms.text: Private health insurance is any health coverage that is not provided by the government. Insurance like Medicaid and Medicare is government-run and is not private. Many people get their insurance from a private company, such as UnitedHealthcare, and that is private health insurance. It can be obtained through an employer or directly from the insurance company.
qs: What is private health insurance?
Is Medicare private insurance?

atoms.title: Employer-sponsored plans are often least expensive
atoms.q: Why are employer-sponsored health plans often the cheapest option?
atoms.text: In most cases, employer-sponsored insurance is the least expensive option because the employer covers part of the monthly cost. Also, some employers are able to get better rates with insurance companies because they buy for so many people. Many employers offer a few plans, such as a PPO with a low deductible or an HDHP with a lower monthly premium.
qs: Is employer health insurance cheaper?
What plan choices do employers usually offer?

atoms.title: Self-employed people need other private options
atoms.q: What if I'm self-employed and can't get employer insurance?
atoms.text: Self-employed individuals such as freelancers, contractors and small business owners do not have access to employer-sponsored plans. They need other private health insurance options. Even someone with access to insurance through work may want to compare other options to be sure they get the best plan.
qs: How do freelancers get health insurance?
What insurance can I get if I'm self-employed?

atoms.title: On-exchange vs. off-exchange ACA plans
atoms.q: What is the difference between on-exchange and off-exchange ACA plans?
atoms.text: On-exchange ACA Marketplace plans are bought through the Marketplace or directly from an insurer, and buyers may qualify for tax subsidies that lower the monthly cost. Off-exchange ACA plans are bought directly from an insurer or through a broker and are not connected to the Marketplace, but they provide the same minimum coverage and essential health benefits. Both are private insurance plans administered by private companies.
qs: What's an off-exchange plan?
Can I get subsidies on an off-exchange plan?

atoms.title: When to choose an off-exchange ACA plan
atoms.q: When do people choose off-exchange ACA plans?
atoms.text: A person will typically need to choose an off-exchange plan if their income is too high to qualify for subsidies, or if their employer reimburses health care costs through an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement (ICHRA) or a Qualified Small Employer Health Reimbursement Arrangement (QSEHRA).
qs: Do I need an off-exchange plan with ICHRA?
What if my income is too high for subsidies?

atoms.title: Short term plans: duration, speed and limits
atoms.q: What should I know about short term health insurance as private coverage?
atoms.text: Short term health insurance provides temporary coverage, typically for almost 12 months. In some states, extended short term health insurance, also called TriTerm Medical, provides 3 consecutive terms for nearly 3 years. Coverage can start quickly, sometimes the next day. However, short term plans may not be best for people with chronic medical needs, as they typically do not cover pre-existing conditions and are medically underwritten.
qs: How long does short term insurance last?
Does short term insurance cover chronic conditions?

atoms.title: TriTerm Medical waiting periods
atoms.q: Are there waiting periods under TriTerm Medical plans?
atoms.text: According to the page's disclaimers, with TriTerm Medical plans no benefits will be paid during the first 12 months for a preexisting condition, and preventive care has a 6-month waiting period. Short term health insurance is described as a short-term, limited-duration policy, not comprehensive health coverage, with fewer benefits and Federal protections than options like those on HealthCare.gov.
qs: Does TriTerm Medical have a waiting period?
Is short term insurance comprehensive coverage?

atoms.title: Supplemental and fixed benefit plans add coverage
atoms.q: What supplemental insurance options complement a major medical plan?
atoms.text: Even the most comprehensive health insurance plans do not cover everything. Supplemental options can add a layer of coverage to a major medical plan, including dental, vision, and accident and critical illness insurance. A fixed benefit plan, also known as fixed indemnity insurance, pays a fixed amount for specific covered services, regardless of the total bill or what other insurance pays. It is a supplement, not a substitute for minimum essential coverage.
qs: What is supplemental health insurance?
Does fixed indemnity replace major medical?

atoms.title: Benefits of choosing private coverage
atoms.q: What are the benefits of private health insurance?
atoms.text: For people who do not qualify for Medicaid or Medicare, private insurance offers many opportunities for coverage, with a variety of options with different monthly costs, copays, risks and benefits. Depending on the plan, benefits may include access to a large provider network, coverage for essential health benefits such as prescriptions, lab services and pediatric care, financial security in an emergency, telemedicine, and wellness incentives.
qs: What do I get with private health insurance?
Does private insurance include telemedicine?

atoms.title: Six factors for choosing a private plan
atoms.q: How do I choose the right private health insurance plan?
atoms.text: Consider each plan's premium, the monthly cost to be a member; copays or coinsurance, what is paid to receive a service or medication; deductible, how much is paid before additional benefits kick in; out-of-pocket maximum, the most paid for covered services in a year; coverage, which services and medications are covered; and network, which providers can be seen. Only the shopper can decide which matters most.
qs: What should I look for when choosing a health plan?
How do I compare health insurance plans?

atoms.title: When is open enrollment for private insurance?
atoms.q: What is open enrollment and when is it?
atoms.text: Open enrollment is a period, usually once a year, when individuals can enroll in or change their health insurance plans. For ACA Marketplace plans, this time is November 1 to December 15, in most states. Many employer-sponsored plans follow the same schedule, but some employers offer open enrollment at different times of the year, so it is important to check with the employer.
qs: When is ACA open enrollment?
When does employer open enrollment happen?

atoms.title: Can I sign up outside of open enrollment?
atoms.q: Can I sign up for private insurance outside of open enrollment?
atoms.text: A person who has had a qualifying life event (QLE) can make changes to an employer-sponsored or ACA Marketplace plan outside of open enrollment. QLEs include marriage, the birth or adoption of a child, or job loss, and begin a special enrollment period, typically 60 days. Short term and TriTerm Medical plans have year-round enrollment, subject to medical underwriting and pre-existing limitations.
qs: Can I buy health insurance outside open enrollment?
How long is a special enrollment period?

atoms.title: Provider networks and plan acronyms
atoms.q: Why do health plans use terms like network, HMO and PPO?
atoms.text: People with health insurance, or shopping for coverage, likely come across the term network, or provider network, and acronyms like HMO, PPO, EPO, POS or HDHP. It may not be completely clear how choosing one over another changes access to medical care and may affect out-of-pocket costs. For many people with employer coverage, the choice comes down to which options are available.
qs: What is a provider network?
What do HMO, PPO and EPO stand for?

atoms.title: What is an HMO plan?
atoms.q: What is an HMO health plan?
atoms.text: HMO plans typically require a person to choose a primary care physician (PCP) in the HMO network, who refers them to other network providers as needed. Care typically must come from providers in the HMO network to use plan benefits, and referrals from the doctor are needed before seeing specialists. Premiums are often lower because the defined network can help control costs, and these plans may offer low or no deductible options.
qs: What is an HMO?
Are HMO premiums lower?
Do HMO plans need referrals?

atoms.title: What is a PPO plan?
atoms.q: What is a PPO health plan?
atoms.text: PPO plans tend to give more flexibility to choose preferred providers. A PPO creates a network of preferred providers, so a person gets the highest level of coverage with providers in the network. Choosing an out-of-network provider likely costs more. Premiums tend to be higher and are commonly paired with a deductible.
qs: What is a PPO?
Do PPO plans cost more?
Can I see out-of-network doctors with a PPO?

atoms.title: What is an EPO plan?
atoms.q: What is an EPO health plan?
atoms.text: EPO plans generally let a person see any network provider they choose, with no requirement to choose a primary care physician or get referrals to see a specialist (this refers to non-gated plans only). EPO plans do not offer out-of-network benefits. A person would likely pay higher deductibles and lower monthly payments compared to other plan types.
qs: What is an EPO?
Do EPO plans need referrals?
Does an EPO cover out-of-network care?

atoms.title: What is a POS plan?
atoms.q: What is a point of service (POS) plan?
atoms.text: A point of service (POS) plan is a health insurance plan that partners with a group of clinics, hospitals and doctors to provide care. A person pays less out of pocket for care within the plan's network. POS plans often require coordination with a primary care provider (PCP) for treatment and referrals, and most have some coverage for out-of-network care, often with a higher copay. They are like a combination of an HMO and PPO plan.
qs: What is a POS plan?
How is a POS different from an HMO?

atoms.title: What is an HDHP?
atoms.q: What is a high deductible health plan (HDHP)?
