atoms.text: With a high deductible health plan (HDHP), it is common to pay lower premiums in exchange for higher out-of-pocket costs. That means paying less each month but more when getting care, compared to other plans.
qs: What is an HDHP?
Does a high deductible plan have lower premiums?

atoms.title: HMO vs. PPO vs. EPO vs. POS: network rules
atoms.q: How do HMO, PPO, EPO and POS plans treat out-of-network care?
atoms.text: HMO plans generally require in-network providers and typically allow out-of-network care in emergencies only. PPO plans usually include out-of-network care, though at a reduced level of coverage. EPO plans may restrict coverage to the plan network, with out-of-network coverage possibly only for emergencies. POS plans generally cover in-network care, and may authorize out-of-network services in limited cases, with less coverage than in-network.
qs: Which plans cover out-of-network care?
Does an HMO cover out-of-network emergencies?

atoms.title: Referral and PCP rules by plan type
atoms.q: Which plan types require a PCP or referrals?
atoms.text: With most HMO plans, a person chooses a PCP and may need a referral to see a specialist. With PPO plans it is less likely a PCP or specialist referral is needed, though some plans may require them. EPO plans are less likely to require a PCP or referral, generally letting people see any in-network provider. POS plans often use a PCP to coordinate care, and need PCP referrals for specialists or out-of-network care.
qs: Do I need a referral with a PPO?
Which plan doesn't require a primary care doctor?

atoms.title: HMO vs. PPO vs. EPO vs. POS: preapprovals
atoms.q: Which plan types require preapproval for services?
atoms.text: HMO plans may require advance approval for certain services, often handled through the PCP. Almost every PPO network requires preapprovals for some services, and because a PPO allows more provider choice, more preapprovals may be needed. EPO plans more likely need preapprovals because no PCP oversees care. POS plans need preapproval for some services, though a PCP will often handle it.
qs: Do PPO plans require preapproval?
Who handles preapproval in an HMO?

atoms.title: How providers are paid by plan type
atoms.q: How are doctors paid under HMO, PPO, EPO and POS plans?
atoms.text: HMO providers either work for the HMO or contract for set rates. PPO networks include providers and facilities that negotiated lower rates, and PPO plans have access to those rates. EPO providers are paid per service; they do not work for or contract with the EPO carrier for a set rate, but have negotiated lower rates for plan members. POS network providers have negotiated rates for members.
qs: How do doctors get paid in an HMO?
What are negotiated rates?

atoms.title: Short term coverage can start next day
atoms.q: Can I get coverage quickly if I need it now?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare describes short term health insurance underwritten by Golden Rule Insurance Company as a fast, flexible solution for temporary coverage. It provides access to large nationwide provider networks through UnitedHealthcare, and coverage can be available as soon as the next day in many cases.
qs: How fast can short term coverage start?
Who underwrites UnitedHealthcare short term plans?

atoms.title: What is a POS health plan?
atoms.q: What is a point of service (POS) plan?
atoms.text: A point of service (POS) plan is a less common type of health insurance that partners with a group of clinics, hospitals and doctors to provide care. A person pays less out of pocket for care within the network. Many POS plans require coordination with a primary care provider (PCP) for treatment and referrals. A POS may suit someone who wants flexibility to see out-of-network providers, is comfortable paying more, and already works with a PCP.
qs: What is a POS plan?
Who is a POS plan good for?

atoms.title: Why it is called point of service
atoms.q: Why is it called a point-of-service plan?
atoms.text: These plans are known as point-of-service plans because each time a person needs health care, which is the time or point of service, they can decide to stay in-network and let their primary care physician manage care, or go outside the network and seek care from a doctor of their choosing.
qs: Why is it called a POS plan?
Can I choose in or out of network each time?

atoms.title: How does a POS plan work?
atoms.q: How does a POS plan work?
atoms.text: POS plans have similarities to both PPO and HMO plans. Like a PPO, POS insurance offers the flexibility to see any provider, but at an added cost, and staying in the network saves money on copays or coinsurance. The only exception is emergency care, which the plan covers in or out of network. Like an HMO, a POS plan requires working with a PCP to coordinate treatment and referrals to specialists, and sometimes for out-of-network providers.
qs: How do POS plans work?
Does a POS cover out-of-network emergencies?

atoms.title: Advantages of a POS plan
atoms.q: What are the advantages of a POS plan?
atoms.text: POS health insurance offers flexibility in provider choice, but may come with some hoops to jump through, like referrals. The three biggest advantages of a POS plan are out-of-network coverage, more providers to choose from, and, if preapprovals are needed, that the PCP takes care of them.
qs: What are the pros of a POS plan?
Does a PCP handle preapprovals on a POS?

atoms.title: POS plan cost considerations
atoms.q: How much does a POS plan cost compared with HMO and PPO?
atoms.text: Typically, POS plan premiums are higher than HMOs, but lower than PPOs. Other cost considerations include how much care a person or family might need during the plan year, and how often they might see specialists or out-of-network providers.
qs: Are POS premiums higher than HMO?
Is a POS cheaper than a PPO?

atoms.title: POS vs. PPO plans
atoms.q: What is the difference between a POS and a PPO plan?
atoms.text: Generally, POS and PPO plans have two main differences. Unlike PPO plans, many POS plans require choosing a PCP to help manage care. And many POS plans require referrals to see specialists or some out-of-network providers.
qs: How is a POS different from a PPO?
What are the main differences between POS and PPO plans?

atoms.title: POS vs. PPO vs. HMO at a glance
atoms.q: How do POS, PPO and HMO plans compare on cost, referrals and PCP?
atoms.text: On cost, POS has a lower monthly premium, PPO a higher monthly premium, and HMO usually lower premiums. Referrals are needed for POS and HMO, not PPO. Out-of-network care is covered under POS and PPO, not HMO. A primary care provider is required under POS and HMO, not PPO.
qs: POS vs PPO vs HMO comparison
Which plan types require a primary care provider?

atoms.title: Do I need a referral with a POS plan?
atoms.q: Do I need a referral with a POS plan?
atoms.text: Yes. To schedule an appointment with a specialist, POS plans require a referral from the primary care provider. A referral may also be needed for some out-of-network providers. For example, to see a dermatologist, the PCP has to submit a referral before an appointment can be scheduled.
qs: Does a POS plan require referrals?
Do I need a referral to see a dermatologist on a POS plan?

atoms.title: What is a PPO health plan?
atoms.q: What is a PPO plan?
atoms.text: A PPO plan is a common type of health insurance that partners with a group of clinics, hospitals and doctors to create a network of preferred providers. A person pays less out of pocket for care within that network. An out-of-network provider can still be seen, but the most coverage comes from staying in the PPO network. PPO plans may suit someone who lives in two different states or travels often within the U.S.
qs: What is a PPO?
Is a PPO good if I travel a lot?

atoms.title: What does PPO stand for?
atoms.q: What does PPO stand for?
atoms.text: PPO means preferred provider organization. The name refers to the plan's network of contracted PPO providers. The plan's preferred providers are those who can offer care at the lowest out-of-pocket cost, compared to out-of-network providers.
qs: What does PPO mean?
Who are preferred providers?

atoms.title: How does a PPO work?
atoms.q: How does a PPO plan work?
atoms.text: A PPO plan pays its contracted providers a set cost to offer certain health care services, so a person pays a lower cost-share, like a copay or coinsurance, within that network. Care outside the network costs more and likely requires submitting an insurance claim. A separate out-of-network deductible must also be met before plan benefits kick in. Some PPO plans have large networks and some have small (narrow) networks.
qs: How do PPO plans work?
Is there a separate deductible for out-of-network care?
Do I file claims with a PPO?

atoms.title: Advantages of a PPO plan
atoms.q: What are the advantages of a PPO plan?
atoms.text: In general, a PPO plan gives more flexibility than some other plan types. Pros include that it can have a large, nationwide provider network, no referrals are needed, there is out-of-network coverage, and there is no requirement to choose a primary care provider.
qs: What are the pros of a PPO?
Why choose a PPO plan?

atoms.title: HMO vs. PPO plans
atoms.q: What is the difference between an HMO and a PPO?
atoms.text: HMO plans only cover services from a network provider, except for emergency care, so an out-of-network visit likely costs the full price. HMO plans typically have lower premiums than PPO plans. An HMO requires referrals, has no out-of-network coverage and requires choosing a primary care provider. A PPO needs no referrals, has out-of-network coverage and does not require choosing a primary care provider.
qs: What's the difference between HMO and PPO?
Which is cheaper, HMO or PPO?

atoms.title: Do I need a referral with a PPO plan?
atoms.q: Do I need a referral with a PPO?
atoms.text: No. One advantage of a PPO plan is that a person does not need a referral to see specialists. A PPO provides the flexibility and coverage to see any provider the member would like to get care.
qs: Can I see a specialist without a referral on a PPO?
Do I need a referral to see a specialist on a PPO plan?

atoms.title: Medicare PPO plans are Medicare Advantage plans
atoms.q: What is a Medicare PPO plan?
atoms.text: People 65 or older may be interested in a Medicare PPO plan, called a Medicare Advantage plan. According to UnitedHealthcare, these work just like an Affordable Care Act Marketplace PPO plan. A person can still get care from out-of-network providers, but only if they accept Medicare.
qs: What is a Medicare PPO?
Can I see out-of-network doctors with a Medicare PPO?

atoms.title: What is a PPO dental plan?
atoms.q: What is a dental PPO plan?
atoms.text: PPO dental insurance is similar to a PPO health plan. A dental PPO plan has a list of preferred dental providers a person can see at a lower cost. A member has the freedom to see any provider, but pays more out of pocket for an out-of-network dental provider.
qs: What is a dental PPO?
Can I see any dentist with a PPO plan?

atoms.title: Medicare PPO plans may include dental coverage
atoms.q: What dental coverage can Medicare PPO plans include?
atoms.text: Medicare Advantage plans come with more dental benefits than people would normally get with Medicare parts A and B alone. PPO Medicare plans can include coverage for things like routine cleanings, fluoride, fillings and crowns, root canals, extractions and dentures.
qs: Does Medicare Advantage cover dental?
What dental services do Medicare PPO plans cover?

atoms.title: What is an EPO health plan?
atoms.q: What is an EPO plan?
atoms.text: An EPO plan is a common type of health insurance that requires care from a certain network of providers. Generally, EPO insurance covers out-of-network care only in emergencies or special circumstances, like during complex treatment or if the EPO network does not have the type of provider needed. A person will likely have a higher deductible and lower monthly payments than with other types of health plans.
qs: What is an EPO?
Does an EPO cover out-of-network care?
Do EPOs have higher deductibles?

atoms.title: What does EPO stand for?
atoms.q: What does EPO stand for?
atoms.text: EPO means exclusive provider organization. The name refers to the rule of staying within the plan's network of select providers. If a person gets care outside the EPO network, they will likely have to pay the full cost of that visit.
qs: What does EPO mean?
What happens if I go outside my EPO network?

atoms.title: An EPO combines features of HMOs and PPOs
atoms.q: How does an EPO work?
atoms.text: EPOs can be thought of as a combination of HMO and PPO plans. Like a PPO, most EPO plans offer the freedom to see any network provider without a referral and typically do not require choosing a primary care provider (non-gated plans only). Without a PCP sending referrals, a person may have to get preapproval for certain services. Like HMOs, EPOs do not offer out-of-network coverage.
qs: How is an EPO like a PPO?
Do EPO plans need preapproval?

atoms.title: Gated vs. non-gated EPO plans
atoms.q: What is the difference between a gated and non-gated EPO plan?
atoms.text: With a gated EPO plan, a person will typically need a referral from a PCP to see a specialist. With a non-gated EPO plan, generally no referral is needed to see specialists, if the provider is in the network. A person should check the specifics of their plan's benefits to learn whether referrals are needed before seeing a specialist.
qs: What is a gated EPO?
Do I need a referral with a non-gated EPO?

atoms.title: Advantages of an EPO plan
atoms.q: What are the advantages of an EPO plan?
atoms.text: EPO insurance offers some benefits like those of PPO and HMO plans, such as flexibility and lower costs. Advantages include no referrals needed (non-gated plans only), usually no requirement to choose a primary care provider, and generally lower out-of-pocket costs than a PPO plan. An EPO may suit someone who wants to choose providers without referrals while staying within the network.
qs: What are the pros of an EPO?
Are EPOs cheaper than PPOs?

atoms.title: EPO vs. PPO plans
atoms.q: What is the difference between an EPO and a PPO?
atoms.text: One major difference is that unlike PPO plans, EPO plans do not offer coverage for out-of-network care. Because of that limitation, EPO plans usually have lower out-of-pocket costs than PPO plans. On referrals, an EPO needs none if the plan is non-gated, and a PPO needs none. On choosing a primary care provider, an EPO usually does not require it and a PPO does not.
qs: What's the difference between EPO and PPO?
Which has lower costs, EPO or PPO?

atoms.title: Do I need a referral with an EPO?
atoms.q: Do I need a referral with an EPO?
atoms.text: Typically, EPO insurance gives a person the freedom to see any network provider without a referral, which can make getting care simple and convenient. However, with gated EPO plans, a person may need to get referrals from their PCP. They should check their specific plan benefits to see if a referral is needed before seeing a specialist.
qs: Can I see a specialist on an EPO without a referral?
Do I need a referral on a non-gated EPO plan?

atoms.title: What is a dental EPO plan?
atoms.q: What is a dental EPO plan?
atoms.text: EPO dental plans work just like EPO health plans. Generally, a person can see any dental provider in their EPO network without a referral, but should check plan details to be sure. Getting dental care outside the plan's network will cost more, possibly the whole bill.
qs: What is a dental EPO?
Do dental EPO plans need referrals?

atoms.title: What is a high deductible health plan?
atoms.q: What is a high deductible health plan (HDHP)?
atoms.text: A high deductible health plan (HDHP) is a type of health insurance plan that offers lower premiums in exchange for higher out-of-pocket costs. With an HDHP, a person pays less each month, but more when they get care compared to other health plans.
qs: What is an HDHP?
Do high deductible plans have lower premiums?

atoms.title: Who should consider an HDHP
atoms.q: Who should enroll in a high deductible health plan?
atoms.text: HDHPs may be a good fit for someone who is in fairly good health and typically sees their doctor only once a year for preventive care. Factors to consider during the plan year include how often a person plans to see their doctor, how many tests or screenings they think they will need, whether they plan to use a health savings account (HSA), and whether their employer contributes to the HSA.
qs: Is an HDHP right for me?
Who benefits from a high deductible plan?

atoms.title: Any plan type can be an HDHP
atoms.q: How is an HDHP different from a PPO, HMO, POS or EPO?
atoms.text: HDHP is a way to describe any health insurance plan with a high deductible. As long as a plan includes a minimum deductible that meets the limit for that year, it is considered an HDHP. Any plan can be a high deductible health plan, whether it is a PPO, HMO, POS or EPO plan.
qs: Can an HMO be a high deductible plan?
Is HDHP a plan type or a deductible level?

atoms.title: HDHPs are HSA-eligible plans
atoms.q: What is an HSA-eligible health plan?
atoms.text: High deductible health plans are also called HSA-eligible plans. They are the only type of health insurance that can be paired with a health savings account (HSA). HSAs can help pay for certain out-of-pocket health care costs and get a person closer to reaching their deductible. An HSA comes with perks such as tax-free saving, employer contributions and the freedom to take the HSA along when switching jobs.
qs: Can I have an HSA with any plan?
What is an HSA-eligible plan?

atoms.title: How an HDHP works step by step
atoms.q: How does an HDHP work?
atoms.text: High deductible health plans help protect against really high-cost, even unplanned, services such as hospital stays, surgeries and complex treatment. Until the network deductible is reached, a person pays all health care costs. After that, the cost of covered care is split with the plan through copays or coinsurance. After reaching the network out-of-pocket maximum, the plan picks up the tab for future covered services.
qs: How does a high deductible plan work?
What happens after I meet my deductible?

atoms.title: HDHP example with a $1,700 deductible
atoms.q: Can you give an example of how an HDHP works?
atoms.text: As an example, a high deductible health plan has a network deductible of $1,700. After a surgery and a hospital stay, the member may reach that deductible. They then split the cost of covered services with the plan and pay 20% of the bill. After a few more doctor visits and some high-cost tests they could reach the out-of-pocket maximum, and the plan would pay for all covered services until the end of the plan year.
qs: How much would I pay with a $1,700 deductible?
Example of deductible and coinsurance

atoms.title: Does an HDHP cover preventive care?
atoms.q: Does a high deductible plan cover preventive care?
atoms.text: Even though a high deductible health plan has higher out-of-pocket costs, high deductible health plans typically cover preventive care, like an annual wellness exam. This includes things like vaccines, and tests and screenings for certain health conditions.
qs: Is my annual physical covered on an HDHP?
Are vaccines covered on a high deductible plan?
Do high deductible plans cover preventive care?

atoms.title: Advantages of an HDHP
atoms.q: What are the advantages of an HDHP?
atoms.text: If a person plans to rarely see their doctor throughout the plan year, an HDHP may be a good option. Advantages of a high deductible health plan include lower premiums compared to other plans and the option to pair with an HSA.
qs: What are the pros of a high deductible plan?
What are the advantages of an HDHP?

atoms.title: Disadvantages of an HDHP
atoms.q: What are the disadvantages of an HDHP?
atoms.text: A high deductible health plan is not for everyone or every family. A person may not benefit if they frequent their doctor's office or anticipate unplanned urgent care visits, like for sick kids, especially if they do not plan to use an HSA. Disadvantages can include expensive out-of-pocket costs if more care is needed than planned, and deductibles that can be very high.
qs: What are the cons of an HDHP?
When is a high deductible plan a bad idea?

atoms.title: Choosing between plan types and an HDHP
atoms.q: How should I decide whether an HDHP is right for me?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare suggests first deciding whether a PPO, HMO, POS or EPO plan is preferred. Then decide whether a high deductible health plan version is right. High deductible health plans can be a great fit if they match a person's care needs, so all options should be compared before choosing a plan.
qs: How do I pick between HMO, PPO and HDHP?
What should I decide first when choosing a plan?

atoms.title: What is an HMO health plan?
atoms.q: What is an HMO plan?
atoms.text: A health maintenance organization (HMO) plan is one common type of health insurance that typically comes with a specific network of providers. With an HMO plan, a person has to stay in the HMO network to use plan benefits and needs a referral from their doctor before seeing specialists or getting medical equipment (like a wheelchair). Out-of-pocket costs are usually lower than other types of health insurance.
qs: What is an HMO?
How does an HMO plan work?
Are HMO plans cheaper?

atoms.title: What does HMO stand for?
atoms.q: What does HMO stand for?
atoms.text: HMO stands for health maintenance organization. The name comes from the goal of this kind of plan, which is to help maintain a person's health. As a way to keep costs low, HMO plans focus on preventive care to help people get and stay healthy, because the healthier a person is, the less care they are likely to need.
qs: What does HMO mean?
Why is it called a health maintenance organization?

atoms.title: An HMO uses a local provider network
atoms.q: How does an HMO work?
atoms.text: HMO plans contract with a group of local providers to offer certain health care services. Members are limited to this local network for their care needs, and some HMO plans require members to live or work in the plan's service area to sign up. HMO providers can be thought of as a local care team, and an HMO plan will not cover visits with out-of-network providers.
qs: Do I have to live in a certain area for an HMO?
Can I see any doctor on an HMO?

atoms.title: HMO plans require choosing a primary care provider
atoms.q: Do HMO plans require a primary care provider?
atoms.text: With HMO insurance, a person is required to choose a primary care provider (PCP) as their main doctor. Some people enjoy having a PCP because they value building a relationship with their doctor. A member sees their PCP for all care needs and pays the plan's cost-share, like a copay or coinsurance.
qs: Do I need a PCP with an HMO?
What does a primary care provider do?

atoms.title: HMO plans cover out-of-network care only in emergencies
atoms.q: Does an HMO cover out-of-network care?
atoms.text: It is important to know which providers are in an HMO plan's network. If a person gets care from an out-of-network provider, such as a doctor, surgeon or lab for bloodwork, they are required to pay the full cost of that service. The only time an HMO plan will cover out-of-network services is for emergency care.
qs: Will my HMO pay if I see an out-of-network doctor?
Are emergencies covered out of network on an HMO?

atoms.title: Advantages of an HMO plan
atoms.q: What are the advantages of an HMO plan?
atoms.text: The main advantages of an HMO health plan include usually lower premiums, deductibles and cost-shares compared to other types of health plans; a PCP to help coordinate care; and no need to file health insurance claims. An HMO plan may be a good fit for someone who does not travel much and typically does not see specialists.
qs: What are the pros of an HMO?
Is an HMO good for someone who rarely sees specialists?

atoms.title: HMO vs. POS plans
atoms.q: What is the difference between an HMO and a POS plan?
atoms.text: Unlike HMO plans, POS health plans offer some coverage for certain out-of-network care. Both plan types require referrals and require choosing a primary care provider. For the question of out-of-network coverage, the answer is no for an HMO and yes for a POS.
qs: How is a POS different from an HMO?
Which has out-of-network coverage, HMO or POS?

atoms.title: Do I need a referral with an HMO?
atoms.q: Do I need a referral with an HMO?
atoms.text: Yes. A big difference between HMO plans and some other types of health insurance is that a person needs a referral from their PCP before they can see a specialist or get certain medical equipment. For example, if someone visits their PCP for back pain, the PCP has to submit a referral for them to see a physical therapist before they can make that appointment. For some, this extra step can cost time and money.
qs: Do HMOs require referrals to see a specialist?
Why do I need a referral?

atoms.title: Medicare HMO plans are Medicare Advantage plans
atoms.q: What is a Medicare HMO plan?
atoms.text: People 65 or older may be interested in a Medicare HMO plan, called a Medicare Advantage plan. According to UnitedHealthcare, these work just like individual and family HMO plans with one important difference: the Medicare HMO plan has coverage for out-of-network services, as long as those providers accept Medicare.
qs: What is a Medicare HMO?
Does a Medicare HMO cover out-of-network doctors?

atoms.title: What is a dental HMO plan (DHMO)?
atoms.q: What is a dental HMO plan?
atoms.text: Dental HMO insurance is similar to an HMO health plan. It focuses on preventive care and encourages regular visits to the dentist, which helps keep out-of-pocket costs lower than other dental plans. To take advantage of the low costs, a member must see a network dental provider, or pay for out-of-network dental care. A referral from the primary dentist is needed for specialty dental work.
qs: What is a DHMO?
Do dental HMOs need referrals?

atoms.title: Purpose of health insurance and cost variables
atoms.q: What affects how much I pay for health insurance?
atoms.text: Health insurance exists to help offset the costs of medical events, whether planned or unexpected. A number of factors may play a role in how much you pay for health insurance. Some costs vary based on your situation, like your age, where you live and even some of your habits. These are only a few of the variables that come into play when costs are calculated.
qs: Why does health insurance cost what it does?
What factors change my health insurance price?

atoms.title: What can make costs lower or higher
atoms.q: What makes health insurance cost more or less?
atoms.text: In the United States, health insurance costs may be lower if you are younger or have fewer health issues. Costs may be higher if you are age 50 and over, because you may experience more health issues; if you use tobacco; or if you include your spouse or dependents, because you are charged for each person covered by your plan.
qs: Does my age affect my health insurance premium?
Do tobacco users pay more for insurance?
Does adding my spouse raise my cost?

atoms.title: Out-of-pocket costs not paid by insurance
atoms.q: What are the types of health insurance costs?
atoms.text: Within health insurance there are a number of costs not paid by insurance, also known as out-of-pocket costs. They include premiums, deductibles, coinsurance and copayments. Understanding how these costs work, including the difference between a high deductible plan and a low deductible plan, is important before you choose a plan.
qs: What are out-of-pocket costs in health insurance?
What costs do I pay besides my premium?

atoms.title: Programs that help pay for health insurance
atoms.q: Can I get help paying for my health insurance?
atoms.text: There are many federal programs designed to help people cover the costs of health insurance. They range from Medicare and Medicaid to Affordable Care Act (ACA) or Marketplace plans, COBRA and Dual Eligible plans.
qs: What programs help pay for health insurance?
Are there subsidies for health insurance?

atoms.title: Ways to save on health care costs
atoms.q: How can I save on health care costs?
atoms.text: There are a number of ways to save on health care costs. Even simple choices, like going to providers in your health plan network, may help you reduce costs significantly. It may also be worthwhile to add a supplemental plan to your main health plan to help reduce costs, such as dental, vision or a fixed benefit health plan.
qs: How do I lower my health care costs?
Does a supplemental plan help reduce costs?

atoms.title: What an HSA is
atoms.q: What is a health savings account (HSA)?
atoms.text: A health savings account (HSA) is a place to put money away, pretax, to save for medical expenses ranging from standard medical costs to self-care treatments, first aid items and medical equipment. An HSA is owned by the employee and remains with them even after leaving a company.
qs: What is an HSA?
Can I keep my HSA if I leave my job?

atoms.title: What an HRA is
atoms.q: What is a health reimbursement account (HRA)?
atoms.text: A health reimbursement account (HRA) works in a similar way to an HSA. However, contributions can only be made by an employer, and the employer owns any unused funds if the employee leaves the company.
qs: What is an HRA?
Who contributes to a health reimbursement account?

atoms.title: What an FSA is
atoms.q: What is a flexible spending account (FSA)?
atoms.text: A health care flexible spending account (FSA) lets you set aside money, before it is taxed, to help pay for qualified medical, dental and vision care expenses. It is one of the account types you may be able to choose during open enrollment, alongside HSAs and HRAs.
qs: What is a flexible spending account?
How does an FSA save money on taxes?

atoms.title: Preventive and diagnostic coverage differ
atoms.q: Why does it matter if care is preventive or diagnostic?
atoms.text: Insurance coverage is usually different based on the type of care. Preventive care, like well exams and screenings, is often covered at 100% with $0 out-of-pocket costs when you see a network provider. Coverage for diagnostic care, when you have symptoms your doctor needs to diagnose, could have additional costs and will vary depending on your plan.
qs: Are annual checkups free with insurance?
Why might diagnostic tests cost more than screenings?

atoms.title: Programs exist to help with insurance costs
atoms.q: What help is available if I'm struggling to afford health insurance?
atoms.text: Many programs were created to help individuals who have limited or moderate income and resources get the care they need when they need it. The Affordable Care Act (ACA) was designed to help individuals and their dependents get health insurance coverage when they might not otherwise have been able to afford it. ACA subsidies can go toward paying health insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs.
qs: How can I get help paying for health insurance?
What is the Affordable Care Act designed to do?

atoms.title: Who qualifies for ACA subsidies
atoms.q: Who qualifies for ACA subsidies?
atoms.text: People who qualify for ACA subsidies have a household income that falls within a certain range, do not have access to affordable coverage through their employer, and are not eligible for coverage through the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), TRICARE, Medicaid or Medicare.
qs: Do I qualify for health insurance subsidies?
Can I get ACA subsidies if my employer offers coverage?

atoms.title: What a premium tax credit is
atoms.q: What's a premium tax credit and how does it work?
atoms.text: Premium tax credits are offered through the Health Insurance Marketplace to reduce the monthly payments, or premiums, you pay to your insurance plan and to cap the amount an individual or family must pay for health insurance. The size of the credit is based on a sliding scale, so people with lower income get a larger credit. The credit is sent directly to your insurance company.
qs: How do premium tax credits work?
Who gets a bigger premium tax credit?

atoms.title: What cost sharing is
atoms.q: What is cost sharing in health insurance?
atoms.text: Cost sharing is sharing medical costs with your insurance company: you pay some costs out of pocket and your insurance company pays some costs. You are cost-sharing when you pay deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. Cost-sharing only applies when you pay part and your insurance pays part; for example, you pay $0 for preventive care covered at 100%, and you pay the full amount for a service that is not covered or if you choose an out-of-network provider.
qs: What does cost sharing mean?
What costs do I share with my insurer?

atoms.title: What cost-sharing reductions are
atoms.q: What are cost-sharing reductions?
atoms.text: Cost-sharing reductions, also called decreased cost-sharing or 'extra savings,' are part of the Affordable Care Act and help people save on out-of-pocket costs. People who qualify may have a lower out-of-pocket maximum and lower copays and deductibles. They are in place to help people get the care they need.
qs: What are ACA extra savings?
Can I get a lower deductible with cost-sharing reductions?

atoms.title: Who is eligible for Medicare
atoms.q: Who is eligible for Medicare?
atoms.text: Medicare is the federal health insurance program for people who are age 65 or older; younger than 65 with a qualifying disability and on Social Security disability for at least two years; any age with a diagnosis of End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) or Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease); or receiving Railroad Retirement benefits.
qs: Who qualifies for Medicare?
Can I get Medicare before 65?

atoms.title: What Medicaid is
atoms.q: What is Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicaid is a federal-state public health insurance program that provides coverage to low-income children, adults and people with disabilities. Medicaid is managed at the state level, and the rules vary from state to state.
qs: What is Medicaid?
Are Medicaid rules the same in every state?

atoms.title: What CHIP is
atoms.q: What is the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP)?
atoms.text: The Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) is another national health insurance program alongside Medicaid. It covers uninsured children from low-income families who are not eligible for Medicaid. Medicaid, by contrast, is a federal-state program covering low-income children, adults and people with disabilities.
qs: What does CHIP cover?
Who qualifies for CHIP?

atoms.title: What a Dual Special Needs Plan is
atoms.q: What are Dual Special Needs Plans (D-SNP)?
atoms.text: Special Needs Plans (SNP) are a special category within Medicare Advantage that combine the benefits of Original Medicare (Parts A and B) with prescription drug coverage (Part D) in one plan. A Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan, often called a D-SNP, provides health benefits to people who qualify for both Medicaid and Medicare, with benefits customized to specific needs and possible access to special programs, specialists and care coordinators.
qs: What is a D-SNP?
What does a dual eligible plan offer?

atoms.title: When you can use COBRA
atoms.q: What is COBRA and when can I elect it?
atoms.text: The Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) was enacted as a short-term insurance solution if you lose your job or your hours are reduced. You can elect COBRA if you lost coverage because your work hours were reduced; you quit or lost your job (unless it was 'gross misconduct'); you are transitioning between jobs; the covered employee dies; you are going through a divorce; you turn 26; or you become eligible for Medicare. Typically you can keep COBRA for up to 18 months.
qs: How long does COBRA last?
Can I get COBRA if I quit my job?
What qualifies me for COBRA?

atoms.title: What an FSA is and how it works
atoms.q: How do FSAs work?
atoms.text: A flexible spending account (FSA) is a tool offered by many employers as part of their benefits package to help employees set aside money during the plan year to pay for out-of-pocket costs and catch a tax break. Employers set the maximum you can contribute, which cannot exceed the IRS limit. An FSA is not a savings account, and if you leave your job you cannot take your FSA with you.
qs: How does an FSA work?
Can I keep my FSA if I leave my job?

atoms.title: FSA forfeiture, carryover and grace period
atoms.q: What happens to unused FSA money?
atoms.text: If you do not use the full amount you elected to contribute by the end of the calendar year, you could lose, or forfeit, your FSA dollars. To protect employees, many companies allow a carryover of unspent FSA money or a grace period to use prior year funds for new claims up to 2 1/2 months into a new plan year. Any amount left after that is generally no longer available to you.
qs: Do I lose my FSA money at the end of the year?
Is there a grace period for FSA funds?

atoms.title: 2026 health care FSA contribution limits
atoms.q: What are the FSA contribution limits for 2026?
atoms.text: Beginning January 1, 2026, IRS contributions to a health care FSA (HCFSA) are limited to $3,400 each year, a $100 increase from the 2025 limit of $3,300. The limit is per person, so each spouse in the household may contribute up to the limit. For the 2026 plan year an individual can also contribute up to $3,400 to a limited purpose FSA (LPFSA). Your employer may elect a lower limit.
qs: How much can I put in my FSA in 2026?
Can my spouse and I each contribute to an FSA?

atoms.title: 2026 health care FSA carryover limit
atoms.q: How much FSA money can I carry over into 2026?
atoms.text: For a plan ending December 31, 2025, up to $680 of health care FSA funds can be carried over to the 2026 plan year. Any amount that rolls over into the 2026 plan year does not affect the maximum limit that employees can contribute.
qs: What is the FSA carryover limit?
Does FSA carryover reduce my 2026 contribution limit?

atoms.title: 2026 dependent care FSA limits
atoms.q: What is the dependent care FSA limit for 2026?
atoms.text: The dependent care FSA limit for 2026 depends on how you file. It is $7,500 per year if you are married and filing a joint return or a single parent, and $3,750 per year per parent if you are married and filing separately.
qs: How much can I put in a dependent care FSA?
What is the DCFSA limit if I file separately?

atoms.title: Three types of FSAs
atoms.q: What types of FSAs are there?
atoms.text: There are three types of FSAs: health care FSA, limited-purpose FSA and dependent care FSA. Each type has a different set of rules for what you can spend the money on. For example, you cannot use health care FSA funds to pay for daycare, because that requires a dependent care FSA.
qs: What are the different kinds of FSA?
Can I use a health care FSA for daycare?

atoms.title: Health care FSA eligible expenses
atoms.q: What can I pay for with a health care FSA?
atoms.text: A health care FSA uses pre-tax dollars to pay for eligible medical, dental and vision expenses not covered by your health plan, and the annual amount is available on the first day of the plan. Eligible expenses include copays and coinsurance, medications, dental care, vision care, over-the-counter items like first aid supplies and blood pressure monitors, and family planning needs.
qs: What does an FSA cover?
Can I use FSA money on day one of the plan year?

atoms.title: FSA items that need a prescription or LMN
atoms.q: Which FSA items need a prescription or Letter of Medical Necessity?
atoms.text: Some products and services are health care FSA eligible only if a doctor prescribes them for a specific need. For example, an FSA may not cover a multivitamin for general health, but a doctor can write a prescription or Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN) so an FSA covers iron supplements for someone with anemia. With a prescription or LMN, your health care FSA may cover gym memberships, fitness equipment and trackers, supplements, dermatology treatments and weight-loss programs.
qs: Can I use my FSA for a gym membership?
What is an LMN for an FSA?

atoms.title: What a limited-purpose FSA is
atoms.q: What is a limited-purpose FSA?
atoms.text: A limited-purpose FSA lets you set aside pre-tax earnings at the beginning of the plan year to help pay for eligible dental and vision expenses only. Because funds are used only for out-of-pocket dental and vision expenses, you can contribute to a limited-purpose FSA while also contributing to a health savings account (HSA), which lets you reserve more money in your HSA for retirement or other expenses.
qs: Can I have an FSA and an HSA?
What does a limited-purpose FSA cover?

atoms.title: What a dependent care FSA covers
atoms.q: What can I pay for with a dependent care FSA?
atoms.text: A Dependent Care FSA (DCFSA) is an account of pre-tax dollars used to pay for eligible dependent care services when you or your spouse work or are looking for work. The care must be for an eligible dependent, typically a child or another legal dependent such as an adult with disabilities. Qualifying care includes before and after school care, daycare, babysitters and nannies, preschool, and summer and school break camps.
qs: Can I pay for summer camp with an FSA?
Does a dependent care FSA cover care for an adult relative?

atoms.title: Tax benefits of a health care FSA
atoms.q: What are the tax benefits of an FSA?
atoms.text: Putting money into an FSA offers tax advantages. The amount you contribute is pre-taxed, meaning you save whatever percentage you would have paid in federal taxes if the money had not been deducted from your paycheck. Your employer saves on taxes too, by avoiding a payroll tax.
qs: How does an FSA save on taxes?
Does my employer save money with an FSA?

atoms.title: How to enroll in a health care FSA
atoms.q: How do I enroll in a health care FSA?
atoms.text: If your employer offers an FSA, then at the beginning of a plan year you decide how much to allocate to it. Think carefully about this estimate, because you cannot change the amount unless your employment changes. Once you decide on an amount and set up the FSA, it is automatically deducted from your paycheck and deposited into the account. You will either receive a debit card tied to the account or submit receipts to the FSA administrator for reimbursement.
qs: How do I sign up for an FSA?
Can I change my FSA amount during the year?

atoms.title: What an HRA is
atoms.q: What is a health reimbursement account (HRA)?
atoms.text: A health reimbursement account or arrangement (HRA) is an account your employer funds so you can reimburse yourself for certain medical, dental or vision expenses. As an account-based health plan, an HRA can help you stretch the value of your health care dollar for eligible health care expenses and over-the-counter items.
qs: What is an HRA?
Who funds a health reimbursement account?

atoms.title: Employers own and set the rules for HRAs
atoms.q: Who controls an HRA?
atoms.text: Your employer owns your HRA and sets it up for you, unlike a flexible spending account (FSA) or health savings account (HSA), where you contribute money. Your employer sets the rules and decides the amount, and you are not allowed to make contributions to your HRA. Your employer also decides the list of medical expenses that will be covered.
qs: Can I contribute to my HRA?
Who decides what my HRA covers?

atoms.title: What employers typically use HRAs for
atoms.q: What are HRAs usually set up to pay for?
atoms.text: Most employers set up HRAs for their employees to pay for expenses not typically paid for by health plans. These are medical and pharmacy expenses that may be paid out of pocket before meeting a deductible, as well as coinsurance after meeting a deductible.
qs: Can an HRA help me pay my deductible?
Does an HRA cover coinsurance?

atoms.title: HRA tax advantages
atoms.q: Are HRA reimbursements taxable?
atoms.text: Reimbursement from an HRA for eligible medical expenses is generally not considered taxable income. You usually receive the full amount and do not have to pay federal or state income taxes on the money. UnitedHealthcare does not provide tax advice and you should contact a tax advisor for your specific situation.
qs: Do I pay tax on HRA reimbursements?
Is an HRA tax-free?

atoms.title: Unused HRA funds and leaving your employer
atoms.q: What happens to unused HRA money?
atoms.text: Your employer can set up the plan so that unused HRA funds roll over from year to year, but this is not a requirement, so you might lose unused funds. If you leave your employer and have unused funds in your account, they can keep the money.
qs: Do HRA funds roll over?
Can I take my HRA with me if I quit?

atoms.title: What you can buy with HRA funds
atoms.q: How can I use the money in my HRA?
atoms.text: You can use HRA funds for eligible medical expenses, as determined by the IRS and your employer. Some employers allow only services covered by your health plan, and some also allow dental, vision or other services. Examples of expenses HRAs may help pay include deductible payments, copays, routine doctor visits, hospital expenses, dental care, blood pressure monitors, vision care including eyeglasses, contact lenses and exams, prescription drugs and blood glucose monitors.
qs: What can I buy with HRA money?
Does an HRA pay for glasses?

atoms.title: How to access HRA money
atoms.q: How do I access my HRA money?
atoms.text: Your employer decides how you access your HRA, and it will likely be one of two ways. With most plans you do nothing, because the plan reimburses your network doctor directly. Otherwise, you pay for expenses up front and then request reimbursement.
qs: How do I get reimbursed from my HRA?
Do I pay first and then get paid back by my HRA?

atoms.title: How to enroll in an HRA
atoms.q: How do I enroll in an HRA?
atoms.text: You can enroll in an HRA, if your employer offers one, during your open enrollment period. Outside of open enrollment, you can sign up when you first join a company or if you experience a qualifying life event. Contact your employer to learn whether the account is available to you, and if you have experienced a qualifying life event, call the number on your member ID card.
qs: When can I sign up for an HRA?
Can I add an HRA after a life event?

atoms.title: What an HSA is and who can open one
atoms.q: What is a health savings account and who is eligible?
atoms.text: A health savings account (HSA) is a financial account designed to help you save for qualified health care expenses. Not just anyone can open an HSA: you must be enrolled in a high deductible health plan (HDHP), and not every HDHP is HSA qualified. As defined by the IRS, the plan must have a higher deductible than typical individual health insurance plans and a maximum out-of-pocket limit that includes deductibles, copays and coinsurance.
qs: Who can open an HSA?
Do I need a high deductible plan for an HSA?
Is every HDHP HSA-qualified?

atoms.title: 2026 HSA limit for individual coverage
atoms.q: What is the 2026 HSA contribution limit for an individual?
atoms.text: For 2026, an individual with coverage under a qualifying high-deductible health plan (deductible not less than $1,700) can contribute up to $4,400 to an HSA for the year, up $100 from 2025. The maximum out-of-pocket for such a plan is capped at $8,500. Each year the IRS sets the limit for how much individuals can contribute to these tax-advantaged accounts.
qs: How much can I put in my HSA in 2026?
What is the HSA limit for one person?

atoms.title: 2026 HSA limit for family coverage
atoms.q: What is the 2026 HSA contribution limit for family coverage?
atoms.text: For 2026, an individual with family coverage under a qualifying high-deductible health plan (deductible not less than $3,400) can contribute up to $8,750 to an HSA for the year, up $200 from 2025. The maximum out-of-pocket for such a plan is capped at $17,000.
qs: What is the family HSA limit for 2026?
How much can a family contribute to an HSA?

atoms.title: HSA catch-up contribution at age 55
atoms.q: Can I contribute extra to my HSA as I get older?
atoms.text: When you turn 55, you can contribute an extra $1,000 each year to your HSA, called a catch-up contribution. If you and your spouse are both over the age of 55, you can each contribute $1,000, but your spouse will need to open their own HSA for their portion.
qs: What is the HSA catch-up contribution?
Can my spouse and I both make catch-up contributions?

atoms.title: Ownership and rollover advantages of an HSA
atoms.q: What are the advantages of an HSA?
atoms.text: With an HSA you own the account, not your employer, and you make deposits like you do with other personal bank accounts, though your employer might add money too. There is no 'use-it-or-lose-it' policy: the funds roll over year to year and stay with you regardless of whether you leave your job or retire. You can also invest your funds.
qs: Do I keep my HSA if I leave my job?
Do HSA funds roll over every year?

atoms.title: HSA tax advantages and withdrawals
atoms.q: How are HSAs taxed?
atoms.text: Money you contribute to an HSA is tax-deductible, which reduces your taxable income, and interest or income on invested funds is tax-free. If you are under 65 and use the money for qualified medical expenses, you can withdraw it tax-free. If you are over 65, you can withdraw tax-free for medical expenses or use the money for non-medical expenses and pay regular income tax. UnitedHealthcare does not provide tax advice.
qs: Are HSA withdrawals taxable?
What happens to my HSA at age 65?

atoms.title: Penalty for non-qualified HSA withdrawals
atoms.q: What happens if I use my HSA for non-medical expenses before 65?
atoms.text: If you cash out HSA money before you are 65 and do not use it for qualified medical expenses, you will have to pay taxes on the amount, and you could be hit with a hefty 20% tax penalty.
qs: Is there a penalty for withdrawing HSA money early?
What is the HSA withdrawal penalty?

atoms.title: What HSA funds can pay for
atoms.q: What expenses can I pay for with an HSA?
atoms.text: HSA funds are pre-tax dollars that can go toward copays for medical visits, alternative health treatments, period supplies and more. HSA eligible expenses fall into groups such as medical appointments and services, prescription and over-the-counter medications, menstrual care and family planning, natural and alternative care, vision and dental care, and certain vitamins and supplements. The IRS determines the list of qualified medical expenses, and some items need a prescription or Letter of Medical Necessity.
qs: What can I buy with my HSA?
Can I use my HSA for dental and vision?

atoms.title: Letter of Medical Necessity for HSA spending
atoms.q: What is a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN)?
atoms.text: A Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN) is a simple letter from a doctor describing why you need a specific service or product and what condition you will use it to treat or prevent. With an LMN you may be able to use HSA funds for items such as gym memberships and fitness equipment, some supplements and vitamins, red light therapy devices, saunas and cold plunges, weight-loss programs and air purifiers.
qs: Can I use my HSA for a gym membership?
How do I get a Letter of Medical Necessity?

atoms.title: Using an HSA for childcare
atoms.q: Can I use an HSA to pay for childcare?
atoms.text: Childcare and other dependent care are not HSA eligible expenses. However, a type of Flexible Spending Account (FSA), the dependent care FSA, allows you to use pre-tax dollars to pay for things like daycare, babysitters and summer camps. You may be able to have both an FSA and an HSA.
qs: Can I pay for daycare with my HSA?
Can I have an FSA and an HSA at the same time?

atoms.title: Optum Bank HSA options
atoms.q: Where can I open an HSA with UnitedHealthcare?
atoms.text: To find your HSA options, check with your employer or your health plan documents. If an HSA is not available that way, you can explore options at Optum Bank, which is described as the UnitedHealthcare bank of choice.
qs: How do I open an HSA?
What is Optum Bank?

atoms.title: How you get an HSA, HRA or FSA
atoms.q: How do I get an HSA, HRA or FSA?
atoms.text: To get a health savings account (HSA), you must have a high deductible health plan that meets a deductible amount set by the IRS. You get a health reimbursement account (HRA) when you sign up for the plan, if your employer offers this type of health plan. A flexible spending account (FSA) is established through your employer and does not have to be tied to a health plan.
qs: How do I qualify for an HSA versus an FSA?
Does an FSA require a health plan?

atoms.title: Who funds an HSA, HRA or FSA
atoms.q: Who contributes to an HSA, HRA and FSA?
atoms.text: You fund an HSA, contributing pre-tax money via payroll deductions up to annual limits, and your employer, family and others can also contribute. An HRA is funded entirely by your employer, and you cannot put your own money into it. With an FSA, you contribute via payroll deductions and your employer can also contribute.
qs: Can my employer contribute to my HSA?
Who pays into an HRA?

atoms.title: What you can spend each account on
atoms.q: What can I spend HSA, HRA and FSA money on?
atoms.text: HSA funds can only be used for qualified medical expenses, which does not include paying for premiums. You can use an HRA for premiums and medical expenses. An FSA can be used for eligible medical and dependent care expenses, but health insurance premiums do not qualify, and the amount you can spend is capped.
qs: Can I pay premiums with an HSA?
Can an HRA pay health insurance premiums?

atoms.title: Which account stays with you after a job change
atoms.q: Which account can I take with me if I leave my job?
atoms.text: If you leave your job, you can take your HSA with you, because once you have established an HSA it is yours forever and stays with you if you change employers, change health plans or retire. You cannot take an HRA with you when you go, because it belongs to your employer.
qs: Do I keep my HSA when I change jobs?
Does an HRA go with me if I quit?

atoms.title: Tax advantages of HSAs, HRAs and FSAs
atoms.q: What are the tax advantages of an HSA, HRA and FSA?
atoms.text: HSA tax benefits include tax-deductible contributions, and account holders can build up the HSA by earning tax-free interest and tax-free investment returns; spending on qualified out-of-pocket medical expenses is also tax-free. An HRA is tax-free for both you and your employer. With an FSA, you do not pay federal, state or Social Security taxes on this money.
qs: Which health account has the best tax benefits?
Are FSA contributions taxed?

atoms.title: HSA savings, limits and rollover
atoms.q: How much can I save in an HSA over time?
atoms.text: Every dollar you contribute to and save in an HSA is tax-free, and spending HSA dollars on qualified out-of-pocket medical expenses is also tax-free. There is no limit to how much you can save over time, but there are annual contribution limits. Since it is your HSA, the money stays with you even if you change employers or health plans, or retire, and unused funds continue to roll over year to year.
qs: Is there a limit on how much I can have in my HSA?
Does HSA money roll over?

atoms.title: FSA use-it-or-lose-it rule
atoms.q: Can I lose money in an FSA?
atoms.text: Flexible spending accounts may follow the use-it-or-lose-it rule, meaning that if you do not spend your FSA funds within your plan year, you may not be able to carry them over to the next. It is a good idea to avoid putting more money into your FSA than you can spend in a plan year.
qs: What is the FSA use-it-or-lose-it rule?
How much should I put in my FSA?

atoms.title: Using an FSA and HRA together
atoms.q: Can I use an FSA and an HRA together?
atoms.text: You can use an FSA and an HRA together. If you have an FSA, expenses typically come from that account first, and funds from the HRA are then used to cover other medical expenses. Using an HSA, HRA or FSA in combination may or may not be possible depending on your circumstances, because of the possibility of double-dipping.
qs: Can I have both an FSA and an HRA?
Which account pays first, an FSA or an HRA?

atoms.title: Using an FSA and HSA together
atoms.q: Can I use an FSA and an HSA at the same time?
atoms.text: It is uncommon to have an FSA and HSA at the same time, but not impossible. One exception is pairing an HSA with a limited-purpose FSA, also called an HSA-compatible FSA or post-deductible FSA. You can use the limited-purpose FSA only for certain expenses, like dental or vision care, until you reach your health plan's deductible, which saves more of your HSA dollars for future expenses.
qs: Can I have an HSA and an FSA?
What is an HSA-compatible FSA?

atoms.title: Using an HRA and HSA together
atoms.q: Can I use an HRA and an HSA together?
atoms.text: You can use an HRA and an HSA at the same time if you are enrolled in a high deductible health plan (HDHP), but the IRS has specific rules as to how they work together. For example, you cannot use HSA funds to cover medical expenses that were reimbursed by your employer in an HRA. You can also use them together if you opt out of your HRA reimbursement of qualified medical expenses, while keeping reimbursement for premiums.
qs: Can I have an HRA and an HSA?
Can I use HSA funds for expenses my HRA reimbursed?

atoms.title: Ways to save on quality health care
atoms.q: How can I save money on health care?
atoms.text: Just like everyday shopping, there are ways to save money on health care. You may be able to get cost estimates before you get care for certain conditions, like pregnancy care, an elective surgery or an MRI. You can also choose providers in your health plan network to take advantage of the lower costs your health insurance carrier has negotiated for you.
qs: How do I lower my health care costs?
Can I get a price estimate before surgery?

atoms.title: Estimate costs with online member tools
atoms.q: How can I look up health care cost estimates online?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare members can sign in to their health plan account to find average costs for providers in their network, including doctors, hospitals, office visits, mental health services, labs and convenience care. They can also find the average cost for specific treatments in their area and quality ratings and reviews for providers, hospitals or facilities.
qs: Where can I see what a procedure will cost?
Can I see provider quality ratings online?

atoms.title: Network providers lower your costs
atoms.q: Why do network providers cost less?
atoms.text: When doctors and facilities are in the UnitedHealthcare network, they have agreed to provide services at a discount, so your costs will be lower when you choose their services. Providers who are not in your health plan network could charge more, which means their services could cost you more or may not be covered at all. UnitedHealthcare members have access to a large provider network that includes more than 1.2 million physicians and care professionals and 6540 hospitals and care facilities nationwide (UnitedHealthcare E&I national network, Q1 2022).
qs: Do in-network doctors cost less?
What happens if my doctor is out of network?

atoms.title: What a Prescription Drug List is
atoms.q: What is a Prescription Drug List (PDL)?
atoms.text: A Prescription Drug List (PDL) is your health plan's list of drugs and how they are covered. If you take medications regularly, it is important to watch for PDL updates, because changes to the list can sometimes change your costs. You can sign in to your member account or call the number on your member ID card to view your pharmacy benefit and PDL.
qs: What is a PDL?
Can my drug costs change if the drug list changes?

atoms.title: Prescription savings tips
atoms.q: How can I save on prescriptions?
atoms.text: If home delivery is included in your benefit, you may be able to order up to a 90-day supply of medication you regularly take, usually with no charge for standard shipping within the U.S., which may save you money. When your doctor prescribes medication, look at your PDL, and ask about a lower cost alternative if the drug your doctor chooses is too expensive or is not covered.
qs: Can I get a 90-day supply delivered?
What if my prescribed drug is too expensive?

atoms.title: Schedule yearly preventive care visits
atoms.q: Why should I schedule yearly preventive care?
atoms.text: Seeing your doctor for regular preventive care can pay off because it may help detect issues early, when health conditions are typically more treatable. Preventive care includes all your regular doctor visits, meaning any annual checkups and screenings. You can prepare for preventive visits and get a list of screenings you might need.
qs: Is a yearly checkup worth it?
What counts as preventive care?

atoms.title: Choose the right level of care
atoms.q: How can I choose care options that cost less?
atoms.text: Choosing the right level of care can help you save, and some locations may charge more for the same services. Call your primary care provider or family doctor first, because they have your records and may offer same-day appointments. For non-emergency care you could consider an urgent care center, a convenience care clinic or an online doctor visit, which may save time and money compared to an ER visit.
qs: Should I go to urgent care or the ER?
Who should I call first when I need care?

atoms.title: Up to $2,000 saved versus an ER visit
atoms.q: How much can I save by choosing urgent care over the ER?
atoms.text: Knowing your care options may help you save both time and money, up to $2,000 for some health plans, compared to an ER visit. The estimate is based on 2019 average allowed amounts charged by UnitedHealthcare network providers, an estimated $2,000 difference between the average emergency room visit and the average urgent care visit. Actual payments may vary by benefit coverage. In an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.
qs: How much cheaper is urgent care than the ER?
Is an ER visit more expensive than urgent care?

atoms.title: Virtual visits can cost less
atoms.q: Are virtual visits cheaper than an office visit?
atoms.text: With virtual visits, also called telehealth services, you can talk with a doctor online using your mobile device or computer. You can get treatment options and even prescriptions for medications, if needed, and it is usually less costly than an office visit. Sign in to your member account or call the number on your member ID card to learn about your benefit for virtual visits.
qs: Is telehealth cheaper than going to the doctor?
Can I get a prescription from a virtual visit?

atoms.title: Common cost terms to know
atoms.q: What do common health insurance cost terms mean?
atoms.text: Health insurance terms can be confusing, and knowing the jargon may help you control costs and make decisions. Common cost terms covered include premium, deductible, copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket limit, referral and prior authorization. UnitedHealthcare also points to a common terms list and the Just Plain Clear glossary for other terms you do not know.
qs: Where can I find a health insurance glossary?
What is a referral or prior authorization?

atoms.title: UnitedHealthcare app for estimating costs
atoms.q: Can I estimate costs in the UnitedHealthcare app?
atoms.text: Members can use the UnitedHealthcare app on a mobile device to get instant access to manage health plan details, estimate costs, find network providers and more. They can also sign in using a mobile browser.
qs: What can I do in the UnitedHealthcare app?
Can I find network providers in the app?

atoms.title: What a premium is
atoms.q: What is a health insurance premium?
atoms.text: To keep your plan active, you will likely pay a monthly premium, which is your way to access the plan. If you have an employer-sponsored health plan, your premium is likely deducted from your paycheck. If you bought an individual plan, you pay the insurer.
qs: What is a premium?
Is my premium taken out of my paycheck?

atoms.title: Paying premiums on Medicare and Medicaid plans
atoms.q: How do I pay premiums on a Medicare or Medicaid plan?
atoms.text: If you have a UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan or prescription drug plan with a monthly premium, you have several options for paying your premium. If you have a Medicaid plan, contact your state's Medicaid program to learn whether any premium may apply.
qs: How can I pay my Medicare Advantage premium?
Do I pay a premium on Medicaid?

atoms.title: What a deductible is
atoms.q: What is a deductible?
atoms.text: A deductible is the amount you pay out of pocket for your care before your insurance plan starts to pick up the tab. Like car insurance, it is an amount you agree to contribute before insurance kicks in. Typically, the higher the deductible, the lower the premium, and the lower the deductible, the higher the premium.
qs: What is a health insurance deductible?
Does a higher deductible mean a lower premium?

atoms.title: High deductible plans suit healthy individuals
atoms.q: Who is a high deductible health plan good for?
atoms.text: A high deductible health plan (HDHP) may be ideal for healthy individuals who do not foresee having many medical expenses in the coming year. Higher deductible plans typically come with lower premiums.
qs: Should I choose a high deductible plan?
Is an HDHP right for me if I'm healthy?

atoms.title: What coinsurance is
atoms.q: What is coinsurance?
atoms.text: After you have met your deductible, depending on your plan, you may pay coinsurance for some services. Coinsurance is a percentage you pay after meeting your deductible. Some of the most common percentage breakdowns are 80/20 and 90/10.
qs: What does 80/20 coinsurance mean?
When do I start paying coinsurance?

atoms.title: What a copayment is
atoms.q: What is a copay and how is it different from coinsurance?
atoms.text: A copayment, or copay, is different from coinsurance. It is a fixed amount you pay for a covered service. It is common to have separate copay rates for different types of care, for example a primary care visit versus a specialist like a dermatologist, and you may also pay a copay for prescriptions. You will often pay your copay at the time of service.
qs: What is a copay?
Do I pay a copay at the doctor's office?

atoms.title: What an out-of-pocket maximum is
atoms.q: What is an out-of-pocket maximum or limit?
atoms.text: Your out-of-pocket maximum or limit is the most you have to pay for covered services within a plan year, including your deductible and any copays and coinsurance. It does not include your monthly premium payments or anything you spent on services not covered by your plan.
qs: What is an out-of-pocket max?
Do premiums count toward my out-of-pocket limit?

atoms.title: How a health plan works through the year
atoms.q: How do health plan costs work step by step?
atoms.text: 1) At the start of the plan year you pay 100% of covered health services until you meet your deductible. 2) After that, your plan shares costs through coinsurance, for example you pay 20% and the plan pays 80%. 3) You may also pay a fixed copay for certain services, like a doctor's appointment. 4) Coinsurance and copays count toward your out-of-pocket limit, but premiums do not. 5) After you reach the limit, your plan pays 100%.
qs: How does health insurance work from start to finish?
What happens after I meet my deductible?

atoms.title: Premium and deductible trade-off
atoms.q: How do premiums and deductibles trade off?
atoms.text: Some plans have higher premiums and lower deductibles. Others have lower premiums and higher deductibles. A monthly premium keeps your plan active, while a deductible is what you pay for covered care before your plan starts to pay. Weighing the two helps you pick a plan that fits your budget and expected care needs.
qs: Should I pay a higher premium for a lower deductible?
How do premiums and deductibles compare?

atoms.title: What coinsurance is
atoms.q: What is coinsurance?
atoms.text: Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost of a covered service. Until you reach your deductible, you pay 100% of out-of-pocket costs. After you meet your deductible, you and your insurance company each pay a share of the costs that add up to 100 percent. Coinsurance is your share, or the percent you pay, of the cost for covered services after you meet your deductible.
qs: What does coinsurance mean?
When does coinsurance start?

atoms.title: Typical coinsurance percentages
atoms.q: What is a typical coinsurance percentage?
atoms.text: Typical coinsurance ranges from 20% to 40% for the member, with the health plan paying the rest. For example, with 20% coinsurance, a member pays 20% of the cost of a covered service after meeting the deductible and the plan pays the remaining 80%. Cost-sharing percentages vary depending on your plan.
qs: How much is coinsurance usually?
What does 20% coinsurance mean?

atoms.title: How coinsurance works
atoms.q: How does coinsurance work?
atoms.text: If your doctor visit costs $100 and you have met your deductible, a coinsurance payment of 20% would be $20 out of pocket. Your insurance would then pay the rest of the allowed amount, which is $80. Your coinsurance benefit does not apply until after you have reached your deductible. Until then, you pay 100% of the cost.
qs: How much would I pay with 20% coinsurance on a $100 visit?
Do I pay coinsurance before my deductible?

atoms.title: Copay versus coinsurance
atoms.q: What's the difference between coinsurance and copays?
atoms.text: Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost of a service, while a copay is a fixed rate. A copay is a flat dollar amount typically paid at the time of service and does not count toward your deductible in most plans. Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost if you have met your deductible and is billed by the provider, whom you pay directly. Both count toward your out-of-pocket maximum.
qs: Is coinsurance or a copay better?
Do copays and coinsurance count toward my out-of-pocket max?

atoms.title: 80/20 coinsurance example
atoms.q: Can you show an example of 80/20 coinsurance?
atoms.text: Jake's health plan has 80/20 coinsurance, meaning that after he has met his deductible, his plan pays 80% of covered costs and he pays 20%. Jake has already met his $1000 deductible for the year and schedules a $100 visit with his primary doctor. His health plan pays $80 for the visit and Jake pays the remaining $20.
qs: What would I pay with 80/20 coinsurance after my deductible?
How is coinsurance calculated on a doctor visit?

atoms.title: Using coinsurance knowledge to plan costs
atoms.q: How can understanding coinsurance help me plan?
atoms.text: Knowing how coinsurance works can help you add up potential costs more accurately when you plan for the year or choose a health plan during open enrollment. Comparing potential medical costs across different types of plans may help make sure you are covered for different scenarios. Some plans, like fixed benefit health insurance, can help you manage potential out-of-pocket costs from your main health insurance plan.
qs: How do I estimate my yearly health care costs?
Can a fixed benefit plan help with coinsurance?

atoms.title: What a copay is
atoms.q: What is a copay?
atoms.text: A copay, or copayment, is a fixed amount you pay for a covered health care service, usually at the time you receive the service. It is common to have separate copay rates for different types of care. For example, the copay to see your primary care doctor may differ from the copay to see a specialist, like a dermatologist. Sometimes you might pay a copay for prescriptions.
qs: What is a copayment?
Do I pay a copay for specialists?

atoms.title: How copays work
atoms.q: How do copays work?
atoms.text: Copay amounts, such as $15 or $20 for a doctor visit, can vary depending on the provider and service. With health plans that have copays, which not all do, you know exactly what you have to pay ahead of time, which can help you manage health care costs. For most plans, your copay does not apply toward your deductible.
qs: Do copays count toward my deductible?
How much is a typical copay?

atoms.title: Some services have a $0 cost share
atoms.q: Are any services covered with no copay?
atoms.text: Some services may be covered at no additional cost, or $0 cost share, such as annual wellness exams and certain other preventive care services. Copay amounts for other services can vary depending on the provider and service.
qs: Is my annual physical free?
Do I pay a copay for a wellness exam?

atoms.title: Copay versus coinsurance
atoms.q: What's the difference between a copay and coinsurance?
atoms.text: A copay is a fixed rate while coinsurance is a percentage of the cost of a service. A copay is a flat dollar amount typically paid at the time of service, and it does not count toward your deductible in most plans. Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost if you have met your deductible, billed by the provider whom you pay directly. Both count toward your out-of-pocket max.
qs: Is a copay the same as coinsurance?
Which counts toward the out-of-pocket max?

atoms.title: Example: copay for primary care then specialist
atoms.q: Can you show how copays and coinsurance work together?
atoms.text: Jake visits his primary care doctor about a rash and pays his plan's $25 copay at the front desk. His doctor refers him to a dermatologist, and his $25 copay does not cover specialist visits, so he pays an additional fee. If Jake has not met his deductible, the dermatology bill is applied to his deductible. If he has met it, he pays only coinsurance, a percentage of the cost, and his plan pays the rest.
qs: Will I owe more than my copay if I see a specialist?
How do copays and deductibles interact?

atoms.title: Managing costs with copays
atoms.q: How can understanding copays help me choose a plan?
atoms.text: Knowing how copays work can help you add up potential costs more accurately when you are planning for the year or choosing your health plan during open enrollment. Comparing potential medical costs across plan types may help make sure you are covered for different scenarios. Some plans, like fixed benefit health insurance, can help you manage potential out-of-pocket costs from your main health insurance plan.
qs: How do copays factor into choosing a plan?
Can fixed benefit insurance offset my copays?

atoms.title: What a health insurance premium is
atoms.q: What is a health insurance premium?
atoms.text: A health insurance premium is the monthly price you pay for your policy, or the monthly cost of your health insurance. The cost can be influenced by the type of plan you have, your age, your lifestyle and more. Typically, a lower deductible means a higher premium, and vice versa. Other factors, such as where you live and your age, are also considered in setting your premium.
qs: What is a premium?
What determines my health insurance premium?

atoms.title: How premiums are paid
atoms.q: How do I pay my health insurance premium?
atoms.text: If you have your own health plan from the Marketplace, you will likely pay your premium each month. If your insurance is through an employer, your premiums will likely be taken out of your paychecks.
qs: Is my premium deducted from my paycheck?
Do I pay premiums monthly on a Marketplace plan?

atoms.title: Only five factors can set premium cost
atoms.q: What factors can legally affect my health insurance premium?
atoms.text: Under health care law, only five specific factors can influence how much a health insurance premium costs. Premium cost can be influenced by the type of plan you have, your age, where you live and your lifestyle, and tobacco users pay quite a bit more for premiums than non-users.
qs: How are health insurance premiums calculated?
What can affect my premium by law?

atoms.title: Factors insurers cannot use to set premiums
atoms.q: What can't affect my health insurance premium?
atoms.text: Insurance companies cannot include some factors when setting prices. One is sex, so men and women cannot be charged a different price for the same plan. The other is health status or medical history, which means health plans must cover services for pre-existing conditions.
qs: Can insurers charge more for pre-existing conditions?
Can women be charged more for health insurance?

atoms.title: Ways to lower your premium
atoms.q: Can I lower my health insurance premium?
atoms.text: If you have an ACA Marketplace plan, you might qualify for tax credits or cost-sharing reductions, which could lower your premiums. Tobacco users pay quite a bit more for premiums than non-users, so quitting may help. If you do not go to the doctor often and it makes sense for your health needs, you might consider switching to a plan with a lower premium.
qs: How can I reduce my health insurance premium?
Do tobacco users pay higher premiums?

atoms.title: How to choose the right plan and premium
atoms.q: How do I choose the right health insurance plan and premium?
atoms.text: Understanding health insurance helps you choose the right plan. Get familiar with the different types of insurance, insurance costs and financial subsidies. Look through your medical history to see what you have paid for and compare it against your options. If you have a doctor you want to stick with, check the provider directory to make sure they are in the network.
qs: How do I pick a health plan and premium?
What should I check before picking a premium?

atoms.title: What an out-of-pocket limit is
atoms.q: What is an out-of-pocket limit?
atoms.text: An out-of-pocket limit, also called an out-of-pocket maximum, is the maximum amount you could pay for covered services in a plan year, which is a 12-month coverage period. The terms mean the same thing. After you meet your out-of-pocket limit, your health plan usually pays 100% of the rest of your covered services for the rest of the year, which helps you plan ahead for health care costs.
qs: Is an out-of-pocket max the same as an out-of-pocket limit?
What is the most I could pay in a year?

atoms.title: What counts and what does not count
atoms.q: What counts toward my out-of-pocket limit?
atoms.text: Typically, copays, your deductible and coinsurance all count toward your out-of-pocket limit. Things like your monthly premium, balance-billed charges and anything your plan does not cover, such as out-of-network costs, do not count. If your provider charges more than the plan's allowed amount, you may have to pay the difference, which is called a balance-billed charge.
qs: Do premiums count toward my out-of-pocket maximum?
Does my deductible count toward the out-of-pocket max?
Does out-of-network care count toward the limit?

atoms.title: Allowed amount and its other names
atoms.q: What is the allowed amount for a covered service?
atoms.text: The plan's allowed amount may also be called the eligible expense, payment allowance or negotiated rate. If a provider charges more than the plan's allowed amount, you may have to pay the difference, known as a balance-billed charge.
qs: What does allowed amount mean?
What is a negotiated rate?
